verdict.note: The role only reads and drafts, so least privilege means taking the update and delete tools out of the agent's configuration. Logging, confirmation dialogs and business-hours windows are compensating controls. They leave the blast radius of a capability the role never needs exactly where it was.

stem: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?

options.text: Log every update and deletion for later audit
Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
Restrict deletions to business hours
Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely

explain: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (A) and confirmations (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (C) narrows the window without closing it.

verdict.note: The only thing that changed was the document refresh, and the stem says model version, prompts and latency are unchanged, so start at ingestion: chunking, index integrity and whether the embedding model matches. Confident but wrong answers are what plausible but irrelevant retrieved context produces. Blaming the model, the prompt or temperature points at layers the change never touched.

stem: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?

options.text: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
The model, which may have degraded overnight
The system prompt wording
The temperature setting

explain: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (B), unchanged prompt (C), and sampling (D) do not correlate with the refresh.

verdict.note: Forty tools loaded up front are already bloating prompts and hurting selection, so the fix is to give each agent a small toolset scoped to its task and load the rest on demand (tool search, namespacing, deferred loading). Cutting descriptions short trades selection quality for tokens. A mode-switch mega-tool hides the forty behaviours from tool selection, and capping the platform at ten drops a stated requirement.

stem: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

options.text: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors
Limit the platform to ten capabilities

explain: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (D) sacrifices the requirement.

verdict.note: These are two known, differently shaped jobs. Policy Q&A with citations needs one retrieval-augmented call. Decline letters built from structured decision data need a templated workflow, which also keeps regulated letter content deterministic. Each gets its own evals and governance. An autonomous multi-agent system or one all-tools agent couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning assumes labelled data and a customization path the stem never gives.

stem: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

options.text: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents
One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
A single fine-tuned model for both

explain: Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (A) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

verdict.note: The pattern choice turns on structural fit. The intake path is known in advance, so a code-defined workflow is cheaper, auditable and reliable, and autonomy earns its cost only where the path emerges at runtime. 'Workflows always win' is also wrong: the portal's counter-trap says a path that emerges at runtime, with recoverable errors, justifies an agent.

stem: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

options.text: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general
Workflows always outperform agents
The team lacked time to build an agent
The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path

explain: The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (A) and universal claims (B) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (C) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

verdict.note: Subjective quality becomes measurable through a rubric of the failure modes that matter, a labelled set built with counsel, and mixed grading: a rubric LLM judge calibrated against those human labels, plus ongoing expert review. Also fix a pass threshold in advance (L7). Counting complaints measures too late, and matching against a single reference fails every valid paraphrase.

stem: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?

options.text: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
Ship and count complaints
Exact string match against one reference summary per clause
Grade outputs by length

explain: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (C) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (D) measures nothing.

verdict.note: A prompt change is a production change. Run it on the regression eval set first, then A/B it on real traffic against the current prompt, with the primary metric, guardrail metrics and stopping rule fixed beforehand. Ideally the A/B starts at capped exposure. Demos and team votes are anecdotes, and a full rollout with a feedback banner is an experiment with no control group.

stem: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?

options.text: Roll it out; demos are representative
Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
Ask the team to vote
Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner

explain: Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

verdict.note: The binding constraint is that no PHI may reach the provider at all, so a BAA alone would not satisfy it. The control has to strip or tokenise PHI before the API call and re-associate results locally. De-identifying free text is imperfect, so logging and boundary audits are the matching detective control. A system-prompt instruction acts only after the data has already crossed, and blocking free text fails a business need that a compliant design can meet.

stem: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?

options.text: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary
Blocking free-text queries entirely

explain: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (A) is not a control, model instructions (B) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (D) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

verdict.note: Reframe the ask around the outcome of the whole process: model plus routed human review, with measured error rates, costs and the trade-off curve made explicit for the sponsor to decide on. Promising 99.9%, refusing to discuss numbers and quietly redefining accuracy each fail L8. 'Confidence-routed' has to mean calibrated signals from the system combined with consequence rules, never the model's self-rated confidence (T-SELFCONF).

stem: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?

options.text: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap
Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher
Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit

explain: Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

verdict.note: Drift across teams is fixed with a shared, version-controlled baseline: committed project CLAUDE.md and settings, shared skills (custom commands are now merged into skills), a `.mcp.json` with env-var secrets, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top. User-level config never propagates. Memorisation and prohibition change nothing about the configuration itself.

stem: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?

options.text: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
Let each engineer keep personal settings only

explain: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

verdict.note: Residency is met by where the workload runs, not by contracts, logging settings or encryption, so Bedrock in the customer's own account and region is the best option. Strictly, Bedrock inference runs in AWS-owned model deployment accounts in the same Region that model providers cannot access (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/data-protection.html). The data therefore stays inside the AWS boundary rather than literally inside the customer's account. Use in-region or geography-bound inference profiles, not global cross-Region profiles.

stem: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

options.text: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region
The Claude API with request logging disabled
Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit

explain: A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (A), disabled logging (C), and transport encryption (D) all still involve the data leaving the account.

verdict.note: When identity, billing and audit must run through existing Google Cloud controls, consume Claude through Google Cloud's own model platform so IAM, billing and audit logs apply natively. Bedrock creates a second control plane, and replicating controls around the direct API duplicates them and drifts. Naming has changed: Google now brands Vertex AI as Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Claude docs say 'Google Cloud's Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI' (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/google-vertex-ai), but the answer is unchanged.

stem: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?

options.text: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
Use the Claude API and replicate the controls
Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
Let each team choose its own path

explain: Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, replication (B) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance.

verdict.note: A single internal gateway in front of Claude is valuable because cross-cutting concerns (authentication, rate limits and budgets, logging, model routing) are enforced and changed in one place. It does not by itself cut token cost or remove the need for evals, and the extra hop usually adds latency.

stem: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?

options.text: It reduces token cost
It removes the need for evaluation
It guarantees lower latency
Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place

explain: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (A) or remove the need to evaluate (B), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

verdict.note: The caller's 2-second synchronous timeout is shorter than the work, so change the call shape: accept the request, return a job ID immediately, and deliver by callback or polling. Forcing a 2-second answer or downsizing the model degrades the reasoning the task needs. Raising the legacy timeout assumes the fixed constraint can change.

stem: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?

options.text: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously
Force the model to answer within two seconds
Increase the legacy timeout
Use the smallest model available

explain: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, D) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (C) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

verdict.note: Cross-cloud equivalence is a requirement to define and then verify. Decide which behaviours must match, pin model versions, and score each platform as its own eval slice, because feature availability, model versions and endpoints can differ by platform. Identical prompts do not guarantee identical behaviour, and cost or proximity says nothing about consistency.

stem: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?

options.text: Using identical prompts in both
Establishing which behaviors must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
Choosing the cheaper platform for both
Deploying to whichever region is nearest

explain: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behavior, and cost (C) and proximity (D) do not address consistency.

verdict.note: For a financial approval process, first establish where accountability sits: which decisions must stay with a named person (separation of duties, sign-off authority). That boundary decides what may be automated and where human-in-the-loop gates go. Model choice, token cost and schedule all come after it.

stem: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?

options.text: Which model to use
The expected token cost
Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person
Whether the agent can be built in the available time

explain: Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (A), cost (B), and schedule (D) are all downstream of that boundary.

verdict.note: Complexity is a running cost, so extra capability has to be bought by a stated requirement, functional or non-functional (L4). Capability for its own sake, team preference and speculative 'future flexibility' all pay that cost without a justification.

stem: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?

options.text: The more capable design, since capability is the point
The design the team finds more interesting
The design with more components, for future flexibility
Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity

explain: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.

verdict.note: A control that regulation requires needs a guarantee, so it must be enforced deterministically outside the model (code, validation gate, permission). High eval accuracy, a disclaimer to the regulator or a larger model only make correct behaviour more likely. None of them turns a tendency into a guarantee.

stem: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?

options.text: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator
Acceptable if a larger model is used

explain: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behavior cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (B), disclosure (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

verdict.note: Over-engineering means components that no stated requirement depends on. Multiple models (tier routing), an eval suite and a human approval step are each justified whenever a requirement calls for them, so their presence alone signals nothing.

stem: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?

options.text: It uses more than one model
Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
It has an evaluation suite
It includes a human approval step

explain: Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (A), evaluation (C), and approval steps (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

verdict.note: Readiness is a measured claim against a success criterion agreed in advance, on representative data. An impressive demo or team consensus is an impression, and a cost estimate does not show that the system works. By the portal's gates, production additionally needs SLOs, rollback, on-call and a named owner, but C is the necessary condition among these options.

stem: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?

options.text: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
Agreement from the engineering team
A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
A completed cost estimate

explain: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (A), consensus (B), and cost (D) do not establish whether the system works.

verdict.note: A set built only from cases the system already gets right measures the wrong distribution. It inflates the score and hides exactly the failures you need to find, and a bigger sample does not fix a biased one. The eval set needs to be representative and held out, refreshed from production traffic, and scored by the slices that matter.

stem: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?

options.text: It gives a reliable measure of quality
It is acceptable if it is large enough
It only matters for regulated systems
It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter

explain: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

verdict.note: The failure is a behaviour nobody measures, so the fix has to measure it. A regression suite covering the behaviours that must not be lost, rerun on every prompt, model or index change, catches the loss before rollout. Changing one thing at a time helps you tell which change caused a result, but it cannot detect a behaviour you never test. Closer review and fewer changes lower the odds without catching anything.

stem: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behavior. How is this best prevented?

options.text: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviors the system must not lose
Changing one thing at a time
Reviewing changes more carefully
Limiting how often prompts change

explain: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (B) and careful review (C) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

verdict.note: Earlier eval results hold only while the things that drive behaviour stay the same: the model, the prompt, the input distribution and the requirement. A change to any of them should trigger re-evaluation. Waiting for an incident finds the problem late, a calendar schedule has nothing to do with what actually changed, and a cost change says nothing about correctness.

stem: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?

options.text: Only a reported incident
A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
A fixed annual schedule
A change in cost

explain: Any change to the things that determine behavior invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (A) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (D) does not affect correctness.

verdict.note: Audit and data protection both bind here. First find out what evidence the audit actually needs, then capture only that, with redaction at capture, access control and a bounded retention period. This follows the portal's 'redact at capture, not later' rule and GDPR minimisation. Logging everything raw ignores the PII risk, a flat refusal overrides the audit owner, and 'responses only' is an arbitrary rule made without knowing the requirement.

stem: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?

options.text: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence
Refuse, since logging creates risk
Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
Log responses only

explain: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (A) and blanket refusal (B) ignore one side, and a partial rule (D) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

verdict.note: Retrieved text stays data the whole way through, and the control that lasts is least privilege: the model cannot go beyond its tools and permissions whatever the text persuades it to try. Signature scans and screening are useful extra layers, as Anthropic's guardrail docs say, but they can be bypassed and are not guarantees. 'Ignore embedded instructions' is only a prompt, and encryption protects the channel, not the content.

stem: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?

options.text: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel
It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content

explain: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (A) and prompt instructions (B) are bypassable, and transport security (C) says nothing about the content.

verdict.note: The organisation that deploys an automated decision owns its outcomes, through a named business owner who accepts the residual risk (portal guide 5.5). That is why where automation stops and humans take over is an architectural decision. The model provider supplies a capability, one engineer's authorship does not carry the organisation's responsibility, and automating a decision does not remove accountability for it.

stem: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?

options.text: The organization that deployed the workflow
The model provider
The engineer who wrote the prompt
Nobody, since the output was automated

explain: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D).

verdict.note: Give the sponsor the one measure that bears on the decision they face, for example errors per month by case type against the agreed bar, and say what it leaves out. A bare headline accuracy hides the failing slices, and a public benchmark does not measure your task. Refusing to summarise fails the executive audience.

stem: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?

options.text: Provide the headline accuracy figure
Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated
Explain that quality cannot be summarised
Provide the model's benchmark score

explain: A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark score (D) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (C) fails the sponsor.

verdict.note: Going from 10 users to 2,000 changes the input mix, the edge cases, the load and the support load. The architect's first job is to name which pilot assumptions will not survive that change, which then shapes the production exit criteria (SLOs, rollback, monitoring owner). Licences and training belong downstream, and a bigger model answers a question nobody has diagnosed.

stem: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

options.text: The cost of additional licenses
The need for a larger model
Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
The training schedule

explain: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licenses (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

verdict.note: A system decays after handover because it drifts, and only continuing ownership catches drift. That means a named owner running a defined routine of evals, monitoring and updates, which matches the portal's 'named monitoring owner who accepts the handoff in writing'. Documentation and training are one-off artefacts that age, and a warranty covers defects, not drift.

stem: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?

options.text: Full documentation at delivery
A longer warranty period
Training every user
A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update

explain: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than drift.

verdict.note: Each task gets the cheapest or smallest tier that clears its own measured bar, confirmed with evals, and the hard slices are routed upward. Using one model everywhere assumes every task has the same requirements. 'Largest' or 'newest' everywhere pays for capability that most tasks do not need.

stem: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?

options.text: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
One model for everything, for simplicity
The largest model for everything, for safety
The newest model for everything

explain: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

verdict.note: Treat context as a budget split deliberately between instructions, retrieved material and working state. Filling it dilutes attention, raises cost and causes mid-context facts to be missed, and this matters well beyond long documents (agent sessions, tool results). A bigger window does not fix a poor allocation. Filter for relevance, clear stale tool results and compact instead.

stem: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?

options.text: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
A limit that only matters for long documents
A setting to raise when quality drops

explain: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

verdict.note: Prompts that drive production behaviour need the same lifecycle as code: versioned, owned, reviewed, and gated by evals on every change. This matches the portal's versioned template, Skill or shared module. Giving one team all the prompting does not add versioning or evals, freezing the prompts blocks improvement, and moving them into the system prompt changes where they live, not how they are governed.

stem: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?

options.text: Appoint one team to own all prompting
Freeze the prompts
Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
Move all prompts into the system prompt

explain: Prompts that determine production behavior deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (A) may not fit the organization, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and relocation (D) does not address governance.

verdict.note: Conventions carry over when they live in the repository (committed CLAUDE.md, project settings, shared skills) and are reviewed alongside the code. Emailed policies and one-off training fade, and approving every use adds friction without passing on any practice. If a managed CLAUDE.md or a plugin distributing shared skills were offered, it could beat per-repo copies for org-wide guidance, but neither is an option here.

stem: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?

options.text: A written policy circulated by email
A one-off training session
Requiring approval for each use
Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code

explain: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (C) creates friction without conveying practice.

verdict.note: Judge enablement by the outcomes it was adopted to move (cycle time, escaped defects, lead time) measured against a pre-agreed baseline. Headcount trained, licence utilisation and tool-call volume only show uptake, not benefit.

stem: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement program is working?

options.text: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
The number of people trained
License utilization
The volume of tool calls

explain: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilization (C), and activity (D) measure uptake rather than benefit.

verdict.note: When the same tool works well in one codebase and poorly in another, the gap usually lies in what each repo supplies: committed CLAUDE.md, documented conventions, and ways for the agent to verify its changes. That is a defect class no model tier can infer away. Training assumes a people gap the stem never mentions, and a rewrite is a fix chosen before any diagnosis.

stem: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?

options.text: Whether the team needs more training
Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
Whether a larger model would help
Whether the legacy service should be rewritten

explain: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

verdict.note: A large catalogue that changes daily is document-style knowledge, so it belongs in a retrieval index refreshed as the catalogue changes, with the answer grounded in what is retrieved. Nightly fine-tuning does not reliably inject facts, 40,000 documents will not fit sensibly in a system prompt, and browsing the public site adds autonomy for no benefit. Caveat: truly live fields such as stock or price should come from the system of record through a tool (CS-D1-04).

stem: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalog that changes daily. Which architecture fits?

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the catalog nightly
Load the catalog into the system prompt
Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalog changes, with the model answering from retrieved context
An autonomous agent that browses the public website

explain: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

verdict.note: The degradation began at the re-index, so look first at the layer the change touched: chunking, the embedding model and its configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently (for example, mixed embedding versions or dropped metadata). The generation prompt, model version and UI were not changed, so they drop out first.

stem: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?

options.text: The generation prompt
The model version
The user interface
Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently

explain: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

verdict.note: When wrong tool picks grow with the size of the catalogue, cut what each agent sees: scope toolsets by role or task and load the rest through progressive discovery (tool search or deferred loading). Shortening every description removes the signals the model needs to choose, mode-switch mega-tools only move the ambiguity into parameters, and a bigger model does not fix a structural problem.

stem: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

options.text: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
Shorten all tool descriptions
Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
Replace the agent with a larger model

explain: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

verdict.note: You make subjective quality measurable with a rubric aimed at the failure modes that matter, applied at scale by an LLM judge that is calibrated and regularly audited against human labels on a labelled set. Exact match suits crisp fields, not free-text summaries. Output length is a proxy, and raw thumbs-up counts are biased and do not diagnose anything.

stem: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?

options.text: Exact match against reference summaries
A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
Average output length compared to references
User thumbs-up counts alone

explain: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

verdict.note: A prompt change is a production change. It passes the offline regression eval first, then runs as a controlled A/B test against the current prompt with metrics and stopping rules fixed in advance under capped exposure, and only then rolls out wider. Shipping and watching complaints, or rolling out with a feedback form, uses detection where prevention is needed, and a team vote is not evidence.

stem: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?

options.text: Ship it and monitor complaints
Team vote followed by rollout
Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
Rollout with a feedback form

explain: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

verdict.note: The stem says PHI must never reach the provider, so the control has to sit before the data crosses the boundary: de-identify or tokenize, keep the re-identification map local, and audit it. A user policy (A) or a prompt instruction (B) cannot stop PHI from being sent, and structured-only search (C) drops the free-text requirement.

stem: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?

options.text: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
Restricting the feature to structured queries only
A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing

explain: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

verdict.note: Routing by consequence and by a calibrated confidence signal puts scarce reviewer time where errors are likely or costly. Reviewing everything at scale turns into a rubber stamp, a random 10% ignores where risk sits, and complaint-driven review finds harm only after customers feel it. Read 'confidence' as a calibrated signal from the system, never the model's own self-rating (see T-SELFCONF).

stem: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?

options.text: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
Review every output regardless of risk
Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
Review only what users complain about

explain: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

verdict.note: The sponsor owns the decision and needs honest evidence: results by document type, the aggregate, how it was measured, and the end-to-end outcome after human review. Cherry-picking (A) or weighting the average to look good (D) hides the failing slices, and refusing to give a number (C) leaves the owner nothing to decide on.

stem: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?

options.text: The highest observed number
Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review
A refusal to quantify
An average weighted to look favorable

explain: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

verdict.note: GDPR shapes the architecture through what personal data flows in and how long it stays: minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)), purpose limitation (Art. 5(1)(b)) and erasure on request (Art. 17), which has to reach logs, caches and indexes too. Latency targets, programming language and the number of providers are engineering choices, not GDPR obligations.

stem: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?

options.text: Response latency targets
The choice of programming language
Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
The number of model providers

explain: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

verdict.note: Take the lowest pattern rung that works. A document intake path known in advance belongs in a code-defined workflow, which is cheaper, testable and auditable. The other options are false generalisations: workflows are not always more accurate, agents can process documents, and context use depends on the design, not the pattern.

stem: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?

options.text: Workflows are always more accurate
Agents cannot process documents
Workflows use less context
The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable

explain: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

verdict.note: A large prefix that is identical on every request is exactly what prompt caching is for. Put it first, place the breakpoint at its end, and cache reads cut both time-to-first-token and input cost. Splitting it, summarising it at request time or recasting it as few-shot examples keeps the cost or adds a call, and risks dropping required policy text.

stem: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?

options.text: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
Splitting the preamble across two requests
Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
Moving the preamble into a few-shot block

explain: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

verdict.note: An ADR preserves why a decision was made: the context and constraints, the options considered, the trade-offs and the consequences. A final design with no alternatives, a list of people or a timeline cannot tell a future team why the other options were rejected.

stem: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?

options.text: The final design only
The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
The team members involved
The implementation timeline

explain: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

verdict.note: To pin an incident to a layer (retrieval, tool, prompt or model), traces must capture tool calls, retrieved context and decision points under correlation IDs, alongside the outputs. Outputs alone, aggregate latency or user feedback show that something failed but not where.

stem: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?

options.text: Final outputs only
Aggregate latency metrics only
Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
User feedback only

explain: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

verdict.note: Adoption lasts when the setup lives in version control: committed CLAUDE.md, project settings and .mcp.json with env-var secrets, shared skills and commands (a plugin can package them), plus an onboarding path new engineers follow. Recordings, chat channels and one-to-one coaching depend on individuals and drift.

stem: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?

options.text: A recorded walkthrough
A shared chat channel
Individual coaching sessions
Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow

explain: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

verdict.note: Least privilege shrinks the blast radius. Split read from write, remove write access from roles that do not need it, and put an approval gate on the writes that are needed. Logging only detects, a cautious prompt is not enforcement, and a business-hours window leaves the capability in place.

stem: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?

options.text: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
Logging modifications for later review
Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
Running the agent during business hours only

explain: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it

verdict.note: Keeping inference inside the client's AWS boundary decides the surface: Claude in Amazon Bedrock is AWS-operated and called from the client's account under its IAM and CloudTrail. For region, use a regional endpoint or geographic inference profile, not the global endpoint. Claude Platform on AWS is reached and billed through the AWS account but Anthropic runs its inference, so it does not qualify, and a DPA or logging settings do not change where processing happens.

stem: A client requires that inference run inside their own AWS account. What does this determine?

options.text: The model family only
That a data processing agreement is sufficient
Deployment through Amazon Bedrock in the client's account and region
That request logging must be disabled

explain: Running inside the client's own cloud boundary is what the requirement describes. A contract (B) and logging settings (D) do not keep the data in the account, and the model family (A) is a separate choice

verdict.note: Deploying on the platform the enterprise already governs means its IAM, billing and Cloud Audit Logs apply without being rebuilt. Google has since renamed Vertex AI to Agent Platform, but Claude is still served there under Google Cloud controls, so the key holds. Rebuilding controls on the direct API, adding a second cloud, or letting each team choose all create duplicate or missing governance.

stem: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud wants identity and audit handled by existing controls. What follows?

options.text: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
Use the Claude API and rebuild the controls
Use Bedrock for feature parity
Let each team decide

explain: Aligning with the governed platform makes existing controls apply without duplication. Rebuilding (B) drifts, a different cloud (C) creates a second control plane, and per-team choice (D) removes governance

verdict.note: A single internal gateway is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once: authentication, rate limits and budgets, logging and model routing. It does not lower unit prices, it adds a network hop rather than guaranteeing lower latency, and it replaces no evaluation.

stem: What is the main architectural benefit of routing all model traffic through one internal service?

options.text: Lower token prices
It removes the need for evaluation
It guarantees lower latency
Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are applied consistently in one place

explain: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once. It does not change unit price (A), remove evaluation (B), or reduce latency (C)

verdict.note: Complexity costs you continuously in failure surface, operations and spend, so extra capability has to be bought by a stated requirement (L4). Headroom, team preference and 'flexibility' from extra components are speculative and pay that cost with no requirement behind them.

stem: Two designs both satisfy the requirement; one is materially simpler. What decides?

options.text: The more capable design, since headroom is valuable
Whether any stated requirement needs the extra capability, against the ongoing cost of complexity
Whichever the team prefers to build
The one with more components, for flexibility

explain: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Headroom (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (D) pay that cost without justification

verdict.note: A control the design must guarantee cannot depend on probabilistic model behaviour. Enforce it deterministically outside the model: code, a validation gate or a permission layer (L3). High accuracy, a larger model or a documented residual risk still leave only a tendency, and a required compliance control is a gate, not a risk you can accept.

stem: A required compliance control depends on the model behaving correctly. What is the correct judgment?

options.text: Acceptable if measured accuracy is very high
Not acceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
Acceptable with a documented residual risk
Acceptable if a larger model is used

explain: A control that must hold needs a guarantee, which probabilistic behavior cannot supply. High accuracy (A), documentation (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee

verdict.note: The delegation boundary keeps decisions that carry accountability, such as consequential customer-affecting ones, with a person and automates the rest by consequence and reversibility. Anthropic's Usage Policy also requires human review for high-risk consumer-facing uses. Test scores, budget and an unexamined client request say nothing about who answers for the decision.

stem: Where should the boundary of automation be drawn in a solution that makes customer-affecting decisions?

options.text: Wherever the model performs well in testing
As far as the budget allows
At whatever the client requests
Where accountability for the decision sits, keeping those decisions with a person

explain: Accountability determines what may be automated at all, and that boundary is an architectural decision. Test performance (A), budget (B), and unexamined requests (C) do not address responsibility

verdict.note: Production readiness is a measured claim against a bar agreed in advance, on data that represents real traffic (L7). A demo proves only feasibility, team sign-off is not evidence, and a cost model does not show that the system works. The portal's production gate also adds SLOs, rollback and a named owner (CS-D6-12).

stem: What must exist before a solution is declared production-ready?

options.text: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
A successful demonstration
Sign-off from the engineering team
A completed cost model

explain: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar. A demonstration (B), consensus (C), and cost (D) do not establish whether it works

verdict.note: An eval set made only of cases the system already passes is biased: it overstates quality and hides exactly the failures that matter. A larger set does not fix the bias, and the problem is not limited to regulated contexts. Draw eval sets from real demand plus edge and adversarial slices.

stem: An evaluation set contains only cases the system already handles. What is the effect?

options.text: It provides a reliable quality measure
It is fine if it is large
It overstates performance and conceals the failures that matter
It matters only in regulated contexts

explain: An unrepresentative sample measures the wrong distribution, and size does not correct bias. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix it (B), and the problem is general (D)

verdict.note: Audit and data protection are both real obligations. First establish what the audit needs (which events and fields, and for how long), then log that with minimisation or redaction at capture and access control. Blanket logging, blanket refusal and an arbitrary prompts-versus-responses split each ignore one side.

stem: How should a request to log every prompt and response for audit be handled?

options.text: Implement it, since audit takes precedence
Decline, because logging creates risk
Log responses but not prompts
Establish what the audit requires, because prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data

explain: Audit and data protection are both real, and the design must serve the audit purpose without retaining more than warranted. Blanket action (A) or refusal (B) ignores one side, and an arbitrary split (C) is unjustified

verdict.note: The organisation that deploys an automated decision is accountable for its outcomes, and a named business owner holds the residual risk. The provider supplies a capability, one engineer writing the prompt does not take on organisational responsibility, and automation never removes accountability.

stem: Who is accountable when an automated Claude workflow produces a harmful decision?

options.text: The model provider
The engineer who wrote the prompt
The organization that deployed it
No one, because the decision was automated

explain: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes. The provider (A) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D)

verdict.note: Give the sponsor the metric tied to the decision they have to make, and say plainly what it leaves out (L8, CS-D1-02). A headline accuracy figure hides which cases fail and what they cost. A benchmark score was not measured on your traffic. Refusing to give a number fails the audience.

stem: A sponsor asks for one number that shows whether the solution is working. What is the right response?

options.text: Give the headline accuracy figure
Give the measure tied to the decision they face, and state what it does not cover
Explain that this cannot be reduced to a number
Give the model's benchmark score

explain: A useful metric matches the decision and is honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark (D) can mislead, and refusing (C) fails the sponsor

verdict.note: Going from 10 users to 2,000 is a stage gate. The first job is to check which pilot assumptions (input mix, how often edge cases appear, support load, quality per slice) still hold at scale. License cost, model size and training plans all depend on knowing what breaks.

stem: A ten-user pilot is about to expand to two thousand users. What should the architect raise first?

options.text: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
License cost
Whether a larger model is needed
The training rollout plan

explain: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and surfacing those is the architect's contribution. Cost (B), model size (C), and training (D) follow from knowing what breaks

verdict.note: Choose a model per task on eval evidence: the cheapest tier that clears that task's agreed bar, with only the hard slice routed upward (CS-D2-01). One model for everything ignores that the tasks differ. The counter-trap (low volume, costly errors) can justify a top tier for one task, but the choice is still made per task.

stem: How should a model be chosen for a solution containing several distinct tasks?

options.text: Match each task to the smallest model meeting its requirement, and evaluate the choices
One model everywhere, for simplicity
The largest model everywhere, for safety
The newest model everywhere

explain: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate on evidence. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit

verdict.note: Context is a finite budget, split on purpose between instructions, retrieved material and working state (CS-D2-08). Filling the window dilutes recall and raises cost. A bigger window does not fix a bad split.

stem: How should the context window be treated in a production design?

options.text: As capacity to fill as completely as possible
As a budget allocated deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
As a concern only for long documents
As a setting to increase whenever quality drops

explain: Context is scarce and its allocation drives quality, so it is designed. Filling it (A) dilutes, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix allocation

verdict.note: Team conventions last when they live in version-controlled project config (CLAUDE.md, shared skills) and get reviewed with the code (CS-D7-02). This is guidance, not a guarantee that must hold on every machine, so managed settings are not needed (T-REACH does not apply). For guidance across the whole org, a managed CLAUDE.md or a plugin can ship the same content centrally.

stem: An organization wants consistent Claude Code practice across dozens of repositories. What is most durable?

options.text: A policy document circulated once
A single training session
Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
Requiring approval for every use

explain: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (D) adds friction without conveying practice

verdict.note: Being able to explain behaviour to an auditor is a property of the architecture: code-defined steps, deterministic rules, logged intermediate outputs and controls someone can inspect (CS-D1-06, CS-D1-08). Model family and cost do not make behaviour traceable. Region answers residency, which is a different obligation.

stem: A client will not accept a solution whose behavior cannot be explained to their auditor. What does this constrain?

options.text: The model family only
The cost model
The architecture, which must make decisions traceable and the controls inspectable
The deployment region

explain: Auditability is an architectural property covering tracing and inspectable controls. Model family (A), cost (B), and region (D) do not by themselves make behavior explicable

verdict.note: Without an abstraction, provider-specific request formats, model IDs and feature availability spread through the application code, so moving later is expensive. Token cost, accuracy and latency come from the model and the configuration, not from how tightly the code is coupled.

stem: What is the main risk of building directly against a single cloud's model service with no abstraction?

options.text: Moving later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
Higher token cost
Lower accuracy
Slower responses

explain: Coupling determines the cost of change, which is the architectural concern. Cost (B), accuracy (C), and latency (D) are not consequences of the coupling itself

verdict.note: Residency is a legal gate. It is met by where processing and storage happen: a region- or geography-bound deployment or endpoint for each jurisdiction (PF-GOV-01). Cost and latency cannot be weighed against it, and encryption in transit protects the data but does not keep it in the region.

stem: A solution must serve users in two regions with different data residency rules. What follows?

options.text: One deployment in the cheaper region
A single deployment with encryption in transit
Whichever region has the lowest latency
Separate deployments whose data stays within each region's boundary

explain: Residency is satisfied by keeping the data within each boundary. A single deployment (A, B) moves data across it, and latency (C) does not address the rule

verdict.note: 'As accurate as possible' is not a target you can design or test against. Discovery has to turn it into a measurable bar tied to what an error costs (CS-D6-01, CS-D1-02). Defaulting to maximum capability spends money without a target, and deferring the question builds before anyone agrees what success means.

stem: A requirement is stated as make it as accurate as possible. What should the architect do?

options.text: Choose the largest model and optimise from there
Establish the accuracy the use case actually needs and what an error costs
Build the most complex design the budget allows
Defer the question until after the pilot

explain: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be made concrete. Defaulting to maximum capability (A, C) spends without a target, and deferring (D) leaves the design unanchored

verdict.note: When two components pass on their own but fail together, suspect the contract between them: schema, edge cases and error semantics. Confirm it from traces of the failing handoffs (L5) before you change anything. Retrying hides the defect, and a bigger model or more components does not define the interface.

stem: Two components each work correctly but the system fails intermittently at their boundary. What does this suggest?

options.text: One component needs a larger model
The contract between them is underspecified, particularly for edge and error cases
The system needs more components
The failure is transient and can be retried

explain: Boundary failures between correct components point at the contract. Capability (A) and more components (C) do not define the interface, and retrying (D) hides it

verdict.note: Keeping data creates legal and security obligations, so you need a stated purpose and a retention period before storing anything. CS-D5-11 lists 'logging everything forever' as a distractor. Treating storage cost or speed as the main issue puts a compliance gate on a cost scorecard.

stem: A design proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely. What should the architect raise?

options.text: Nothing, retention is always safer
That storage is expensive
That it will slow the system
Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations retention creates

explain: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it. Treating retention as free of risk (A) is the error, and cost (B) and speed (C) are minor by comparison

verdict.note: Only a check that does not depend on the model catches a confident error on consequential outputs: the system of record, deterministic validation, or a human (CS-D5-05). Self-reported confidence and asking the model to double-check are not independent. Two models agreeing assumes their errors are uncorrelated.

stem: How should a solution handle the case where the model is confident and wrong?

options.text: Design so that consequential outputs are verified against something independent of the model
Trust the confidence signal
Ask the model to double-check
Use two models and take the agreement

explain: Independence is what catches confident error. Confidence (B) is not evidence, self-checking (C) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (D)

verdict.note: An aggregate rate means something only once you know which cases make up the 6% and what each failure costs (CS-D1-02, T-AGGREGATE). Model version, eval token cost and run time say nothing about the risk. Ideally the result is also judged against a threshold agreed in advance (L7).

stem: An evaluation shows 94% accuracy. What else must be known before this is actionable?

options.text: The model version only
The token cost of the evaluation
What the 6% look like, and what each failure costs
How long the evaluation took

explain: A headline rate is only meaningful alongside the shape and cost of the failures. Version (A), cost (B), and duration (D) do not describe the risk

verdict.note: A new model version invalidates earlier measurements, so re-run the eval suite before the version reaches production traffic, then roll out to capped exposure (CS-D4-08). Monitoring and rolling back on complaints only detect the problem after users are hit. Pin dated snapshot IDs rather than aliases so that upgrades happen only when you choose.

stem: What should happen when a model version is updated beneath a production solution?

options.text: Nothing, versions are compatible
Increase monitoring for a week
Roll back automatically if complaints rise
Re-run the evaluation suite before the change reaches production traffic

explain: A change to the thing that determines behavior invalidates prior measurement. Assuming compatibility (A) is unsafe, and monitoring (B) or reacting to complaints (C) detects after users are affected

verdict.note: A useful answer names the specific decisions that carry accountability or cannot be verified, and says what automating them would risk, judged by reversibility, blast radius and cost of error (CS-D5-06). The stakeholder can act on that and revisit it later. Generic claims about readiness or risk, or blaming the budget, give them nothing to act on.

stem: A stakeholder asks why the solution cannot simply be fully automated. What is the most useful answer?

options.text: That the technology is not ready
That automation is always risky
Which specific decisions carry accountability or are unverifiable, and what automating them would risk
That the budget does not allow it

explain: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited. Generic claims about readiness (A) or risk (B) are not, and budget (D) is not the reason

verdict.note: A handoff survives when the operating team can measure and maintain the solution and a named owner is accountable: eval suite, criteria, owner and a re-check routine (CS-D6-11). Code, a prompt list and a recorded demo are artefacts with no way to verify them.

stem: What should be handed over with a solution so it survives its first year?

options.text: The source code
The evaluation suite, the criteria, the owner, and the routine for re-checking
A recorded demonstration
A list of prompts used

explain: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain, with someone responsible. Code (A), a demonstration (C), and prompts (D) are artefacts without the means to verify them

verdict.note: If nothing was deployed and the model version is pinned, the layer that changed is the input: traffic mix, user behaviour, source data or upstream tools (T-LAYER). Confirm it by comparing traces of failing and passing requests (CS-D4-14). One caveat: if the app calls a model alias, the model can change without a deploy.

stem: A team reports the solution has become worse, but nothing was deployed. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The inputs or the surrounding usage changed
The model degraded on its own
The prompts wore out
The evaluation was wrong originally

explain: Behavior changes with what is fed to it, and distribution drift is the usual cause. Models do not degrade unprompted (B), prompts do not wear out (C), and the original evaluation is not the first suspect (D)

verdict.note: Prompts that decide production behaviour need a code lifecycle: versioned, owned, reviewed and gated by evals on every change (CS-D2-12). Editing in place or in a shared document lets changes through with no review or eval. Freezing the prompts assumes inputs and needs never change.

stem: How should prompts that determine production behavior be managed?

options.text: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on change, like code
Edited in place when someone notices a problem
Kept in a shared document for easy editing
Frozen after launch

explain: Anything that determines production behavior needs the lifecycle of code. Ad hoc edits (B) and open documents (C) invite unreviewed change, and freezing (D) blocks improvement

verdict.note: Show value as movement in the delivery outcomes (cycle time, escaped defects) the tool was adopted for, against a baseline agreed before rollout (CS-D7-04). Invocations, seats onboarded and hours in the tool measure activity, not benefit.

stem: An organization asks how to measure whether Claude Code is worth the license cost. What should be measured?

options.text: Number of tool invocations
Change in the delivery outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
Number of users onboarded
Hours spent in the tool

explain: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated. Invocations (A), onboarding (C), and time in tool (D) measure usage rather than benefit

verdict.note: Of these options, missing committed project context (a CLAUDE.md with conventions, structure and build/test commands) is the common cause the team can fix (CS-D7-02). The 'most often' claim is the community's, not a documented fact. Anthropic's best practices also stress giving Claude a way to check its own work, such as tests, but that option is not offered here.

stem: What most often blocks a team from getting good results from Claude Code on an existing codebase?

options.text: The size of the repository
The programming language
The absence of committed context describing the conventions and structure
The number of contributors

explain: Missing project context is the usual cause, and it is the one the team can fix. Size (A), language (B), and contributor count (D) do not by themselves prevent good results

verdict.note: A cache hit needs an identical prefix, built in the order tools, then system, then messages. So a session ID near the top breaks every request's hit, and so does a changing tool order. Shortening the policy changes what a miss costs, not the hit rate, and it can even drop the prefix below the minimum cacheable length. Output limits and request region play no part in prefix matching.

stem: An application's system prompt is stable but its cache hit rate sits at only 40%. Which TWO changes are most likely to raise it?

options.text: Move the session identifier from the top of the prompt to the end
Shorten the static policy block so that it takes up rather fewer tokens
Keep the tool definitions in a fixed order across every request
Raise the maximum output tokens allowed on each of the requests
Send all requests from a single region so they stay grouped

explain: The cache matches by prefix: it is reused from the first character up to the first change. Everything variable goes after everything stable, and the order of the tool definitions is part of that prefix. Why not the others: B reduces tokens but does not change the hit rate; D is output, not prefix; E plays no part in the matching.

verdict.note: A reviewer that shares the author's session or reasoning inherits its blind spots, so it confirms the code instead of challenging it. The fix is an independent reviewer instance with a fresh context. A longer prompt or a bigger model leaves that anchoring in place, and D contradicts the stem, which says the reviews run and simply find nothing.

stem: Reviews of AI-authored pull requests almost never raise findings, yet defects keep reaching production. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The reviewer shares the context and assumptions that produced the code
The review prompt is too short to describe what quality means here
The model used for the review is smaller than the one used for authoring
The team merges before the automated review has finished running

explain: A reviewer anchored to the reasoning that produced the code inherits its blind spots. That is why the review is done from a fresh context, separate from the session that wrote it. Why not the others: B and C are configuration tweaks that do not touch the anchoring; D would be a process problem visible in the timings.

verdict.note: Observe before you change anything. Traces of the affected sessions show whether the divergence starts in the input, the retrieved context, the tool description or the prompt. Rewriting descriptions guesses at the cause. Disabling the tool or rolling back would be justified only if the stem showed active harm, which it does not.

stem: An agent in production starts calling an unexpected tool on a minority of requests. What does the on-call engineer do first?

options.text: Read traces of the affected sessions to locate where the choice diverges
Rewrite the tool descriptions, since ambiguity is the most usual explanation
Disable the tool until someone can reproduce the behaviour in staging
Roll the whole service back to the release from the previous quarter

explain: Diagnose before intervening. Traces show whether the deviation originates in the input, in what was retrieved, in the tool description or in the prompt. Why not the others: B guesses the cause; C and D are big interventions with no evidence that they target the problem.

verdict.note: Committed, versioned project config (CLAUDE.md, project settings, .mcp.json) gives a new hire the team's proven setup on day one. Training teaches generic technique without the team's context, read-only access delays productivity, and personal user config never propagates, so it recreates the drift.

stem: A developer joins a team that works with AI assistance daily. What gets them productive fastest?

options.text: The shared project configuration and standards the team already uses
A training session covering prompt techniques and their trade-offs
Read-only access for the first weeks, until they know the codebase
Their own configuration, so they can work the way they prefer

explain: Shared, versioned configuration is the onboarding mechanism: the person inherits proven practice on day one, without depending on someone explaining it to them. Why not the others: B teaches technique without giving them the team's context; C postpones productivity; D reproduces fragmentation.

verdict.note: Moving up to an agent is justified when the path cannot be listed in advance: interventions with no repeatable pattern, and steps that only become clear part-way through. Volume and cost can be handled inside any pattern, and prestige is not an architectural driver. The portal's full test also asks that errors be recoverable and guardrailed, so check that before handing the path to an agent.

stem: A fixed workflow for supplier onboarding now fails on roughly a fifth of cases, where staff step in manually to finish the job. Which TWO signals would justify moving this stage to an autonomous agent?

options.text: The number of onboarding requests per week has roughly doubled since launch
The manual interventions follow no repeatable pattern the team can list
The steps differ per supplier and only become clear part-way through
Leadership wants the solution to look more advanced to the board
The cost per request has risen along with the added volume

explain: Autonomy is justified when the path cannot be enumerated in advance. Interventions that follow no listable pattern and steps that only appear part-way through the process are exactly that condition. Why not the others: A and E are scale and cost: they are solved within any pattern; D is prestige, not an architectural driver.

verdict.note: In hub and spoke, the coordinator owns sequencing, halting and the single ordered audit record, which peer handoffs cannot guarantee. Fraud rules are a specialist's job, and in a regulated process they belong in deterministic code. Output formatting is internal to each agent, and model versions are configuration pinned in advance, not a runtime orchestration choice.

stem: A supervisor coordinates four specialist agents in a regulated claims process. Which TWO responsibilities belong to the supervisor rather than to the specialists?

options.text: Deciding the order the specialists run in and when to stop the chain
Applying the rules that determine whether a claim is fraudulent
Recording the ordered outcome of every step for the audit trail
Formatting each specialist's own output for its internal use
Choosing which model version each specialist should call at runtime

explain: The supervisor provides sequencing and a single point where the order of decisions is recorded. That is precisely what a peer-to-peer scheme cannot guarantee. Why not the others: B is the specialist's work; D is internal to each agent; E is a configuration decision fixed in advance, not orchestration at run time.

verdict.note: Decomposition pays off when each step gets focused context and passes structured output that a gate can check. A bigger model is capability, not structure. Keeping the giant prompt, or merging the steps back into one call, restores the single-prompt defect.

stem: An architect is splitting a long analysis task into sequenced subtasks. Which TWO practices make the decomposition real rather than cosmetic?

options.text: Passing structured output between steps so each one can be checked
Giving every step only the context that step actually needs
Running each of the steps on the largest model in the family
Keeping the original prompt intact and appending the steps
Merging the steps back into one call once quality has improved

explain: Decomposing serves two purposes: each step receives focused attention and each intermediate output can be verified. Without structured output between steps, the chain becomes a black box again. Why not the others: C confuses capability with structure; D leaves the giant prompt intact; E undoes the decomposition.

verdict.note: A sponsor funds outcomes: hours of handling removed (efficiency) and measured improvement against a contractual SLA (the performance pillar). Tool counts, parameter counts and prompt-variant counts measure the build, not the value, and none of them would change the investment decision.

stem: A sponsor asks the architect to justify the investment in business terms. Which TWO framings belong in that justification?

options.text: Hours of manual handling removed from the process each month
The number of tools currently registered in the agent's catalogue
Improvement measured against a contractual response-time SLA
The parameter count of the model the team ended up selecting
The number of prompt variants the team wrote during the build
