explain: The value pillars are efficiency, productivity, cost, transformation and SLA compliance. Hours freed up and improvement against a contractual SLA are measurable and matter to whoever is paying. Why not the others: B, D and E are metrics of the build, not of the outcome; none of them changes an investment decision.

verdict.note: One augmented call is the lowest rung, and it is enough when the task is a single transformation and all the context it needs fits alongside the request. Several contributing specialists point to multi-agent, a next step that depends on the previous result points to an agent, and separately audited steps point to a workflow.

stem: Which TWO conditions indicate that a single augmented model call is enough, with no workflow or agent around it?

options.text: The task is one transformation whose context can be supplied up front
Several specialists must contribute before the output is complete
Any reference material needed fits alongside the request itself
The next step depends entirely on what the previous step happened to return
Each step has to be recorded separately for an external auditor

explain: A single augmented call is enough when there is one transformation and the necessary context fits alongside the request. It is the lowest rung of the ladder and is chosen whenever it suffices. Why not the others: B calls for multi-agent; D calls for an agent; E calls for a workflow with discrete steps.

verdict.note: Nobody can tell whether accuracy moved because the loop is open: real outcomes and corrections never come back as evaluable data. The portal adds that the loop needs a named owner who acts on it. Caching cuts cost, a reviewer model prevents some errors but measures nothing over time, and a volume or latency dashboard tracks the machine, not correctness.

stem: A quoting solution was designed as input, processing, and output, with no further stage. Six months in, nobody can say whether quote accuracy has improved or degraded. What is missing from the architecture?

options.text: A feedback stage that captures outcomes into an evaluable dataset
A caching layer that lowers the cost of repeated quotes
A second model that reviews every quote before it goes out
A dashboard reporting quote volume and average processing time

explain: The fourth segment of an end-to-end architecture is feedback: corrections and production signals come back converted into evaluable data. Without that there is no way to know whether quality is moving. Why not the others: B lowers cost; C adds review but still measures nothing over time; D again measures the machine, not correctness.

verdict.note: When input classes need clearly different handling, classify first and route each class to its own path, so lookups stay cheap and fast and deep analysis is kept for disputes. A do-everything agent pays for the complex case on every lookup, one merged prompt degrades both tasks, and two products split the user experience for no technical reason.

stem: An assistant handles two kinds of request: simple status lookups that arrive constantly, and complex disputes that need deep analysis. Which design serves both?

options.text: A router that classifies the request and sends it down the fitting path
One agent with every tool available, deciding what to do per request
A single prompt long enough to cover lookups and disputes together
Two separate products, each with its own interface and its own login

explain: When there are clearly distinct input categories, classifying first and routing lets you handle the simple cases cheaply and quickly, and reserve deep analysis for what needs it. Why not the others: B pays the cost of the complex case on every trivial query; C mixes two tasks in one prompt; D splits the user experience unnecessarily.

verdict.note: Programmatic gates between steps catch a bad result where it starts and stop it spreading, and A already includes the gate before the write. A check only at the end finds errors after they have been carried through the chain, a check only on input misses what the process generates, and self-checking is an instruction, not a control.

stem: A pipeline extracts data, transforms it and writes it to a system of record. Where does validation belong?

options.text: After each step, so a bad result never reaches the following one
At the very end, right before the write to the system of record
Only at the start, validating the input document that arrived
Nowhere: the model is instructed to check its own work as it goes

explain: Validating between steps is what turns a chain into something debuggable: the error is detected where it originates and does not contaminate what follows. It is the main reason to decompose. Why not the others: B detects it once it has already been carried along; C does not cover what the process generates; D entrusts the guarantee to an instruction.

verdict.note: Separate agents earn their place through specialisation that one agent cannot reconcile (distinct sources, tools and context) and through real independence that allows parallel runs. Budget, prestige and volume never justify a split. The split is also not T-ORGCHART, because the three angles are separated for technical reasons, not because they are three teams.

stem: A due-diligence review must cover environmental, legal and financial angles. Which TWO facts justify separate agents rather than one?

options.text: Each angle needs its own sources, tools and specialist context
The three reviews do not depend on each other and can run at once
The client is paying enough to cover the extra orchestration cost
The board asked for the most advanced architecture on the market
The volume of reviews per quarter has grown steadily since last year

explain: Multi-agent design earns its place when the sub-tasks call for different specialisations and tools, and when they are independent and can run in parallel. Why not the others: C is budget; D is prestige; E is scale, solvable within any pattern.

verdict.note: Two real levers: state which instruction wins when two conflict, and keep guardrails structurally apart from long reference material. Anthropic's docs put long documents at the top with instructions after them, and use XML tags to separate the two. They also advise dialling back aggressive 'CRITICAL/MUST' wording on current models, and repetition dilutes the prompt. 'More likely to hold' is still probabilistic, so any rule that must always hold needs enforcement in code.

stem: Which TWO practices make the guardrails written into a system prompt more likely to hold?

options.text: Stating explicitly what takes precedence when two instructions conflict
Placing the guardrails at the start or end, apart from reference material
Writing the guardrails in a noticeably more emphatic and commanding tone
Repeating each guardrail once inside every section of the prompt
Assuming the guardrail also covers the cases it does not mention

explain: Two real levers: explicit precedence when there is a conflict, and position outside the middle of the context, structurally separated from the reference material. Why not the others: C is superstition; D inflates and dilutes; E is an assumption, not a practice.

verdict.note: Cut the passages that add nothing (more precise retrieval, confirmed by retrieval evals so recall does not drop) and stop paying full price for the repeated prefix (caching). Dropping citations removes traceability, downsizing everything ignores fit, and truncating passages cuts required content mid-thought.

stem: A team must cut token spend on a retrieval-heavy assistant without losing answer quality. Which TWO moves fit that goal?

options.text: Retrieve fewer but better-targeted passages for each question asked
Drop the citations from the answer so the output comes out shorter
Cache the stable instruction block that every request shares already
Switch every workload in the product to the smallest model available
Truncate each retrieved passage to its first two sentences

explain: You cut what adds nothing and stop paying twice for what is repeated. More precise retrieval and a cached prefix lower cost without touching quality. Why not the others: B removes traceability; D sacrifices quality blindly; E cuts the content off in the middle of the idea.

verdict.note: Step-by-step reasoning earns its tokens where several criteria intersect: checking one clause against three policies, and weighing signals that conflict. Field extraction, translation with a supplied glossary and a fixed JSON conversion are direct transformations, where explicit reasoning adds cost and latency without accuracy.

stem: Which TWO tasks are the best candidates for chain-of-thought prompting?

options.text: Pulling the invoice number and the issue date out of a scanned paper document
Deciding whether a contract clause conflicts with three internal policies
Translating a paragraph with a supplied glossary of approved terms
Estimating a project's risk from several partly conflicting signals
Converting a list of names into a fixed JSON structure for import

explain: Step-by-step reasoning pays off where there are chained steps and criteria that intersect. Comparing a clause against several policies and weighing contradictory signals are exactly that. Why not the others: A, C and E are direct transformations: explicit reasoning only adds cost and latency.

verdict.note: With equivalent quality measured on this task, take the cheapest tier that clears the bar and keep evaluating after the switch. Ideally that bar was agreed in advance and every slice clears it. Staying on the top tier ignores the evidence, a 50/50 split pays for a hedge nobody asked for, and dropping to the smallest tier has no measurement behind it.

stem: A summarisation feature runs on the largest model in the family. Evaluation shows a mid-tier model matches its quality on this task at a third of the cost. What should the architect do?

options.text: Move the feature to the mid-tier model and keep the evaluation running
Stay on the largest model, since summary quality varies a lot with the input
Split the traffic evenly between both models to hedge against a drop
Move to the smallest model, since the mid-tier one is not the cheapest

explain: With equivalent quality measured, you choose the smallest model that reaches the threshold and keep the evaluation running to confirm it keeps reaching it. Why not the others: B ignores the measurement that already exists; C makes behaviour unpredictable without evaluating; D steps down a rung with no evidence that that model meets the bar.

verdict.note: Zero-shot stays the default while it clears the bar. Examples cost tokens on every request and can anchor varied inputs to their surface patterns, so add them only to fix a measured format or ambiguity defect. A larger model spends capability where there is no problem.

stem: A classification task has eight well-defined categories and clear written definitions for each. Accuracy is already high without examples. What follows?

options.text: Keep it zero-shot and spend the tokens on the definitions instead
Add few-shot examples anyway, since they always improve accuracy
Add one example per category to make the prompt more consistent
Move to a larger model to protect the accuracy already achieved

explain: Examples cost tokens on every request. If the definitions are already sufficient and accuracy is high, adding them pays a cost without buying anything. Each technique is applied according to measured benefit. Why not the others: B is an absolute rule that does not hold; C inflates the prompt without evidence; D spends capacity where there is no problem.

verdict.note: Compaction keeps the conversation inside the window without losing what decides the answer: summarise the old turns and keep identifiers, amounts and commitments verbatim. Blind truncation silently drops facts, a bigger window only delays the problem, and starting over loses the thread.

stem: A support conversation runs long and the earliest messages start falling out of the window. What preserves quality?

options.text: Summarise the older turns and keep the decisive facts verbatim
Let the oldest turns drop, since recent context matters more
Move to the model with the largest window and keep everything
Start a new conversation whenever the window gets close to full

explain: Summarising the old turns and keeping verbatim what is decisive (identifiers, amounts, commitments) combines both things: it fits in the window and you do not lose the data point that breaks the answer if it is missing. Why not the others: B discards information without criteria; C pushes the problem back a few turns; D drops the thread of the conversation.

verdict.note: This is the 'unless' branch of remove-don't-guard: the role keeps the capability. So scope its credentials to the least privilege needed, and gate the irreversible delete before it runs. Make sure that approval is not a rubber stamp. Weekly log review only detects damage after it happens, and 'careful' wording or a rename only nudges the model.

stem: A support agent has a tool that can delete customer records. Which TWO changes reduce the blast radius without removing the capability from the platform?

options.text: Scope the tool's credentials so it can only reach the support dataset
Require an explicit approval step before any delete call executes
Add the word 'careful' to the tool description so that the model hesitates
Log every delete after the fact so the team can review them weekly
Rename the tool so the model is less likely to select it by mistake

explain: Least privilege plus a gate before the irreversible action. One limits what it can reach; the other requires human intervention before executing. Why not the others: C and E are text suggestions, not controls; D is detection after the deletion.

verdict.note: MCP pays off when several consumers need the same system (A) and its catalogue keeps changing (B). The owning team maintains one server, and every client discovers the current tools at runtime instead of re-wiring its own direct integration. C, D and E each describe a single stable consumer, where a direct API call is simpler (CS-D3-16 'unless'). B alone would not justify MCP; it tips the balance together with A.

stem: An architect is choosing between MCP and direct API integration for a new internal system. Which TWO facts about the situation point to MCP?

options.text: Three separate AI applications will need the same access to this system
The team owning the system will keep adding and retiring endpoints
The integration is a single deterministic call inside a nightly job
The system is only ever queried by one service the team owns
Only the data engineering team will ever query this system directly

explain: MCP pays off when there are several consumers and the catalogue changes often: the team maintains its server once and everyone reuses it. Why not the others: C, D and E describe a single, stable consumer, which is the case for direct integration.

verdict.note: To reconstruct a failed session you need a correlation ID joining every span (A) and the content of each step: retrieved chunks, plus tool arguments and results (B). C is presentation and E is deployment metadata. D, a full payload for every session, is what the portal rejects at scale: keep a light record for every request and full traces for failures and flagged slices (CS-D3-10).

stem: A platform team is defining what every agent session must emit for observability. Which TWO elements matter most for finding failures later?

options.text: A correlation identifier that ties every step of one session together
The retrieved context and tool inputs and outputs for each step
The colour-coded severity level of each message shown to the end user today
A copy of the full prompt and response stored for all sessions
The name of the engineer who last deployed the service version

explain: Without a correlation identifier a session cannot be reconstructed, and without the retrieved context and the tool calls you cannot see where it broke. Why not the others: C is presentation; D is precisely what does not scale and is done by sampling; E is deployment metadata.

verdict.note: 'Topically related but not answering' is a precision problem and a unit problem. A re-ranker scores each candidate against the actual question (A), and chunking on complete ideas makes sure a passage can hold the answer at all (B). Re-ranking only helps when the right passage is already among the candidates, which is why B complements it. Raising k to 50 (C) adds noise, temperature (D) leaves retrieval untouched, and a titles-only keyword index (E) throws away the body text.

stem: A RAG assistant returns passages that are topically related but rarely answer the question. Which TWO changes address this directly?

options.text: Add a re-ranking stage that reorders candidates before they are used
Tune chunk boundaries so each passage carries one complete idea
Increase the number of passages retrieved from five up to fifty
Raise the temperature so the model paraphrases the sources more
Replace the vector index with a keyword index built over document titles

explain: Bringing back related but useless material is a problem of what is retrieved and in what order. Re-ranking fixes the order; cutting by complete idea fixes the retrieved unit. Why not the others: C floods the context; D does not change what is retrieved; E discards the semantic search that does work.

verdict.note: Per-user credentials become mandatory when visibility differs per user (A) and untrusted content can steer the model (B). A prompt-level 'only this user's files' check can be talked around, so the credential itself must be unable to reach other users' documents. C and D are the T-AUTHZ counter-case, where everyone sees the same data or a single user sees everything and one read-only identity is fine. E confuses context capacity with access control.

stem: An assistant reads documents that belong to individual users. Which TWO conditions make per-user credentials mandatory rather than optional?

options.text: Each user may only see the subset of documents assigned to them
A prompt injection in a document could redirect what the agent asks for
All documents in the corpus are already public in the company
The assistant is used by a single administrator with full access
The corpus is small enough to fit entirely in the context window

explain: When visibility differs per user and there is a path for manipulating the model, the only reliable boundary is that the credential cannot reach what that user is not allowed to see. Why not the others: C, D and E describe scenarios where there is no separation to protect.

verdict.note: Chunking defects show up in what the retrieved unit contains: a rule without the exception from the next paragraph (A), or fragments that start and stop mid-thought (B). Run-to-run variance (C) comes from sampling, and latency growing with corpus size (D) is index scale or infrastructure. Refusing questions outside the corpus (E) is correct grounded behaviour, not a defect.

stem: Which TWO symptoms suggest that a RAG pipeline's chunking strategy is the problem, rather than the model or the prompt?

options.text: Answers cite a rule but miss the exception stated in the next paragraph
Retrieved passages start mid-sentence and end before the point lands
The same question returns different answers on repeated and identical runs
Latency rises sharply whenever the corpus grows past a certain size
The assistant refuses questions that fall outside the indexed corpus

explain: Chunking gives itself away when the retrieved piece does not contain the complete unit of meaning: the exception that sat right next to it is missing, or the fragment starts and ends in mid-air. Why not the others: C is sampling variability; D is index scale; E is correct behaviour.

verdict.note: Selection accuracy that falls as the catalogue grows is a tool-design and scoping problem. Design tools around agent tasks rather than one per endpoint, and load their definitions on demand through tool search or deferred loading (CS-D3-18). A bigger model (B) or a 'think first' instruction (C) still leaves forty overlapping choices in context. One generic dispatcher that takes an endpoint name (D) moves the confusion into a string parameter and loses the typed schemas.

stem: A team wants to expose forty internal endpoints to an agent. Tool-selection accuracy in testing drops sharply past roughly a dozen tools. What is the sound design response?

options.text: Group the endpoints into task-oriented tools and load them on demand
Register all forty tools and rely on a more capable model to choose
Register all forty and instruct the model to think before selecting one
Expose one generic tool that accepts the endpoint name as a parameter

explain: Tools are designed to be task-oriented, not as a mirror of the internal API, and only those relevant to each request are presented. The complexity stays on the system side, where it is deterministic. Why not the others: B buys capability without reducing the confusion; C adds latency to every call; D discards typed interfaces and makes errors harder to detect.

verdict.note: Tenant isolation is an authorization boundary, so it is enforced in the retrieval query. A mandatory tenant filter on chunk metadata means another client's passages never enter the context (CS-D3-05). B and D make the model the gatekeeper, and C treats relevance ranking as access control. The filter value must come from the authenticated caller, never from an argument the model chooses.

stem: A retrieval index holds documents from many client organisations. What keeps one client from ever seeing another's content?

options.text: Filter by tenant at query time using metadata on every chunk
Instruct the model to answer only from the requesting client's files
Keep one index and rely on relevance to surface the right documents
Ask the model to check the client name before quoting a passage

explain: Isolation between tenants is resolved in the query, not in the prompt: if the metadata filter does not return the document, the model cannot cite it even if it wanted to. Why not the others: B and D leave the separation in the hands of an instruction; C trusts relevance to act as access control.

verdict.note: This is still document knowledge that needs semantic search, but it must be fresh within minutes. Change-triggered incremental indexing (upsert or delete each edited document) meets that, and a periodic full rebuild repairs missed events and drift. It is the T-LIVESTATE rightWhen case: event-driven re-indexing is right for documents, while transactional state belongs in a system-of-record call. B misses the stated freshness, C worsens it on purpose, and D gives up semantic retrieval.

stem: A knowledge base gets edits all day long, and the assistant must reflect them within minutes. What indexing approach fits?

options.text: Incremental indexing triggered by each change, with a periodic full rebuild
A nightly full rebuild, which is simpler to operate and to reason about
Cache answers for an hour so the load on the index stays predictable
Retrieve straight from the source database and skip the index entirely

explain: Freshness within minutes calls for incremental indexing triggered by the change, plus a periodic full rebuild that corrects accumulated drift. Both pieces together. Why not the others: B arrives hours late; C deliberately worsens freshness; D loses semantic search.

verdict.note: Three tools whose descriptions open the same way is an overlap problem in a small set. State what each tool returns and where its boundary sits (A), and merge or retire the ones that really duplicate each other (B), as CS-D3-02 and the T-MEGATOOL rightWhen clause say. Catalogue order (C) is an arbitrary nudge, splitting further (D) adds more surface for confusion, and calling all three (E) multiplies calls, cost and context.

stem: An agent confuses three tools whose descriptions all begin with 'Looks up records'. Which TWO changes fix the selection?

options.text: State what each tool returns and where its boundary sits
Merge or retire the tools whose scope genuinely overlaps
Order the catalogue so the most used tool appears first
Split each tool further so every case has a dedicated one
Have the agent call all three and compare what comes back

explain: Selection fails through overlap and ambiguity: you make each tool's boundary explicit and eliminate the overlaps at the root. Why not the others: C institutionalises an arbitrary preference; D enlarges the surface for confusion; E multiplies calls and cost.

verdict.note: A trustworthy ongoing signal combines real production outputs scored against stable criteria on a schedule (A) with downstream user corrections fed back into the eval set (B), which closes the loop (CS-D1-03). Rerunning the frozen pre-launch suite (C) keeps measuring an old distribution (CS-D4-06). Support-team impressions (D) are anecdote. 'No repeat question' (E) is an ambiguous proxy nobody has shown to track quality.

stem: A team is adding production evaluation to a live assistant. Which TWO practices give a trustworthy ongoing signal?

options.text: Score a sampled slice of real production outputs on a fixed schedule
Capture downstream user corrections and feed them into the dataset
Re-run the pre-launch suite unchanged every quarter and compare
Ask the support team whether the assistant feels better than last month
Count how many sessions ended without the user asking again

explain: Production evaluation lives on two sources: a sample scored against stable criteria and the real corrections users make downstream. Why not the others: C always measures the same old distribution; D is anecdote; E is a weak and ambiguous proxy.

verdict.note: Both keyed levers remove work that adds no quality. Caching a stable prefix cuts input processing and time to first token. Dropping chain-of-thought, or lowering the thinking effort, on simple extraction steps removes reasoning tokens that do not change the result (CS-D2-07 'unless'). Halving every output cap (D) and pushing reasoning-heavy steps to the smallest tier (E) are blunt cuts that risk the quality floor, and C speeds up releases, not the feature. Measure the dominant term first (L6): caching pays only when a large identical prefix repeats.

stem: A latency-sensitive feature must get faster without a measurable quality loss. Which TWO levers fit?

options.text: Cache the stable prefix so repeated content is not reprocessed
Drop chain-of-thought on the steps that are simple extraction
Cut the evaluation suite so releases can ship more frequently
Reduce the maximum output tokens on every endpoint by half
Move all of the reasoning-heavy steps to the smallest available model

explain: You remove work that adds nothing: the repeated prefix is reused and explicit reasoning is withdrawn from where it does not change the result. Why not the others: C speeds up the release process, not the product; D and E cut capability and do cost quality.

verdict.note: With nothing deployed, input drift means the shape of incoming traffic changed. A new language segment (A) and a doubling of query length (B) are direct evidence of that. A higher bill (C) and steady session growth (E) are volume, not a change in distribution, and a flat p95 (D) only rules out infrastructure. To truly confirm drift, check that failing traces cluster in the new slice (CS-D4-14).

stem: Quality has slipped over three weeks with no deploys. Which TWO findings would confirm input drift as the cause?

options.text: A new customer segment started sending queries in a second language
Average query length has doubled since the start of the period
The billing total for the month came in above the usual range
The p95 latency of the endpoint has stayed flat throughout
The number of daily sessions has grown steadily week over week

explain: Drift means that what comes in has changed: a new language or queries noticeably different in shape are direct evidence that the distribution moved under a system nobody touched. Why not the others: C is a consequence of volume; D rules out an infrastructure problem but does not explain quality; E is growth, not a change of shape.

verdict.note: A judge stays trustworthy when its rubric encodes the guidelines human raters apply (B) and its agreement with expert labels is re-measured on fresh samples (A) (CS-D4-05). Anthropic says LLM judges 'should be closely calibrated with human experts'. Reusing the generator's model version (C) invites self-preference bias, and the judge changes every time the generator is upgraded. A self-revising rubric (D) lets the instrument move its own bar, and scoring only self-flagged outputs (E) biases the sample.

stem: A team is standing up an LLM-as-judge to score tone at scale. Which TWO steps keep the judge trustworthy over time?

options.text: Calibrate its scores periodically against a sample rated by experts
Write the rubric from the same guidelines the humans apply
Use the same model version that generated the output that is being scored
Let the judge revise its own rubric whenever agreement drops
Score only the outputs that the assistant flagged as uncertain

explain: A judge is useful if it applies the same criteria as the humans and if someone checks every so often that it has not drifted. A rubric derived from the real guidelines, plus periodic calibration. Why not the others: C introduces same-author bias; D lets the judge set its own bar; E skews the sample towards the doubtful cases.

verdict.note: A canary shows that a new version does no harm on real traffic before exposure widens. The gates are task quality on canary traffic against the eval bar (A) and safety signals, such as guardrail violations and refusal rates, compared with the baseline (B). Refusals arrive as HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal', so they need their own metric (PF-API-01). Reviewer counts (C) are process, cost savings (D) are the benefit rather than a safety condition, and slice size (E) is a canary setting.

stem: A canary is running for a new model version. Which TWO signals should gate the decision to widen the rollout?

options.text: Task-level scores on the evaluation suite for the canary traffic
Guardrail violations and refusal rates compared with the baseline
The number of engineers who reviewed the release notes ahead of time
The reduction in cost per request the newer version delivers
The size of the canary slice relative to total production traffic

explain: You widen the rollout when task quality holds and the safety controls do not degrade. Those are the two dimensions a canary exists to watch. Why not the others: C is process; D is a benefit, not a safety condition; E is a parameter of the canary itself.

verdict.note: The team wants to know whether the new prompt is better on real traffic. That calls for a concurrent, randomised comparison with the current prompt on a pre-registered metric, sample size and stopping rule: an A/B test. It can run under capped exposure, which is guide 4.3's 'online test under capped exposure'. A canary (B) answers a different question, whether the new version breaks anything, and is often run first. C re-measures the same offline set, and D samples opinions.

stem: A prompt change scored six points better offline. The team wants production evidence before switching everyone. Which mechanism answers the question they are actually asking?

options.text: An A/B test splitting live traffic between the current and new prompt
A canary that exposes the new prompt to a small slice and watches errors
A third offline run of the same suite to confirm the six-point gap
A review session where senior staff compare sample outputs side by side

explain: The question is which of the two versions is better with real traffic, and that is answered by a simultaneous comparison. The canary answers a different question: whether the new version breaks something. Why not the others: C re-measures the same offline distribution; D is sampling opinions.

verdict.note: Summary quality means covering what matters and staying faithful to the source. A reference-free rubric scored against the source document measures both and can run on every output; it is typically an LLM judge calibrated against human labels (CS-D4-04). Length ratio (B) measures compression. Overlap with one reference (C) needs a reference for every output and penalises good paraphrases. Expand clicks (D) are an ambiguous behavioural proxy.

stem: A summarisation feature needs a quality metric that can run on every output. What is the sound choice?

options.text: A rubric scored against the source, checking coverage and faithfulness
Length of the summary compared with the length of the source text
How closely the summary matches one reference summary word for word
How many users clicked to expand the full document after reading

explain: The quality of a summary is coverage of what matters and faithfulness to the source. A rubric applied against the document measures that and can be run on every output. Why not the others: B measures compression, not quality; C penalises good summaries worded differently; D is an indirect and ambiguous signal.

verdict.note: The binding tension is a two-hour suite against frequent prompt edits. Tiered gating resolves it: a fast regression subset on every change catches gross breaks within minutes, and the full held-out suite gates everything that ships, so no release goes out on the subset alone. B works, but it adds no protection at release and costs two hours of feedback per edit. C lets changes ship unevaluated, and D falls back to anecdote.

stem: Prompts change several times a week. Running the full evaluation suite on each change takes two hours. What is the sensible arrangement?

options.text: A fast subset on every change and the full suite before each release
The full suite on every change, since quality cannot be compromised
The full suite once a week, regardless of how many changes shipped
Manual spot checks per change, with the suite reserved for incidents

explain: You separate the fast signal from the guarantee: a subset that runs in minutes catches gross regressions on every change, and the full suite protects what goes to production. Why not the others: B slows the pace of work; C leaves days without a signal; D goes back to anecdote.

verdict.note: A regulated launch needs evidence of both competence and limits. That means an expert-labelled set covering routine and high-risk cases (A), and adversarial cases for policy violations and prompt injection, scored as separate gates (B) (CS-D4-03, CS-D4-04). Vendor benchmarks (C) say nothing about this task or these policies. A curated executive demo (D) is cherry-picked, and a post-launch survey (E) arrives after the risk has shipped.

stem: An assistant will operate in a regulated insurance context. Which TWO components must the pre-launch evaluation include?

options.text: A set labelled by experts covering routine and high-risk cases
Adversarial cases probing policy violations and prompt injection
A comparison of the model against the benchmarks of competing vendors
A demonstration to the executive committee with chosen examples
A satisfaction survey run with users after the system is launched

explain: A regulated domain demands both sides: expert-labelled data that tests competence on the typical and the high-risk cases, and adversarial cases that test that the limits hold. Why not the others: C measures what does not matter here; D is theatre over hand-picked examples; E arrives when the risk has already gone out the door.

verdict.note: 'Must never' is enforced on the output, in code. A validator blocks any date that no logistics lookup returned (A). A required source-record field (B) makes every date traceable, so the validator can check it, or the date is left out. B counts only because it produces a checkable artefact; as a bare instruction it would sit on C's rung. The stem asks what enforces the rule, so the usual preventive-plus-detective pairing does not apply: D only detects after sending, and lower temperature (E) does not limit what the model asserts.

stem: A drafting assistant must never state a delivery date that is not in the logistics system. Which TWO controls enforce that?

options.text: Block any response containing a date that no lookup call returned
Require the model to cite the record its date came from, or omit it
Instruct the assistant in the prompt to avoid inventing dates
Review a weekly sample of sent messages for invented delivery dates
Lower the temperature so the assistant improvises less on its own

explain: An absolute requirement is enforced on the output, not in the instruction. Blocking what is unsupported and requiring the source are two layers of the same preventive control. Why not the others: C is a request in text; D detects after sending; E does not change what the model allows itself to assert.

verdict.note: Put the gate where the action is irreversible and has external impact: the cancellation, approved before it executes (CS-D5-08). Searches and drafts are reversible and internal, so they run freely. Approving every call (B) breeds rubber-stamping and kills the efficiency case. Review after the cancellation (C) comes after the harm, and a random tenth (D) leaves most cancellations ungated.

stem: An agent that books travel has a tool that can cancel existing reservations. Where does the human approval gate belong?

options.text: Before a cancellation executes, while searches and drafts run freely
Before every tool call the agent makes during the booking session
After the cancellation, so that a person can reinstate it if it was wrong
On a random tenth of sessions, sampled for quality assurance

explain: The gate goes where the action is irreversible and has external impact. Low-risk work flows on its own, which is what sustains the business case. Why not the others: B destroys efficiency; C reviews after the damage; D leaves most cancellations uncontrolled.

verdict.note: A is right. The binding constraint is 'at design time': if identity is kept apart from content (pseudonymous IDs, an identity map you can delete or crypto-shredding, redaction at capture), both duties can coexist. The community explanation overstates C: GDPR Art. 17(3)(b)/(e) does let a legal retention duty limit erasure, but only as far as necessary, so refusing outright is still wrong. Free-text content must also be redacted, or the separation does not hold.

stem: A customer exercises their right to erasure. The company keeps full conversation traces for auditing. How is that resolved at design time?

options.text: Separate identity from content so the person can be erased from traces
Delete every trace touching that customer, accepting the audit gap
Refuse the request, since audit obligations override the erasure right
Keep the traces and simply stop associating them with any customer

explain: The two duties coexist if they are designed together: the trail keeps what the audit needs and the identity is deleted or pseudonymised. Retrofitting this afterwards is extremely expensive. Why not the others: B breaks the audit; C assumes a hierarchy that does not exist; D describes the goal without any mechanism.

verdict.note: A is right. A guardrail can fail in two ways, so measure wrongful blocks and missed harms on labelled benign and harmful sets, and let the owner pick the operating point by relative harm (L7, L8). B uses complaints as the metric, C ignores what wrongful blocks cost, and D swaps an enforced check for a request in the prompt (L3).

stem: A guardrail is blocking legitimate requests along with the harmful ones, and users are complaining. What is the correct response?

options.text: Measure both error types on labelled cases and tune where the harm is worse
Loosen the guardrail until users stop complaining about the blocks
Keep it as is: blocking too much is always safer than blocking too little
Move the check into the prompt so the model can use its own judgement

explain: A guardrail has two ways of failing and is calibrated by measuring both on labelled cases. Which one is more tolerable depends on the relative harm in that business, and that is an explicit decision. Why not the others: B uses complaints as the metric; C ignores the cost of wrongful blocking; D trades a guarantee for a request.

verdict.note: A is right. Every processor that touches the data is part of the risk surface, including pass-through services, and each dependency needs a defined failure mode and fallback. A contract or penalty assigns liability after an incident and is not a risk control (compare CS-D5-11: a DPA or SOC 2 letter is evidence about the vendor, not about your data flows).

stem: An architecture routes customer data through three third-party services. What does the risk assessment have to cover?

options.text: Each provider's data handling, plus what happens when one of them fails
The provider with the largest share of the traffic that flows through
Only the provider that stores data, since the others merely pass it on
The contractual penalties agreed with each of the three providers

explain: The entire chain is your risk surface: every subprocessor that touches the data counts, and you need to know what happens when one goes down or degrades. Contracts allocate blame; they do not prevent the incident. Why not the others: B and C leave deliberate gaps; D confuses legal liability with risk assessment.

verdict.note: A is right. When a decision significantly affects someone, they are owed meaningful information about what it was based on and a route to human intervention (GDPR Art. 22(3) and Arts. 13-15; EU AI Act Art. 86 for high-risk systems). A bare notice, an uncalibrated score or the raw system prompt is the wrong artefact for this audience (T-AUDIENCE).

stem: An automated decision affects whether a person receives a benefit. What does the design owe that person?

options.text: An explanation of the basis for the decision and a route to human review
A notice that the decision involved an automated system in some way
The confidence score the model produced when it made the decision
The full system prompt, so the criteria applied are fully transparent

explain: When the decision has an effect on the person, what can be demanded is understanding what it was based on and being able to request human review. That is what transparency means when something is at stake. Why not the others: B gives notice without providing anything actionable; C hands over a number nobody can interpret; D exposes internal logic without making it understandable.

verdict.note: A is right. The defect is sending more personal health data than the analytics purpose needs, so minimise before the data crosses the boundary. Pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR (PF-GOV-06), so stripping is the stronger form, and a transfer abroad still needs a lawful transfer mechanism. Encryption in transit, shorter retention and a privacy notice all leave the payload unchanged (T-COMPLY).

stem: A subsidiary streams full patient support chats, names included, to a quality-analytics vendor abroad. The data protection officer objects.

options.text: Strip or pseudonymise personal data before it leaves the boundary
Encrypt the stream in transit to the analytics vendor's own endpoint
Shorten retention at the vendor from three years down to one year
Add a line to the privacy notice saying that chats may be analysed

explain: The problem is sending more personal data than the purpose requires. Minimising before crossing the boundary solves that, and monitoring keeps working on de-identified content. Why not the others: B protects the transit, not the processing at the destination; C shortens exposure without reducing it; D is notification.

verdict.note: A is right. Fairness through unawareness fails because school district acts as a proxy. The fix is to evaluate outcomes per segment against pre-agreed thresholds, remediate, and keep monitoring per group (CS-D5-12). B treats formal compliance as fairness, C ignores the levers in the application layer, and D hides the harm without fixing it.

stem: A scholarship-scoring assistant rates applicants from certain school districts lower. Names and demographic fields were already stripped from the input.

options.text: Proxies still carry the signal: evaluate by segment and remediate
The system is behaving correctly, since no protected field was used
The base model is at fault and the application layer cannot help it
It is a presentation problem: stop showing the score to reviewers

explain: Removing the explicit attributes does not eliminate bias: the school district carries the same signal. The answer is evaluation by segment, remediation and ongoing monitoring. Why not the others: B confuses formal compliance with fairness; C ignores the levers of the application layer; D hides the harm.

verdict.note: A is right. This is indirect prompt injection, and the violated principle is trust separation: retrieved content is data and carries no instruction authority. Per L3, delimiting it as data lowers the risk but guarantees nothing, so pair it with limits on tool and outbound reach. Internal-only sources (B) can be poisoned too.

stem: A security review finds that a sentence inside an indexed supplier document changed how the agent behaved.

options.text: Retrieved text is untrusted data and holds no instruction authority
Indexes should only contain documents written inside the company
Retrieval must stop whenever a document contains an imperative
System prompts must be encrypted wherever they are stored at rest

explain: The violated principle is trust separation: what is retrieved is untrusted input, is delimited as data and has no instruction authority. Why not the others: B restricts sources without fixing the trust model; C would block legitimate documents; D protects secrets, not behaviour.

verdict.note: A and B are right. When a client arrives with a solution already chosen, discovery recovers the underlying job and fixes a measurable success criterion and threshold before any build step (CS-D1-01). A fixed-price quote, a wireframe and a model shortlist all commit to a design before the problem and target are agreed.

stem: A discovery workshop is being planned with a client who has already chosen a solution. Which TWO outcomes make the workshop worth running?

options.text: A written statement of the business problem behind the requested tool
Agreement on how success will be measured and at what threshold
A signed fixed-price quote for the solution the client asked for
A wireframe of the interface the client pictured beforehand
A shortlist of the model versions the team intends to benchmark

explain: Discovery exists to recover the problem behind the proposed solution and to pin down what success will mean. Everything else depends on those two things. Why not the others: C commits to a price on something not yet validated; D and E are products of design, premature here.

verdict.note: A is right. Commit to what you control, which is when the evidence will exist, and gate the launch decision on pre-agreed criteria (L7, CS-D6-12). B promises a date the evidence may not support, C refuses to plan, and D sets scope without the accountable owner (T-OWNER).

stem: A client asks for a firm launch date before the evaluation dataset exists. What does the architect commit to?

options.text: A date for the evaluation to be ready, and a launch decision gated on it
The requested launch date, with the evaluation work compressed to fit around it
No date at all until every acceptance criterion has been measured
A launch date for a reduced scope chosen by the delivery team alone

explain: You commit to what you control (when the evidence will exist) and tie the launch decision to that evidence. It is expectation management grounded in engineering. Why not the others: B commits to a date that cannot be sustained; C blocks the conversation; D decides the scope without the accountable owner.

verdict.note: A is right. A risk committee judges how the system is controlled, so it needs the decision flow, the controls and the evaluation evidence, told in its own language (portal 6.2: reviewers get the architecture and data flows). A raw system prompt, a disclaimer or a live demo shows neither the controls nor measured behaviour.

stem: A client's risk committee asks to see exactly how the assistant reaches its answers. What does the architect provide?

options.text: The decision flow, the guardrails and the evaluation results, in their language
The system prompt and the model parameters, as the literal answer
A statement that large language models are not fully explainable
A live demonstration, which shows the behaviour better than documents

explain: The committee is not asking for the prompt: it is asking to understand what happens and what controls it. Decision flow, controls and evaluation evidence, told in their language, is what truly answers that question. Why not the others: B delivers material they cannot evaluate; C closes the conversation; D shows behaviour without showing control.

verdict.note: A is right. A pilot proves value, not operation. Going to production adds load, long-tail cases, support, SLOs, rollback and cost at volume, and those go on the table before a date is committed (CS-D6-12). B is pessimism without data, C reruns the stage with no new criteria, and the budget (D) follows from A.

stem: A pilot exceeded its targets and the sponsor wants to roll it out to the whole organisation next month. What does the architect raise first?

options.text: What changes at production scale: load, edge cases, support and cost
That the pilot results will not hold, so expectations must come down
That a second pilot is needed before committing to any rollout
The additional budget the wider rollout is going to require

explain: A successful pilot proves the hypothesis, not the operation. Volume, rare cases, support and cost change in scale, and that is put on the table before committing to the date. Why not the others: B is pessimism without data; C delays without adding new information; D is a consequence, not the conversation.

verdict.note: A is right. An ADR records the options considered and why the alternatives lost, so a later team can check whether the constraint that forced the decision still holds (CS-D6-10). Describing only the system as built (B) loses the why, and the conditions in C and D hollow out the practice.

stem: During design, a promising approach was evaluated and discarded. Should that appear in the documentation?

options.text: Yes: recording why it was rejected stops the team revisiting it blindly
No: documentation should describe the system as it was finally built
Only if the client asks specifically about that particular alternative
Only when the rejected option was the more expensive of the two

explain: That is what the decision record exists for: whoever comes later sees the discarded option and the reason, and does not spend a quarter rediscovering it. It is what makes the handover sustainable. Why not the others: B documents the what without the why; C and D set conditions that hollow out the practice.

verdict.note: A is right. Accuracy can be an SLA term once it is defined as a floor on a named, versioned eval set, with a grader, a sample size and a review cadence (CS-D6-07, portal 6.3). Uptime only (B) drops what the client needs, accepting an undefined target (C) is a promise nobody can enforce, and a penalty regime (D) is a remedy with nothing defined to measure.

stem: A client wants an SLA that covers answer accuracy the same way it covers uptime. How should the architect respond?

options.text: Commit to accuracy measured on an agreed test set, reviewed periodically
Commit to uptime only, since accuracy cannot be guaranteed by contract
Accept the accuracy target and manage it through internal monitoring
Propose a penalty regime, which is what an SLA really comes down to

explain: Accuracy can indeed be committed to if you define what it is measured against and how often it is reviewed. That turns a vague expectation into an agreement both parties can verify. Why not the others: B gives up what the client needs; C accepts without defining the measurement; D jumps to the penalty without defining what is being measured.

verdict.note: A is right. Bring the measured error rate, the rework and the regulatory exposure to the accountable owner with a recommendation, and let them decide with that in hand (L8). B is deception, C withholds material information and deploys the cheapest tier whether or not it fits, and D goes over the owner's head before the conversation has happened (T-OWNER).

stem: A finance director orders the cheapest model for a filing that feeds the regulator. Testing shows it errs materially more often on that task.

options.text: Show the evidence and let the accountable owner choose informed
Use the better model quietly and absorb the difference elsewhere
Comply without comment, since the budget belongs to that director
Take it over their head to the audit committee for a final ruling

explain: The professional move is to quantify quality, rework and regulatory exposure against the savings, recommend, and let whoever holds the responsibility decide. Why not the others: B is deception; C hides material information; D escalates before having the conversation.

verdict.note: A is right. Show the latency budget stage by stage, agree an SLA the pipeline can meet, and use streaming to shorten the wait users perceive. Streaming does not shorten completion time (CS-D3-07, portal 6.3), and where verification gates release you stream progress, not unverified text. B, C and D either promise a speed the pipeline cannot deliver or buy it by removing the stages that justify the system.

stem: A client demands answers in under a second from a pipeline that retrieves, reasons and verifies. Engineering measures three seconds.

options.text: Show the latency budget, agree a realistic SLA and add streaming
Accept the target now and count on later optimisation to close it
Remove the retrieval and verification stages so the target is met
Promise sub-second timing for demonstrations to the client only

explain: Expectations are managed with engineering reality: the latency budget in plain view, an SLA the pipeline can honour, and perceived speed improved with streaming. Why not the others: B signs up to a breach; C sacrifices the capability that justifies the system; D guarantees the gap will show up in production.

verdict.note: A is right. The sponsor funded a business outcome, so the report leads with the success criteria agreed at discovery, measured against the baseline, and keeps tokens, uptime and latency as supporting detail (T-AUDIENCE). Reporting more often or adding technical metrics keeps the misalignment, and dropping the report removes the loop.

stem: Three months after launch the sponsor is losing interest: the monthly report shows tokens, uptime and average latency.

options.text: Lead with the criteria agreed at discovery, technical data behind
Report weekly instead of monthly so the project stays more visible
Add further technical indicators so the report looks more complete
Drop the report and rely on conversations with the sponsor instead

explain: The sponsor funded a business outcome: the report leads with the criteria agreed at discovery and keeps the technical data as backup. Why not the others: B is more of the same at a different frequency; C deepens the misalignment; D eliminates the loop.

verdict.note: A is right. Keep secrets out of version-controlled files and out of the context window, and have configuration reference them as environment variables (for example `${VAR}` expansion in `.mcp.json`, CS-D7-02). This principle carries over from Foundations. One caveat: the agent's shell inherits environment variables, so a secret manager or credential helper plus deny rules on secret files isolates the key better than any listed option.

stem: An AI coding assistant needs access to a service that requires an API key. How is that handled?

options.text: An environment variable the tooling reads, never a file under version control
A configuration file kept out of the repository through the ignore list
A note in the project documentation explaining where to find the key
A key with a short expiry, pasted into the session when it is needed

explain: Secrets go in environment variables and the configuration references them. Everything else ends up, sooner or later, inside a repository or inside a context window. Why not the others: B depends on nobody ever making a single mistake; C documents where the secret is located; D puts it into the model's context.

verdict.note: A and B are right. Reconstructing a past decision needs what the agent saw (a retained trace with its inputs, tool results, and model and prompt versions) and the rules in force that day (an immutable record of the active policy version). Current aggregates (C, E) and a preventive guardrail (D) reconstruct nothing. The retained traces still have to follow retention and redaction rules.

stem: A regulator asks how the bank would reconstruct an agent's decision on a disputed loan eight months ago. Which TWO capabilities answer that?

options.text: Retention of the full session trace, including the data the agent read
An immutable record of which policy version was active that day
A dashboard showing the current month's approval and refusal rates by product
A guardrail that blocks approvals above the delegated credit limit
A quarterly report summarising total volume by product and region

explain: Reconstructing requires knowing what the agent saw and under which rules it was operating on that date. Retained trace plus the policy version in force. Why not the others: C and E are present-day aggregates; D is prevention, useful but it reconstructs nothing.

verdict.note: A and B are right. Residency (where the data is processed and which subprocessors may touch it) and minimisation (which fields leave each region) decide which architecture is lawful, so both are fixed before any data flows. C, D and E are product or unrelated choices with no bearing on compliance.

stem: A hiring assistant will run in three countries with different data-protection regimes. Which TWO decisions belong to the architecture stage?

options.text: Where candidate data is processed and which subprocessors may touch it
What personal fields are stripped before the data leaves each region
Which font and colour scheme the recruiter interface will use
How the weekly summary email to hiring managers will be worded
Which conference the team will present the resulting case study at next year

explain: Data residency and minimisation determine which architecture is legally possible. They are decided before the data flows, not afterwards. Why not the others: C and D are product matters; E has no bearing on compliance.

verdict.note: A and B are right. The receiving team needs the why (decision records that include the rejected alternatives) and a way to check its own changes (eval baselines it can re-run), which matches the portal's handoff pack (CS-D6-11). Prompt-draft history, a demo recording and an unapproved backlog are fragments, not artefacts the team can operate from.

stem: An internal team is taking over a solution built by a consultancy. Which TWO artefacts most reduce the risk of the handoff?

options.text: Decision records explaining why each major trade-off was chosen
Evaluation baselines the team can re-run after their own changes
The full history of prompt drafts explored during development
A recording of the final demonstration given to the steering group
A backlog of features the client requested but never approved

explain: The receiving team needs to understand why the system is the way it is and to be able to verify that their changes do not make it worse. Decision records plus executable baselines. Why not the others: C is history; D belongs to the journey, not to operation; E documents what was not built.

verdict.note: The system meets its technical targets and still fails on adoption, so the first job is diagnosis, not new features. Compare real usage with the success criteria agreed at discovery and ask the intended users where the tool fails their workflow. New features, a bigger model or another launch campaign all change something before anyone knows what is wrong.

stem: Six weeks after launch, adoption is far below plan although the system meets every technical target. Which TWO steps does the architect take first?

options.text: Interview the intended users about where the tool fails their workflow
Compare actual usage against the success criteria agreed at discovery
Add the capabilities the team believes users will find compelling
Increase the model size so responses come back faster and richer
Announce the tool again through a broader internal campaign

explain: The system meets the technical bar and fails the real one, so the evidence lies in usage and in the users. First you understand the gap against what was agreed, then you decide. Why not the others: C, D and E are interventions without diagnosis: they change the product before knowing what is missing.

verdict.note: Shared configuration and prompt standards under version control let proven practice spread to all twelve squads (CS-D7-02). An explicit list of the commands and branches automation may touch limits risk (CS-D7-05). Broad credentials make any mistake bigger, standards published per squad bring the drift back, and adopting every new tool at once adds churn without any evaluation.

stem: A platform team is enabling AI-assisted development across twelve squads. Which TWO measures scale the practice without scaling the risk?

options.text: Keep shared configuration and prompt standards under version control
Define which commands automated tooling may run and on which branches
Grant the tooling broad credentials so squads are never blocked
Let each squad publish its own standards independently
Adopt every new assistant tool in the week it becomes available

explain: Accelerator and brake at once: proven practices inherited through version control, and explicit limits on what automation may execute. Why not the others: C maximises the blast radius; D reproduces fragmentation; E adds churn without evaluation.

verdict.note: This is a choice between two use cases on different value pillars (efficiency versus performance SLA), not a design option that would breach an SLA. So the architect puts a cost on each: the hours saved against the penalties and churn from SLA breaches, and brings that to the decision owner. C assumes, without evidence, that breach costs always exceed the savings. D hands the decision over without any criteria to decide on.

stem: Two use cases are on the table. One saves 200 staff hours a month; the other prevents breaches of a contractual response-time commitment. How should the architect frame the choice?

options.text: Both map to value pillars; the decision needs the cost of each risk
The hours are measurable, so efficiency should always come first
The SLA is contractual, so it always outranks any efficiency gain
Whichever the sponsor prefers, since both are defensible on paper

explain: Efficiency and SLA compliance are distinct pillars and neither wins by default. What decides is how much each risk costs in that business: that is what the architect has to put on the table. Why not the others: B and C make one pillar absolute; D delegates the decision without giving the decision-maker any criteria.

verdict.note: A production chain needs failure behaviour defined in code at the orchestrator for each stage (retry, fall back, or stop and report), as in CS-D1-12's programmatic gates and CS-D5-05's fallback for a failed dependency. A downstream 'repair' stage fixes symptoms in the wrong layer. A bigger model only makes failures rarer. An instruction to skip the stage leaves control flow to the model and silently drops a required step.

stem: In a four-stage chain, the third stage fails on about one request in twenty. What belongs in the design?

options.text: A defined behaviour for that failure: retry, fall back, or stop and report
A fifth stage that reviews the output and repairs whatever looks wrong
A larger model in stage three so the failures become less frequent
A rule telling the model to skip stage three when it cannot complete

explain: A chain in production needs defined behaviour on failure, not just a happy path. Retry, fallback or an explicit stop are design decisions taken beforehand, not during the incident. Why not the others: B patches downstream without knowing what failed; C lowers the frequency but does not define what happens when it occurs; D silently skips a necessary step.

verdict.note: Anthropic's tool-design guidance says to build tools around the tasks the agent must complete, often combining several endpoints into one tool, rather than wrapping every API endpoint. One tool per endpoint bloats the catalogue and makes selection harder. A single pass-through tool with a mode or endpoint parameter loses the typed interface. How stable the backend is has nothing to do with what the agent needs.

stem: An internal API exposes forty endpoints. The team is deciding how to expose it to the agent. What should drive the tool boundaries?

options.text: The tasks the agent needs to accomplish, not the endpoints that exist
One tool per endpoint, so the whole surface stays available to it
A single tool that receives the endpoint name and its parameters
The endpoints the backend team considers most stable over time

explain: Tools are designed per task. Mirroring the internal API transfers its complexity to the model, which is where it is handled worst; grouped by task, the complexity stays on the deterministic side. Why not the others: B produces an excess of capabilities; C discards the typed interface; D uses a backend criterion for an agent decision.

verdict.note: Wake someone only for a sustained, actionable sign that the system is broken, such as a tool error rate that stays above a threshold for several minutes. A single request slower than the median is noise. A rise in week-on-week token spend belongs in a cost review, not a page. One thumbs-down is feedback for the eval loop, not an incident.

stem: An agent platform needs alerting. Which signal deserves a page to the on-call engineer?

options.text: Tool error rate crossing a threshold sustained over several minutes
Any single request that took longer than the median to complete
Daily token spend rising above the same day of the previous week
A user rating one individual answer as unhelpful in the interface

explain: You wake someone up for a sustained condition that indicates the system is broken. A tool error rate above the threshold and sustained is exactly that. verdict.note: The key is right. Submissions fall into known, labelled classes that each need different handling, so a routing workflow fits: a cheap classifier sends each class to its own prompt and the always-human liability class to the adjuster queue. An agent adds cost for a path that never varies, one big prompt dilutes three rule sets, and running every pipeline then picking by self-reported confidence triples cost and routes on an uncalibrated signal.

stem:
A national insurance carrier has a backlog of 40,000 first notice of loss submissions. About 60% are simple auto glass claims that follow one fixed path, 25% are property claims needing a different set of checks, and 15% are complex liability claims that always require adjuster review. The team has six months of labelled historical submissions and a hard 8 second SLA on the customer-facing acknowledgement.

Which architecture gives the best accuracy per dollar for the portion that can be automated?

options.text: Classify each submission with a fast, cheap model, then dispatch it to a claim-type-specific prompt pipeline, with liability claims routed to the human adjuster queue.
Build one autonomous agent with tools covering every claim type and let it decide the handling path on each submission.
Run all three claim-type pipelines in parallel on every submission and select the output with the highest self-reported confidence.
Write one large prompt containing the handling rules for all three claim types and let the model apply the relevant ones.

explain:
This is the routing workflow: inputs fall into known, distinct categories, so classifying first and then optimising a specialist prompt per category improves accuracy for each type without degrading the others. Labelled historical data makes the classifier cheap to build and validate, and the human queue absorbs the category that should not be automated. Routing also keeps the fast path fast, which matters for the 8 second SLA.

Distractor notes:
B: An autonomous agent is the right choice when the handling path cannot be predetermined. Here the categories are known and labelled, so the agent adds latency, cost and behavioural variance for no accuracy gain.
C: Parallelisation by voting is for running the same task several times to raise confidence. These pipelines are mutually exclusive, so running all three triples cost and still needs a selection rule.
D: A single combined prompt is the correct starting point when categories are few and similar. With three genuinely different check sets it dilutes instructions and burns tokens on rules that do not apply.

verdict.note: The key is right. Every packet follows the same steps and regulators can demand a seven-year replay, so the answer is a gated prompt chain that persists each step's input and output. An agent that plans its own path per packet breaks the reproducible audit trail. Ideally the check against underwriting policy is deterministic code rather than an LLM call (CS-D1-08), but A is the only option that gives step-level provenance and gates.

stem:
A mortgage lender must extract 40 fields from loan packets, validate them against underwriting policy, generate a conditions letter, and produce an audit record showing which step produced each value. The steps are the same for every packet and regulators can request a replay of any decision made in the last seven years.

Which design best fits these constraints?

options.text: A prompt chain where extraction, validation and letter generation are separate calls with programmatic gates between them, each step persisted.
An orchestrator agent that plans its own sequence per packet and calls extraction, validation and drafting tools as it sees fit.
A single call with extended thinking enabled and a large max_tokens, producing all 40 fields, the validation verdict and the letter in one response.
An evaluator-optimizer loop where a second model critiques the extraction until it converges.

explain:
The subtasks are fixed and known in advance, which is exactly the condition under which prompt chaining beats agentic approaches: you trade latency for accuracy and get a deterministic, inspectable sequence. Programmatic gates between steps let you fail fast on bad extractions, and each step's input and output can be persisted to satisfy a seven-year replay obligation. Agentic self-planning would make the audit trail vary from packet to packet.

Distractor notes:
B: Orchestrator-workers is the right pattern when subtasks cannot be predetermined. Here they can, and a variable plan per packet undermines the reproducible audit record the regulator expects.
C: One monolithic call is cheapest and lowest latency, and would be right if there were no audit or gating requirement, but it produces no step-level provenance and no place to stop the pipeline on a bad extraction.
D: Evaluator-optimizer suits open-ended generation with clear evaluation criteria, such as translation or copywriting. Field extraction against a fixed policy is better checked by deterministic validation code than by a critic model.

verdict.note: The key is right. Anthropic's multi-agent research post names two conditions that justify subagents here: work that parallelises heavily, and information that exceeds one context window. Multi-agent systems spend more tokens than a single agent, not fewer (about 15x chat usage). Workers that must share tightly coupled state argue against splitting, and no LLM design gives byte-identical output.

stem:
A pharmaceutical competitive intelligence team wants an agent that answers open-ended questions such as 'which competitors changed their phase III endpoints this quarter'. Answering means searching many sources, and the team has proposed a lead agent that spawns parallel subagents. Finance has flagged that token spend must be justified.

Which TWO conditions most justify the multi-agent orchestrator-subagent design over a single agent here? (Select TWO)

options.text: The work is breadth-first and parallelisable, with independent lines of investigation that do not depend on each other.
The information to be examined greatly exceeds what fits in a single context window.
The task requires every worker to share the same evolving context and coordinate tightly on shared state.
The team wants lower total token consumption than a single-agent implementation.
The output must be byte-for-byte reproducible across runs.

explain:
Multi-agent systems earn their cost when work is heavily parallelisable and when the material to examine exceeds a single context window, because subagents compress their own findings before returning them. Both conditions hold for breadth-first competitive research. The cost case has to be made on answer quality, not on token savings.

Distractor notes:
C: Tight coupling on shared state is the classic anti-pattern for multi-agent designs. When agents need the same evolving context, coordination overhead and error compounding outweigh the parallelism.
D: Multi-agent systems consume substantially more tokens than a single agent, not fewer. Anthropic's published figures put multi-agent research around 15 times chat usage.
E: Neither single-agent nor multi-agent LLM systems give byte-for-byte reproducibility. If that were a requirement the answer would be a deterministic workflow, not any agent.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

stem:
A regional bank's KYC analysts need answers grounded in an internal policy corpus of about 120,000 tokens that is revised roughly once a quarter. Query volume is 3,000 per day, latency target is under 4 seconds, and the platform team has no vector database and no budget to run one.

What is the most appropriate retrieval design?

options.text: Place the whole corpus in the prompt behind a cache breakpoint and let the model answer directly from it.
Chunk and embed the corpus into a managed vector store and retrieve the top 20 chunks per query.
Build a contextual retrieval pipeline with contextual embeddings, BM25 and a reranker.
Fine-tune a smaller model on the policy corpus and serve queries from it.

explain:
For knowledge bases under roughly 200,000 tokens the guidance is to put the whole corpus in the prompt rather than build a retrieval system, and prompt caching makes that both fast and cheap on repeated queries. A quarterly revision cadence means the cached prefix stays stable for long periods. This removes an entire piece of infrastructure the team cannot fund or operate.

Distractor notes:
B: Plain vector RAG becomes the right answer once the corpus is well beyond what fits in context, but at 120k tokens it adds infrastructure, a chunking failure mode and retrieval latency for no benefit.
C: Contextual retrieval with BM25 and reranking is the right answer for large corpora where retrieval failures are the dominant error, not for a corpus that fits comfortably in context.
D: Fine-tuning bakes policy into weights, which is the worst fit for content revised quarterly and for a domain where you need to point to the clause you relied on.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval

verdict.note: The key is right. Contextual retrieval puts back the qualifiers that chunking stripped (country, effective date), and indexing the same contextualised chunks in BM25 restores precision on exact codes. Re-ranking then tightens the merged candidate set. Bigger chunks or a higher top-k add volume without fixing either defect, and a bigger model cannot use evidence that retrieval never surfaced.

stem:
A global logistics provider has 4 million tokens of tariff rulings, customs notices and country annexes. Analysts report that the current embedding-only RAG returns chunks that are topically close but missing the qualifier that makes them apply, for example a chunk that states a duty rate without naming the country or the effective date. Precision on exact code lookups is also poor.

Which change addresses both failure modes most directly?

options.text: Prepend a short chunk-specific context blurb to each chunk before both embedding and BM25 indexing, then rerank the merged candidate set.
Increase the chunk size so that each chunk carries more surrounding text.
Raise the number of retrieved chunks from 20 to 100 and let the model filter.
Switch the answering model to the largest available model and enable extended thinking.

explain:
Contextual retrieval fixes exactly the described problem: the chunk-specific context restores the qualifiers stripped by chunking, and indexing that contextualised chunk in both the embedding space and BM25 recovers the exact-match behaviour that embeddings alone lose on codes and identifiers. Reranking the merged candidate set then filters what survives. Published results show the combination reduces retrieval failures substantially more than embeddings alone.

Distractor notes:
B: Larger chunks help when chunks are absurdly small, but they dilute the embedding, raise cost per retrieved chunk and do nothing for the lexical precision problem on codes.
C: Retrieving more chunks trades precision for recall and pushes far more tokens into context, which invites context rot. It masks the retrieval defect rather than fixing it.
D: A stronger answering model cannot use evidence that retrieval never surfaced. This would be the right lever if the retrieved chunks were correct but the reasoning over them was wrong.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval

verdict.note: The key is right. The stem gives both conditions for an evaluator-optimizer loop: clear, checkable criteria and consistent reviewer feedback that can be put into words. The retry cap bounds cost. Routing, orchestrator-workers and sectioning each assume a problem the stem never describes (category differences, a decomposition you cannot predict, a need for speed). Rules that must hold every time, such as the mandatory certification sentence, can also be checked in code.

stem:
A retailer's brand team generates 500 product descriptions a week. They have a written style guide with concrete, checkable rules, for example no superlatives without a substantiating spec and a mandatory sustainability sentence when the product carries a certification. Human reviewers currently reject about a third of first drafts and their feedback is consistent and articulable.

Which workflow pattern fits best?
