options.text: An evaluator-optimizer loop where a generator drafts and a separate critic scores against the style guide until the draft passes or a retry cap is hit.
A routing workflow that sends each product to a category-specific description prompt.
An orchestrator agent that decomposes each description into sections and delegates each to a worker.
Parallel sectioning where one call writes features, one writes benefits, and a third concatenates them.

explain:
Evaluator-optimizer is indicated when there are clear evaluation criteria and when human feedback demonstrably improves the output, both of which are stated here. The style guide gives the critic a concrete rubric, and the retry cap bounds cost. This mirrors the human review loop that already works, so it is cheap to validate against existing reject rates.

Distractor notes:
B: Routing helps when categories need genuinely different handling. Nothing here suggests category-specific prompts are the gap; the gap is guideline compliance on the first draft.
C: Orchestrator-workers is for tasks whose decomposition cannot be predicted in advance. A product description has a known shape.
D: Parallel sectioning speeds up independent subtasks but produces disjointed copy and still has no mechanism for enforcing the style guide.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

verdict.note: The key is right. An agent that contradicts its earlier decisions after hours of tool calls is suffering context degradation. Anthropic documents three long-horizon fixes: compaction, structured notes kept outside the window, and subagents that return condensed summaries. max_tokens caps only output, temperature does not restore recall, and more tools add to the context load.

stem:
A telecom operator runs a network incident agent that works a single incident for six to ten hours, calling diagnostic tools hundreds of times. Engineers report that after several hours the agent starts contradicting decisions it made earlier in the same incident and re-runs diagnostics it already ran.

Which THREE techniques directly address this long-horizon degradation? (Select THREE)

options.text: Compact the conversation when it approaches the context limit, preserving decisions and discarding redundant tool output.
Have the agent write structured notes to persistent storage outside the context window and read them back when needed.
Delegate bounded investigations to subagents that return condensed summaries rather than raw tool output.
Raise max_tokens so the agent can produce longer responses per turn.
Lower the temperature so the agent is more deterministic across the run.
Increase the number of tools available so the agent has more diagnostic options.

explain:
The symptom is context rot: as the window fills, recall of earlier content degrades, so the agent loses its own prior decisions. Compaction, external structured note-taking and subagent delegation are the three long-horizon techniques that keep the working context small and high-signal while preserving the decisions that matter. All three reduce the token count the model must attend to without discarding the substance.

Distractor notes:
D: max_tokens governs the output ceiling. It does nothing about degraded recall over a long input context and, if anything, adds more tokens to the history.
E: Temperature affects sampling variance within a response, not the model's ability to recall a decision made 200 tool calls ago.
F: More tools enlarge the tool definitions in every request and widen the action space. This makes context pressure worse, not better.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

verdict.note: The key is right. The same judgement applies to every listing and a wrong removal is expensive, so voting is the parallelisation that targets the error asymmetry: several runs, agreement required to remove automatically, disagreement escalated. The extra runs cost far less than a $30 appeal. Splitting the policy or the listing strips context the judgement needs, and routing adds machinery for a variation the stem rules out.

stem:
A marketplace must decide whether listings violate a prohibited-items policy. Volume is 90,000 listings a day. Wrongly removing a legitimate seller's listing triggers an appeal that costs about 30 dollars to handle, while missing a genuine violation carries regulatory exposure. The policy is a single document and the same judgement applies to every listing.

Which use of parallelisation is most appropriate?

options.text: Voting: run the same classification prompt several times with diverse framings and require agreement before an automated removal.
Sectioning: split the policy into three parts and run one call per part, then union the flags.
Sectioning: split each listing into title, description and images and classify each independently.
Routing: classify listing category first, then apply a category-specific removal prompt.

explain:
Voting runs the same task multiple times to raise confidence, which is exactly what an asymmetric cost structure calls for: disagreement between runs becomes the signal to escalate rather than auto-remove. That directly reduces the expensive false positive while keeping recall high enough to satisfy the regulatory concern. Sectioning would be the choice if the task decomposed into genuinely independent subtasks, which it does not.

Distractor notes:
B: Splitting the policy into parts is sectioning applied to the wrong axis. Each call would lack the policy context needed to judge, and unioning flags maximises false positives, the outcome you are trying to avoid.
C: Splitting the listing into fields loses cross-field signal, which is where many violations actually live, for example a benign title with a violating image.
D: Routing is appropriate when categories need different handling. The scenario states the same judgement applies to every listing, so the category split adds machinery without addressing the error asymmetry.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

verdict.note: The key is right. Start with the simplest pattern that could work and add autonomy only when evals show it falls short, and build the eval set first so every step up is measured. The eval set presupposes agreed success criteria (portal T-LATER). Irreversible refund writes are the last capability to automate, and frameworks that hide the context window make agents harder to debug.

stem:
A retailer's support leadership has asked for an agentic assistant that can read order history, issue refunds and update addresses. The team has never shipped an LLM feature, has no evaluation harness, and has committed to a demo in five weeks. An architect is asked whether to start with the full agent.

Which TWO recommendations best reflect sound architectural sequencing here? (Select TWO)

options.text: Start with the simplest composable pattern that could work, and add agentic autonomy only when the simpler approach demonstrably falls short.
Build the evaluation set first so that any later increase in system complexity can be justified by a measured improvement.
Implement the full tool-using agent immediately, since retrofitting autonomy later requires rewriting the orchestration layer.
Adopt a framework that abstracts the agent loop so the team never has to reason about what is in the context window.
Give the agent write access to refunds from day one so that the demo shows end-to-end value.

explain:
The consistent guidance is to start with simple prompts, optimise them against comprehensive evaluation, and add multi-step agentic systems only when simpler solutions fall short. For a team with no eval harness, building the evaluation set first is what turns later complexity decisions into evidence-based ones rather than taste. Both recommendations also fit the five-week constraint far better than a full agent build.

Distractor notes:
C: This inverts the guidance and assumes a rewrite cost that good decomposition avoids. A routing or chaining implementation can be extended into an agent loop without discarding the tool layer.
D: Frameworks that hide the agent loop make it harder to see the exact prompt and context being sent, which is precisely what you need visibility into when debugging an agent's behaviour.
E: Irreversible write actions such as refunds are the last capability to automate, not the first. They would be appropriate once evaluation and approval gates exist.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

verdict.note: The key is right. The Citations feature returns cited_text with document and page locations, and the API guarantees those are valid pointers into the supplied documents, which no prompt instruction can do. Structured outputs guarantee only the JSON shape and return a 400 if combined with citations. A second-model check is a costlier after-the-fact control.

stem:
A medical device manufacturer answers regulator questions using a set of submitted PDFs. Every statement in a response must be traceable to an exact passage in a specific document, and the quality team must be able to click through to the page. The team currently prompts the model to 'quote the source' and finds the quotes are sometimes paraphrased or attributed to the wrong document.

What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Enable the Citations feature on the document blocks so the API returns cited text with document and page locations.
Add a stricter system prompt instructing the model to reproduce quotes verbatim and never paraphrase.
Use structured outputs with a JSON schema requiring a quote string and a page number per claim.
Post-process the response with a second model that checks each quote against the source documents.

explain:
Citations returns cited text blocks with concrete document and location pointers that the API guarantees are valid references into the supplied documents, which is stronger than any prompt-level instruction. For PDFs the locations are page numbers, exactly what the click-through requirement needs, and cited text does not count toward output tokens. It is also more reliable at selecting relevant quotes than prompting alone.

Distractor notes:
B: Prompting for verbatim quotes is a reasonable baseline and is what the team already does. It cannot guarantee the pointer is valid, which is the failure they are hitting.
C: Structured outputs guarantee the shape of the JSON, not the truth of the quote or page number inside it. It is also incompatible with citations in the same request.
D: A verification pass catches some errors but doubles cost and latency, and it is a compensating control for a problem the platform already solves natively.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations

verdict.note: The two keyed properties are real: a 50% discount and asynchronous processing within 24 hours. C, D and E are false: results come back in any order and are matched by custom_id, rate limits still apply, and batches do not stream. But prior-authorisation files are PHI, and the current data-retention docs list the Batch API as not HIPAA-eligible, so a HIPAA-enabled org gets a 400 (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/api-and-data-retention). The compliance gate comes before cost: this works only on de-identified files or through a HIPAA-eligible path.

stem:
A healthcare payer wants to re-summarise 2.4 million historical prior-authorisation files to populate a new analytics warehouse. The load runs once, there is no user waiting, the files are already in object storage, and finance wants the cheapest defensible option.

Which TWO properties of the Message Batches API make it the right fit here? (Select TWO)

options.text: Batch requests are priced at a 50% discount to the standard synchronous rates.
Batches are asynchronous with a processing window of up to 24 hours, which suits a job with no interactive consumer.
Batch requests are guaranteed to return in the same order they were submitted.
Batch requests bypass organisation rate limits entirely.
Batch requests support server-sent event streaming so progress can be shown per file.

explain:
The batch discount and the asynchronous processing window are the two properties that match a large one-off backfill with no user waiting, and prompt caching discounts stack on top. Most batches finish well inside the window, and results remain retrievable for a period after creation. Nothing about the workload needs synchronous behaviour.

Distractor notes:
C: Batch results can be returned in any order, which is why each request carries a custom_id you use to match results back to inputs.
D: Rate limits still apply to batch API calls and to in-flight requests. Batching changes price and latency expectations, not the existence of limits.
E: Streaming is not supported for batch requests; results are retrieved as a single results file once the batch ends.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

verdict.note: The key is right. At 46 tools the cause is catalogue size: it bloats every request's payload and widens the choice the model has to make. Scoping tools per domain behind specialist subagents fixes that cause. Longer descriptions and a generic dispatcher are mega-tool band-aids, and tool_choice any treats a symptom nobody reported. Deferred loading with tool search (CS-D3-18) is the other documented fix, but it is not among the options.

stem:
An energy utility's field-operations agent has grown to 46 tools across asset registry, work orders, weather, GIS and safety systems. Engineers report the agent now picks the wrong tool frequently, and every request carries a large tool-definition payload even for trivial questions.

Which architectural change addresses the root cause most directly?

options.text: Group the work into a small number of specialist subagents, each given only the tools for its domain, with the main agent delegating and receiving summaries.
Rewrite all 46 tool descriptions to be longer and more explicit about when not to use them.
Set tool_choice to any so the model must always select a tool rather than answering from memory.
Move all 46 tools behind a single generic execute_operation tool that takes the operation name as a parameter.

explain:
The failure is a context and action-space problem: 46 tool definitions in every request both crowd the context and widen the space the model must discriminate over. Decomposing into specialist subagents with scoped tool access shrinks both, and the summaries returned to the main agent keep its context clean. This is the standard remedy when an agent must interface with numerous complex tools.

Distractor notes:
B: Better descriptions genuinely help and would be the right first move at eight or ten tools, but at 46 longer descriptions make the payload problem worse while barely moving discrimination.
C: Forcing tool use addresses an agent that answers from memory when it should call a tool. That is not the reported symptom, and it will cause spurious calls on trivial questions.
D: A single generic dispatcher hides the schemas the model needs to call the operation correctly, trading a tool-selection problem for a parameter-hallucination problem.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

verdict.note: The key is right. The workload splits cleanly by difficulty, and the simple 80% also carries the tighter latency target. So serve it with the fastest small model and escalate only the rebookings. Capping output or caching the prefix cannot close a 3x gap on traffic dominated by input, and downgrading everything breaks the hard slice.

stem:
A travel platform handles 2 million support messages a month. Around 80% are simple intent classification and templated answers with a sub-second perceived latency target; the remaining 20% are multi-leg itinerary rebookings that need careful reasoning and tolerate several seconds. A single frontier model on everything would exceed the annual budget by roughly 3x.

What is the soundest model strategy?

options.text: Tier the workload: serve the high-volume simple path with the fastest small model and escalate only the complex path to a more capable model.
Serve everything with the most capable model but cap max_tokens aggressively to control spend.
Serve everything with the fastest small model and accept lower quality on rebookings.
Serve everything with the most capable model and enable prompt caching to bring the cost within budget.

explain:
Tiering matches model capability to task difficulty, which is where most of the cost-quality leverage is when a workload splits cleanly by complexity. The simple path also carries the tighter latency target, and the fastest model is the right answer for latency-critical work. Escalation keeps quality where it matters without paying frontier prices on the 80%.

Distractor notes:
B: Capping output tokens reduces cost somewhat but input tokens dominate in a classification-heavy workload, and truncating rebooking answers damages exactly the cases that need room.
C: Uniformly downgrading hits quality on the complex 20%, which is the segment where support failures are most expensive.
D: Caching is a strong lever and stacks with tiering, but a static shared prefix cannot close a 3x gap on its own when the variable per-message content is what drives volume.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview

verdict.note: The key is right. A breakpoint at the end of the 30k static system prompt lets every conversation and every turn read the same cached prefix. B's rationale is overstated, though: thanks to the 20-block lookback, a breakpoint on the latest message does hit the previous turn's entry within one conversation (the docs' multi-turn pattern). Alone, however, it never writes the system-only prefix, so different advisors' conversations cannot share it. Best practice is A plus a second breakpoint on the last message.

stem:
A wealth manager's advisor assistant sends a 30,000 token system prompt containing product rules and disclosure language, followed by a growing conversation. Every request re-reads the same 30,000 tokens. The team wants to cut input cost without changing behaviour.

Where should the cache_control breakpoint go?

options.text: At the end of the static system prompt, so the stable prefix is cached and the varying conversation follows it.
At the end of the most recent user message, so the entire request including the conversation is cached.
At the start of the system prompt, so caching begins as early as possible.
On each tool definition individually, so every tool is cached separately.

explain:
A cache breakpoint marks the end of a prefix, and only a prefix that is byte-identical across requests can be reused. Placing it at the end of the static system prompt captures the 30,000 stable tokens while letting the changing conversation sit outside the cached region. Cache reads are charged at a small fraction of base input price, so this is where nearly all the saving comes from.

Distractor notes:
B: Caching through the latest user message would be correct in a multi-turn design where you cache the growing history incrementally, but placed alone it means the prefix changes every turn and almost never hits.
C: A breakpoint at the start of the system prompt caches essentially nothing, since the cached region is everything up to and including the marked block.
D: Breakpoints are limited per request and tool definitions already sit in the earliest cacheable position. Marking each tool wastes breakpoints without extending the cached prefix.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

verdict.note: The key is right. The prefix is built as tools, then system, then messages, and the docs say any change to tool definitions invalidates the whole cache. Filtering the tools per request therefore forces a fresh write every time. A prompt below the minimum length would show zero cache creation and zero reads, not repeated writes. TTL expiry does not fit steady load, and caches are shared across requests.

stem:
A logistics agent caches a large static system prompt. The team also filters the tools array per request so the model only sees tools relevant to the current shipment mode. Monitoring shows cache_creation_input_tokens on nearly every request and almost no cache reads, despite the system prompt never changing.

What explains the near-zero cache hit rate?

options.text: Tool definitions sit before the system prompt in the cacheable ordering, so changing the tools array on each request invalidates the system prompt cache too.
The system prompt is below the minimum cacheable token length for the model in use.
The default cache lifetime is too short for the request rate, so entries expire between calls.
Cache entries are scoped per request and cannot be shared across separate API calls.

explain:
The cacheable prefix is built in the order tools, then system, then messages, and a change at any level invalidates that level and everything after it. Filtering the tools array per request therefore changes the very start of the prefix and forces a fresh cache write each time. The fix is to send a stable tool set and constrain selection through the prompt or tool_choice instead.

Distractor notes:
B: A minimum-length miss is a real failure mode, but it would show as no caching at all rather than repeated cache creation, and the prompt is described as large.
C: TTL expiry is plausible for sporadic traffic and is worth checking, but it would not explain a consistent pattern on an agent under steady load, and the described cause is upstream of it.
D: Caches are reusable across requests within the same scope; that is the entire point of the feature.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

verdict.note: The key is right. The thinking configuration is rendered into the prompt, so changing budget_tokens always invalidates message-level breakpoints. On models that render the configuration ahead of tools and system, it invalidates the system-prompt cache too. The docs' advice is to pick one budget and hold it stable. On 4.7 and later, budget_tokens is rejected and varying effort has the same effect. Thinking is billed at the normal output rate, caching works with thinking, and throttling would show up as 429s, not higher cost.

stem:
A credit risk agent uses extended thinking and a large cached system prompt. To control spend, an engineer added logic that scales the thinking budget with an estimated question difficulty, so the budget differs between requests. Cost went up rather than down.

What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Changing the thinking budget between requests invalidates the cached prefix, so every request pays a cache write instead of a cache read.
Extended thinking disables prompt caching entirely, so no requests were ever cached.
Thinking tokens are billed at a higher rate than ordinary output tokens, so variable budgets cost more on average.
Cache reads count toward input token rate limits, so the variable budget pushed the workload into throttling.

explain:
Thinking parameters participate in the cached prefix, so varying budget_tokens between requests produces a different prefix hash and forces a fresh cache write each time. With a large system prompt the write cost swamps whatever was saved by trimming reasoning on easy questions. The practical rule is to choose a budget and hold it stable for the life of the conversation.

Distractor notes:
B: Extended thinking and prompt caching work together; the interaction to watch is invalidation on parameter change, not wholesale incompatibility.
C: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens at the normal output rate, so there is no premium rate to blame.
D: For most current models cache reads do not count toward input-token-per-minute limits, and throttling would present as 429s rather than higher cost.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking

verdict.note: The key is right. This is context rot: recall and reasoning degrade as the window fills, so curate the smallest set of high-signal tokens instead of loading everything. That means retrieving just in time, pruning the examples to the ones that discriminate, and sending only the profile fields the task needs. Few-shot examples are not harmful in themselves, long context does not cause refusals, and latency does not cause wrong answers. Dropping the full citizen profile is also data minimisation (CS-D5-10).

stem:
A public sector case-handling assistant loads every policy document, the full user profile, all prior cases for the citizen and a 60-example few-shot block into every request, on the theory that more context is safer. Accuracy on a held-out set is worse than an earlier version that loaded far less.

Which principle best explains the regression and points at the fix?

options.text: Model performance degrades as the context window fills, so the goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens rather than the largest set of possibly relevant ones.
Few-shot examples always harm accuracy once the model has a system prompt, so they should be removed.
Long contexts exceed the model's training distribution and cause it to refuse, so requests should be split.
Loading many documents increases latency, and latency correlates with lower accuracy.

explain:
Context rot is the documented effect that recall and reasoning quality decline as the number of tokens in the window grows, because attention is a finite budget spread across every token. The remedy is curation: retrieve just in time, prune the example set to the ones that discriminate, and keep only the profile fields the task uses. More context is not free, and defaulting to maximal loading is the anti-pattern.

Distractor notes:
B: Few-shot examples remain one of the most effective techniques; the issue is 60 undifferentiated examples crowding the window, not examples as a category.
C: Long context does not cause refusals. The models here support very large windows, and the failure is graded degradation rather than a hard error.
D: Latency does rise with context length, but latency does not cause wrong answers. Conflating the two leads to the wrong remedy.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

verdict.note: The key is right. Server-side tool-result clearing drops old tool outputs once an input-token threshold is crossed (keeping the 3 most recent by default), while the client keeps the full history. The documented pairing with the memory tool warns Claude to save its findings before results are cleared. Two caveats: the memory tool stores data client-side, so 'server-side' is loose, and server-side compaction is now the docs' main strategy for long contexts. Lowering max_tokens, serialising tool calls and raising the thinking budget do not shrink the tool-result footprint.

stem:
A security operations agent triages alerts over shifts lasting several hours, calling log-search tools that return large payloads. It regularly approaches the context limit, and when it does the team restarts it, losing the investigation so far.

Which TWO server-side context management measures directly address this? (Select TWO)

options.text: Enable tool-result clearing so older tool outputs are removed from the prompt once an input-token threshold is crossed, keeping the most recent few.
Give the agent a memory tool so it can persist findings to files before older tool results are cleared.
Reduce max_tokens so each response is shorter and the conversation grows more slowly.
Disable parallel tool use so fewer tool results accumulate per turn.
Increase the thinking budget so the agent reasons more carefully about what to keep.

explain:
Tool-result clearing removes the bulk of what fills an agentic context, old tool outputs, while preserving the recent ones the agent is actively using, and it is applied before the prompt reaches the model so your client keeps the full history. Pairing it with a memory tool is the documented combination: the agent is warned as the threshold approaches and can write findings to durable files, so clearing does not destroy the investigation. Together they let a run continue past what would otherwise be a hard stop.

Distractor notes:
C: Shorter responses slow context growth marginally, but tool results dominate the footprint in this workload and are unaffected by max_tokens.
D: Serialising tool calls does not reduce the total volume of results, it only spreads them over more turns, and it makes the agent slower.
E: A larger thinking budget adds tokens to the turn rather than removing them, and the agent cannot prune its own prompt.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing

verdict.note: Citations and structured outputs can't be combined: turning on citations for document blocks while also setting output_config.format returns a 400 (both the citations and the structured-outputs docs say so, checked 2026-09). So chain them: a citation-enabled call returns source pointers the API has validated, then a schema-constrained call (or code) puts them into JSON. A schema 'quote' field only makes the field exist. It can't prove the quote is in the note.

stem:
A clinical documentation team needs each answer as strict JSON for downstream ingestion, and separately needs every clinical assertion to carry a verifiable pointer into the source note. An engineer configures a JSON schema output format and enables citations on the document blocks in the same request, and the API returns a 400.

What is the correct architectural response?

options.text: Split into two calls: one citation-enabled call to produce grounded prose with source pointers, and a second call that structures those results into the required JSON.
Keep both features enabled but relax the JSON schema by allowing additional properties.
Drop citations and require the schema to include a quote field and a character offset for each assertion.
Drop the JSON schema and parse the citation-enabled prose with a regular expression.

explain:
Structured JSON output and citations are mutually exclusive in a single request because schema-constrained decoding conflicts with the interleaved cited text blocks. Splitting into a grounding call followed by a structuring call preserves both guarantees: the first produces citations the API validates against the documents, the second produces JSON the schema validates. Each call keeps the property that the requirement actually depends on.

Distractor notes:
B: The incompatibility is between the two features, not a schema strictness setting, so loosening the schema does not clear the error.
C: A schema can force a quote field to exist but cannot verify that the quote appears in the source, which is the guarantee the clinical requirement needs.
D: Regex parsing of prose reintroduces exactly the fragility that structured outputs exist to remove, and it will break on the first unusual response.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

verdict.note: Anthropic's reduce-hallucinations guide recommends both. For long documents (>20k tokens), extract word-for-word quotes first and answer only from them. Also say explicitly that 'the document does not address this' is an allowed answer. Higher temperature, longer output and a persona add no grounding.

stem:
A law firm's assistant summarises 80-page discovery documents. Partners report occasional confident statements about clauses that do not exist in the document. The firm will not ship until this is materially reduced, and cost per document can rise moderately.

Which TWO techniques most directly reduce this failure? (Select TWO)

options.text: Instruct the model to first extract word-for-word quotes relevant to the question, then answer using only those quotes.
Explicitly permit the model to answer that the document does not address the question.
Raise the temperature so the model explores more phrasings before settling on an answer.
Increase max_tokens so summaries are longer and cover more of the document.
Add a role prompt describing the model as a meticulous senior litigator.

explain:
Quote extraction before answering grounds the response in text that actually exists in the document, which is the recommended technique for long documents. Explicitly giving the model permission to say it does not know removes the pressure to produce an answer when the document is silent, and it is one of the highest-yield single changes for hallucination rates. Both are cheap and compose well with each other.

Distractor notes:
C: Higher temperature increases variability and makes fabricated detail more likely, not less. Lower temperature would be the direction here.
D: Longer summaries give more surface area for unsupported claims. Length is not the constraint that produces the failure.
E: Role prompting shapes tone and framing and can help marginally, but it provides no grounding mechanism, which is what the failure requires.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

verdict.note: Make the instruction clear first. Every later technique amplifies what the instruction says, so examples of an underspecified task just teach the ambiguity. Once the task and output shape are explicit, few-shot examples (the portal's CS-D2-06 fix for format drift) are the natural second step. Tags help only when the model confuses content with instructions, and the stem doesn't report that.

stem:
A media company's summarisation prompt performs inconsistently. An engineer proposes, in order: adding a role description, adding four worked examples, wrapping the article and the instructions in distinct tags, and rewriting the instructions to state the exact output shape. The team can only do one thing before the next release.

Which should be done first?

options.text: Rewrite the instructions to be explicit and unambiguous about the task and the required output shape.
Add the role description, since persona framing sets the overall register.
Add the four worked examples, since examples subsume written instructions.
Wrap the inputs in tags, since structure is what the model attends to most.

explain:
Clarity is the first technique to apply because every later technique amplifies whatever the instructions say; examples of an ambiguous task teach an ambiguous task. Explicit statements of the task and the required output shape usually produce the largest single improvement and cost nothing at inference time. Examples, structure and role framing are then applied on top of a clear instruction, not as substitutes for one.

Distractor notes:
B: Role prompting is a legitimate technique but it shapes register rather than resolving what the task actually is, so it rarely fixes inconsistency on its own.
C: Examples are powerful and would be the right second step, but examples of an underspecified task encode the ambiguity rather than removing it.
D: Tagging inputs is genuinely useful once prompts get long and mix content with instructions, and would be the right move if the model were confusing article text with directives. That is not the stated symptom.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

verdict.note: Many clients, central authentication, per-user authorization and a single audit point all point to a remote Streamable HTTP MCP server behind the existing gateway. Each user gets an OAuth token issued for that server; the server validates the audience and never passes the token on. stdio only works between processes on one machine, and a shared service credential removes per-user authorization and attribution.

stem:
An investment bank wants to expose an internal positions service to Claude for 600 analysts across three offices. Security requires centralised authentication, per-user authorisation and a single audit point. The service already runs behind the bank's API gateway.

Which MCP deployment shape fits these requirements?

options.text: A remote MCP server using the Streamable HTTP transport, fronted by the gateway with OAuth-issued bearer tokens.
A local MCP server distributed to each analyst's laptop and launched over the stdio transport with a shared service credential.
A local stdio MCP server on each laptop that opens a direct database connection using the analyst's own credentials.
A remote MCP server using stdio over an SSH tunnel from each analyst workstation.

explain:
Streamable HTTP is the transport designed for remote servers serving many clients, and it supports standard HTTP authentication with OAuth-obtained tokens, which is what centralised authn, per-user authz and a single audit point require. Running it behind the existing gateway reuses the bank's control plane rather than duplicating it. Local stdio servers serve a single client per process and put the trust boundary on each laptop.

Distractor notes:
B: A shared service credential destroys per-user authorisation and attribution, and distributing a server binary to 600 laptops multiplies the patching surface.
C: Direct database access from a laptop bypasses the gateway entirely, so there is no single audit point and no central policy enforcement.
D: stdio is a local process transport for communication on the same machine; tunnelling it does not make it the remote transport, and it inherits none of the HTTP authorisation model.

Reference: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture

verdict.note: A server may return a different tool list per caller: the 2026-07-28 MCP caching spec uses cacheScope 'private' for filtered lists that vary per user. Declare tools.listChanged and send notifications/tools/list_changed on the client's subscriptions/listen stream, so a tier change takes effect without a restart. Hiding tools isn't enough on its own; the server must still reject a tools/call for an unlicensed tool.

stem:
A SaaS vendor ships an MCP server that its enterprise customers connect to. Each customer's client must only see the tools their licence tier includes, and tiers change during the contract year without a client restart.

Which protocol mechanism should the design rely on?

options.text: Return a tier-filtered tools list from tools/list, declare the tools listChanged capability, and emit a tools list changed notification when the tier changes so clients refresh.
Return every tool from tools/list and reject unlicensed calls at tools/call with an error.
Encode the licence tier in each tool's input schema and let the model decide which tools it is allowed to use.
Publish one MCP server binary per tier and have customers reinstall when their tier changes.

explain:
Tool listings in MCP are dynamic by design: the server returns whatever tools/list should expose for that caller, and change notifications exist so clients can refresh when the set changes. Declaring the listChanged capability and emitting the notification lets a tier change take effect without a restart. Notifications are best effort, so clients should also re-poll, but the mechanism is the right one.

Distractor notes:
B: Exposing every tool and failing at call time wastes context on tool definitions the customer cannot use and leaks the product roadmap. It is a reasonable fallback only where filtering is impossible.
C: Licence enforcement must be server side. Putting the tier in a schema and trusting the model to respect it is not an authorisation control.
D: Shipping a binary per tier is the workaround you would choose if the protocol had no dynamic listing, which it does. It also forces exactly the restart the requirement forbids.

Reference: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture

verdict.note: MCP servers expose three primitives. Tools are functions the model calls to take action (create a work order). Resources are context data the application supplies (the equipment hierarchy). Prompts are templates the user invokes (the troubleshooting interview). This is Foundations content, applied here to server design.

stem:
A manufacturer is designing an MCP server over its maintenance system. It needs to expose: the ability to create a work order, the current equipment hierarchy that the model should be able to read as reference material, and a standard troubleshooting interview template that engineers invoke by name.

Which THREE mappings to MCP primitives are correct? (Select THREE)

options.text: Creating a work order is a tool, because tools are executable functions the model invokes to take action.
The equipment hierarchy is a resource, because resources are data sources that supply contextual information.
The troubleshooting interview template is a prompt, because prompts are reusable templates that structure an interaction.
The equipment hierarchy should be a tool, because any data the model reads must be fetched through a tool call.
Creating a work order should be a prompt, because it is a repeatable operator workflow.
The troubleshooting template should be a resource, because it is static text stored on the server.

explain:
MCP servers expose three primitives with distinct roles: tools are executable functions that perform actions, resources are data sources that provide contextual information, and prompts are reusable templates that structure interactions. Creating a work order changes state and is therefore a tool, the equipment hierarchy is reference data and is therefore a resource, and a named interview template that a user invokes is a prompt. Getting these boundaries right is what makes a server predictable for any client.

Distractor notes:
D: Resources exist precisely so that contextual data does not have to be modelled as a tool call. Forcing all reads through tools would be the right shape only on a client that supports tools alone.
E: Prompts do not execute actions; they template an interaction. A state-changing operation exposed as a prompt has no execution semantics.
F: Storing the template as a resource makes it data the model may read, not something a user can invoke by name, which is the stated requirement.

Reference: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture

verdict.note: Anthropic's tool-writing guidance says to build tools around the workflow, for example schedule_event instead of list_users, list_events and create_event. One schedule_interview tool keeps the intermediate results out of context and removes the chance to stall halfway through the chain. This isn't the mega-tool trap: A is one typed tool for one job, unlike D's single free-text parameter.

stem:
A staffing agency's scheduling agent must book interviews. The current tool set is list_candidates, list_interviewers, get_availability, create_calendar_event and send_invite. Traces show the agent frequently succeeds on the first four calls then stalls, and each booking consumes far more context than expected.

What is the most effective redesign?

options.text: Consolidate the sequence into a higher-level schedule_interview tool that performs the lookups and the booking internally.
Keep the five tools and add a sixth tool that returns the recommended calling order.
Keep the five tools and force the sequence with tool_choice on each turn from application code.
Merge the five tools into one tool whose single parameter is a natural language instruction.

explain:
Tools should be built around the workflow an agent is actually trying to complete rather than around the underlying API's individual endpoints. Consolidating the chain into one schedule_interview tool removes four round trips, four sets of intermediate results from the context, and four opportunities for the agent to lose the thread. This is the standard remedy when traces show an agent chaining low-level primitives.

Distractor notes:
B: A tool that documents ordering adds another call and another payload while leaving the underlying chain intact. Ordering guidance belongs in tool descriptions, not in a tool.
C: Driving the sequence from application code is a valid design, but it is a workflow rather than an agent, and it does not reduce the context cost of the intermediate results.
D: A single free-text tool discards the typed schema that makes tool calls reliable, converting a tool-selection problem into a parsing problem on the server.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

verdict.note: Return only the data the agent needs, per Anthropic's 'Writing tools for agents'. That means pagination and filtering with sensible defaults, readable identifiers next to the technical ID, and a response_format parameter (concise or detailed). Bare UUIDs force an extra lookup per record. Silent truncation hides what was cut; a truncated response should tell the agent how to narrow its query.

stem:
A CRM MCP server exposes a search_contacts tool that returns full contact records including UUIDs, all custom fields and the complete activity history. The agent typically needs a name, an owner and an ID to pass to the next call. Runs frequently hit the context limit after a handful of searches.

Which set of changes best fits the guidance on writing tools for agents?

options.text: Paginate and filter by default, return semantically meaningful identifiers alongside technical IDs, and add a response_format parameter offering concise or detailed output.
Return the full record but compress it to minified JSON to save tokens.
Return only UUIDs and require the agent to call a second tool to resolve each one to a name.
Truncate every response at a fixed character count with no explanation.

explain:
The guidance is to return only high-signal information, with pagination, filtering and sensible defaults, and to let the agent choose verbosity through a response_format parameter when it genuinely needs the detail. Returning human-meaningful identifiers rather than bare UUIDs keeps the agent oriented while still supplying the technical ID needed for downstream calls. Together these cut the payload without removing the agent's ability to complete the task.

Distractor notes:
B: Minifying JSON saves a small percentage of tokens while leaving the real problem, which is that most of the payload is information the agent does not use.
C: Stripping to UUIDs forces an N+1 pattern of resolution calls, which costs more round trips and more context than returning a name in the first place.
D: Silent truncation is worse than the original problem: the agent cannot tell that data was cut, so truncated responses should include guidance steering toward a more targeted query.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

verdict.note: Five tools all named 'search' can't be told apart. The documented fix is to prefix names by service and resource (jira_issues_search, confluence_pages_search) and give each a description that says what it's for. More reasoning can't separate identical interfaces, and deleting integrations removes capability users need.

stem:
A platform team connects five MCP servers to one assistant: Jira, Confluence, GitHub, Snowflake and an internal deployment service. Each exposes a tool called search. Users report the assistant frequently searches the wrong system.

What is the most appropriate remedy?

options.text: Namespace tool names by service and resource, for example jira_issues_search and confluence_pages_search, and make each description state what the tool is for.
Remove four of the five search tools and route all searching through one server.
Increase the thinking budget so the model reasons longer about which search to call.
Instruct the model in the system prompt to always ask the user which system to search.

explain:
Namespacing groups related tools under common prefixes and is the recommended way to delineate boundaries when many tools coexist, particularly when several servers expose the same generic verb. Naming by service and resource makes the correct choice legible from the name alone, before the model even reads the description. Clear per-tool descriptions then handle the remaining ambiguity.

Distractor notes:
B: Consolidating behind one federating server can be a good design, but discarding four integrations to fix a naming collision removes capability the users need.
C: More reasoning cannot disambiguate five tools that are genuinely indistinguishable by name and description. Fix the interface, not the deliberation.
D: Asking the user every time pushes the cost of the design flaw onto the user and destroys the assistant's usefulness for multi-system questions.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents

verdict.note: Per the rate-limits doc (checked 2026-09), on most current models only input_tokens after the last cache breakpoint and cache_creation_input_tokens count toward ITPM. cache_read_input_tokens don't; Haiku 3.5 is the exception. Caching the identical 180k-token prefix therefore turns most of each request into reads that don't count. Splitting requests or moving blocks sends the same tokens, and a larger context window fixes a per-request limit, not a per-minute one.

stem:
A media monitoring product sends a 180,000 token editorial guideline corpus with every classification request. At peak it issues 900 requests a minute and starts receiving 429 responses on input tokens per minute, well below its request-per-minute ceiling. The corpus is identical on every request.

Which change is most likely to relieve the input token limit?

options.text: Cache the corpus behind a breakpoint, since on most current models tokens served from cache do not count toward the input tokens per minute limit.
Split each request into two calls, each carrying half the corpus, so no single request is as large.
Move the corpus from the system block into the first user message.
Switch to a model with a larger context window.

explain:
Input token rate limits are assessed on uncached input for most current models: tokens read from cache do not count, while cache writes do. Caching a large identical prefix therefore converts nearly all of that 180,000 tokens per request into non-counting reads and can multiply effective throughput several times over. It also cuts cost at the same time.

Distractor notes:
B: Splitting a request in half doubles the request count and sends the same total tokens per minute, so the input token limit is unaffected.
C: Where the corpus sits in the request does not change how many input tokens are billed or counted; it only changes the caching prefix order.
D: A larger context window raises how much you can send per request. It is the right answer when you are hitting a per-request limit, not a per-minute one.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits

verdict.note: The binding constraint is a 60-second load-balancer timeout on a long generation that a person is waiting for. Streaming sends bytes continuously and shows the first tokens quickly. The errors doc recommends it for long requests because some networks drop idle connections. Batch can't serve a citizen who is waiting, and cutting reasoning trades answer quality for a transport problem.

stem:
A government benefits portal generates long eligibility explanations. Requests sometimes take over a minute, and the team's load balancer terminates connections at 60 seconds, producing errors that the user sees as a blank screen even though generation was progressing normally.

What is the correct remedy?

options.text: Stream the response so tokens are delivered incrementally and the connection stays active throughout generation.
Increase max_tokens so the model finishes the explanation in a single fast pass.
Move the workload to the batch API so the timeout no longer applies.
Reduce the thinking budget to zero so generation always finishes inside 60 seconds.

explain:
Streaming delivers incremental events as generation proceeds, which both keeps the connection active past intermediary timeouts and drastically improves perceived responsiveness by showing the first tokens quickly. Long single-shot generations are the canonical case for enabling it. The user-visible symptom, a blank screen followed by an error, is precisely what streaming removes.

Distractor notes:
B: Raising max_tokens lets responses get longer, which makes the timeout more likely rather than less.
C: Batch is asynchronous and appropriate when nobody is waiting. Here a citizen is waiting on a portal, so a 24 hour window is not acceptable.
D: Cutting reasoning to fit an infrastructure timeout trades answer quality for a problem the transport layer should solve.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming

verdict.note: Upload the PDF once through the Files API (now out of beta) and reference its file_id. File content is still billed as input tokens, so the cost and latency saving comes from a cache breakpoint after the document block, which turns each follow-up into a cache read. Batch can't serve an interactive session. Caveat: the Files API isn't ZDR-eligible, so an engagement that requires ZDR would send the document inline and still cache it.

stem:
An audit firm's assistant answers follow-up questions about the same 200-page engagement PDF across a long session. The current implementation base64-encodes and uploads the PDF in every request. Latency and cost per follow-up are far higher than expected.

Which change addresses this best?

options.text: Upload the PDF once through the Files API and reference it by file_id in subsequent requests, with a cache breakpoint after the document block.
Convert the PDF to plain text on the client and send only the pages a keyword search suggests are relevant.
Switch the follow-up questions to the batch API to get the 50% discount.
Reduce the image resolution of the PDF pages before encoding them.

explain:
The Files API lets you upload a document once and reference it by identifier on later requests, removing the repeated upload from the request path. Adding a cache breakpoint after the document block means the document's tokens are served as cache reads on each follow-up rather than reprocessed, which is where the cost and latency go in a long session. The two features are designed to compose.

Distractor notes:
B: Client-side keyword selection is a reasonable strategy for a very large corpus, but here it risks dropping the page the auditor is asking about, and a 200-page document fits comfortably in context.
C: Batch would halve the price but is asynchronous, which is unusable for an interactive follow-up session.
D: Lowering page image quality reduces tokens somewhat but degrades extraction accuracy on exactly the dense financial tables an audit assistant must read.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files

verdict.note: The question asks for a 'platform feature', and the side effect can't be undone. strict: true constrains decoding so tool names and inputs match the schema: right types, required fields present. Also keep validation in the tool handler before the payment intent is created, because strict mode doesn't enforce numeric or string constraints such as minimum or maxLength. C loses only because it corrects after the fact, not because validating in code is wrong.

stem:
A payments platform calls a submit_payment tool. Occasionally the model produces a call with the amount as a string, or omits the currency, and the downstream service rejects it after the payment intent has already been created, leaving orphaned records.

Which platform feature most directly prevents this class of failure?

options.text: Mark the tool as strict so tool names and inputs are constrained to conform to the declared schema.
Add examples of well-formed calls to the tool description.
Validate the arguments in application code and send a corrective follow-up message when they are wrong.
Lower the temperature to reduce variability in the generated arguments.

explain:
Strict tool use constrains generation so that the tool name and input conform to the declared schema, which turns a probabilistic formatting problem into a guarantee. That is the right control when a malformed call has side effects that are expensive to unwind. Application-level validation remains good practice but should not be the only line of defence.

Distractor notes:
B: Examples improve the odds and cost nothing at request time, but they are a soft control and leave a residual failure rate on a path with irreversible side effects.
C: A corrective round trip is the right pattern when strict mode is unavailable or the schema is too complex to compile, but it happens after the orphaned record has been created.
D: Temperature affects sampling variety, not schema conformance, and lowering it does not make a type error impossible.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

verdict.note: The MCP client best practices (2026-07-28) recommend progressive tool discovery, such as a search_tools meta-tool, once tool definitions take up a real share of the context window; they suggest a threshold of 1-5%. Change notifications are opt-in through subscriptions/listen and explicitly best effort, so clients should also respect ttlMs freshness and re-fetch. A list cached forever goes stale; newly found definitions can be added after the cache breakpoint instead.

stem:
An internal developer platform federates 18 MCP servers into one assistant. Loading every tool from every server at session start consumes a large share of the context window before the user has typed anything, and several servers change their tool sets during the day.

Which TWO approaches are consistent with MCP client best practice here? (Select TWO)

options.text: Discover tools progressively rather than loading every server's full tool list up front.
Subscribe to tool list changed notifications where servers support them, while still re-polling periodically because notification delivery is best effort.
Cache the first tools/list response permanently and never refresh it, to keep the prefix stable for prompt caching.
Require every federated server to expose fewer than five tools as a platform standard.
Ask the model to call tools/list itself as its first action in every session.

explain:
Clients that federate many servers are advised to discover tools progressively instead of loading everything at startup, which is exactly the context pressure described. For freshness, servers can declare a listChanged capability and clients can open a notification subscription, but notifications are explicitly best effort across transport reconnects, so periodic polling remains necessary. Together these keep the tool set both small and current.

Distractor notes:
C: Permanently caching the tool list keeps the prefix stable but guarantees stale tools, which is the opposite of the requirement that servers change during the day.
D: Capping tools per server is a governance idea that would sidestep the symptom, but 18 servers at five tools each is still 90 tools, and it constrains legitimate server design.
E: tools/list is a client-side protocol call, not something the model invokes. Making discovery a model action wastes a turn and does not reduce what is loaded.

Reference: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture

verdict.note: Anthropic's eval guidance says to design evals that mirror the real task distribution (edge cases included), automate grading, and 'prioritize volume over quality'. A larger set that grades itself automatically can be re-run on every prompt change, which is the regression check leadership wants. Still set a pass threshold before the first run (L7).

stem:
A utility company's outage-notification summariser is going to production in three weeks. The team has hand-written 12 test cases and grades them by reading each output. Leadership wants confidence that a prompt change has not regressed anything, and the team can spend about two days on evaluation.

How should they spend those two days?

options.text: Generate a much larger set of cases that mirror the real input distribution and structure them so most can be graded automatically.
Expand to 25 hand-graded cases, prioritising depth of human judgement over volume.
Keep the 12 cases and run each one five times to measure variance.
Replace the test cases with a production canary and judge quality from customer complaints.

explain:
Eval guidance is explicit that volume matters more than perfection: a larger set with slightly noisier automated grading beats a small set of immaculate hand-graded examples, because it covers more of the real distribution and can be re-run on every change. Mirroring the actual input distribution, including edge cases, is what makes the signal trustworthy. Automating the grading is what makes regression testing possible at all inside a three-week timeline.

Distractor notes:
B: Hand grading is the highest-quality method but does not scale, and 25 cases still will not cover the distribution. It is the right fallback only when nothing else can judge the output.
C: Measuring variance on 12 cases tells you about stability on 12 cases. It does not extend coverage, which is the actual gap.
D: A production canary measures real users but detects regressions after customers have experienced them, which is unacceptable for outage notifications.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

verdict.note: Anthropic's grading tips are a detailed, specific rubric, a constrained verdict (correct/incorrect or a 1-5 scale), and reasoning before the score, with the reasoning then discarded. Put the compliance team's criteria into the rubric, then check the grader agrees with their labels before trusting it (CS-D4-05). The docs also advise grading with a different model from the one that generated the output, which rules out D.

stem:
A bank uses a model-based grader to score complaint-response drafts. Reviewers find the grader inconsistent: identical drafts receive different verdicts on re-runs, and its scores correlate poorly with the compliance team's own assessments.

Which change to the grader design is most likely to fix this?

options.text: Replace the open-ended quality question with a concrete rubric and a constrained output, and have the grader reason before emitting the verdict.
Increase the grader's temperature so it explores more interpretations before deciding.
Ask the grader to return a free-text paragraph of feedback instead of a score.
Use the same model and the same prompt as the generator so the grader shares its understanding of the task.

explain:
Model-based grading becomes reliable when the rubric is detailed and empirical and the output is constrained, for example a correct or incorrect verdict or a defined scale, rather than an open-ended judgement of quality. Asking the grader to reason first and then emit the verdict improves performance on complex judgements, and the reasoning can be discarded. Encoding the compliance team's actual criteria into the rubric is also what closes the correlation gap.

Distractor notes:
B: Higher temperature increases the inconsistency the team is complaining about. Graders should be run at low variance.
C: Free-text feedback is useful for humans but cannot be aggregated into a regression metric, which is the grader's purpose.
D: Sharing the generator's prompt makes the grader inherit the generator's blind spots and biases, so agreement rises while validity falls.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

verdict.note: This follows the develop-tests guide. Code-based exact match is the fastest and most reliable grader when there is one right answer, like the ICD-10 code. A rubric-based LLM grader suits tone and empathy, once it has been checked against human labels. The guide calls human grading 'slow and expensive. Avoid if possible', so keep humans for calibration and high-stakes spot checks.

stem:
A healthcare intake assistant is evaluated on two dimensions: whether the extracted ICD-10 code exactly matches the coder's gold answer, and whether the patient-facing summary reads with appropriate empathy and avoids alarming language.

Which TWO grading choices are appropriate? (Select TWO)

options.text: Grade the ICD-10 code with code-based exact matching against the gold answer.
Grade the empathy and tone dimension with a model-based grader using a written rubric.
Grade the ICD-10 code with a model-based grader so near-miss codes get partial credit.
Grade the empathy dimension with exact string matching against approved phrasings.
Grade both dimensions by human review only, since clinical content is involved.

explain:
Code-based grading is the fastest and most reliable method and is the right choice wherever the judgement is rule-based, which an exact code match is. Tone and empathy are nuanced judgements that no deterministic rule captures well, which is where model-based grading with a clear rubric earns its place. Matching the grading method to the nature of each judgement is the core skill being tested.

Distractor notes:
C: Partial credit for near-miss codes sounds generous but a wrong ICD-10 code is wrong for billing and clinical purposes, and using a model here introduces noise into the one dimension that is objectively checkable.
D: Exact matching against approved phrasings would force a fixed script and would fail any acceptable paraphrase, so it measures conformity rather than empathy.
E: Human review gives the highest quality but does not scale and cannot be run on every change, so it should be reserved for cases the other methods cannot judge.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

verdict.note: The constraint that decides this is that no baseline exists. Adding an orchestrator adds complexity (L4), and that has to be justified by a measured gain, so the first requirement is a representative eval set with the current single prompt scored on it (CS-D4-01 'unless': measure the baseline first). Load tests and cost models are later gates, and a design doc produces no evidence.

stem:
A team proposes moving their document assistant from a single prompt to an orchestrator with four specialist workers, arguing it will be more accurate. They have no eval set and are working from a handful of anecdotal failures reported in Slack.

What should the architect require before approving the change?

options.text: An eval set representing the real task distribution, with the current single-prompt system scored on it as the baseline.
A load test showing the orchestrator can meet the latency target at peak volume.
A written design document describing how the four workers divide the task.
A cost model showing the orchestrator's projected token spend.

explain:
Added complexity has to be paid for with measured improvement, and without a baseline there is no way to tell whether the orchestrator helps, hurts or merely changes which cases fail. Anecdotal Slack reports are a source of eval cases, not evidence of a systemic gap. Building the eval first also often reveals that a prompt fix closes most of the gap at a fraction of the cost.

Distractor notes:
B: Load testing matters and would be a gate before release, but it answers whether the design is fast enough, not whether it is better.
C: A design document clarifies intent but does not produce evidence. It is necessary later, not sufficient now.
D: A cost model is one half of a cost-benefit case; without a measured benefit there is nothing to weigh it against.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

verdict.note: An agent eval should grade the end state against explicit criteria, because many valid tool paths lead to an equally good shortlist. Step count and tool error rate are useful as diagnostics, not as pass conditions (Anthropic multi-agent research write-up). Temperature 0 does not make trajectories deterministic once tool results vary, an order-free tool-set check is still a process assertion, and weekly human sampling cannot gate a change.

stem:
A procurement agent researches suppliers and produces a shortlist. The team's current eval asserts an exact expected sequence of tool calls. It fails constantly because the agent reaches equally good shortlists by different routes, and engineers now ignore the eval.

How should the eval be restructured?

options.text: Grade the end state against criteria the shortlist must satisfy, and separately track trajectory metrics such as tool error rate and step count as diagnostics rather than pass conditions.
Pin the agent's temperature to zero so the trajectory becomes deterministic and the existing assertions pass.
Assert on the set of tools used, ignoring order, so any permutation passes.
Replace automated evaluation with weekly human review of a sample of runs.

explain:
Agentic evaluation should judge whether the agent reached an acceptable end state, because many valid paths lead to the same good outcome and asserting on one of them produces a brittle test that engineers learn to ignore. Trajectory data is still valuable, but as diagnostics that explain why a run was slow or expensive rather than as pass criteria. Separating outcome grading from process telemetry is what makes an agent eval durable.

Distractor notes:
B: Zero temperature does not make an agent deterministic once tool results and external systems vary, and it would mask legitimate path diversity rather than evaluate outcomes.
C: Order-insensitive tool-set assertions are still process assertions, and they break as soon as the agent legitimately solves a case with one fewer tool.
D: Human review is a useful complement for catching edge cases, but weekly sampling cannot gate a change and does not restore the regression signal.

Reference: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

verdict.note: TTFT (4.9 of 6.2 s) is the dominant term, so trimming unused prompt content attacks it directly (L6). Streaming fits because a person is watching (CS-D3-07 'unless'). Caution: the item's rationale overstates streaming. It only removes the roughly 1.3 s after the first token and cannot turn the 4.9 s blank screen into an immediate response; prompt caching (not offered) is the other TTFT lever.

stem:
A retail chat assistant is judged too slow by users. Instrumentation shows the median total generation time is 6.2 seconds and the median time to first token is 4.9 seconds. The product owner insists the answers themselves are the right length.

Which TWO changes address the reported experience most directly? (Select TWO)

options.text: Enable streaming so users see output as it is produced instead of waiting for the full response.
Shorten the prompt by removing redundant instructions and context that the task does not use.
Increase max_tokens so the model does not have to plan around a ceiling.
Move the workload to the batch API to reduce load on the synchronous endpoint.
Raise temperature so the model commits to a phrasing sooner.

explain:
Time to first token is nearly the whole of the perceived wait here, so streaming converts a 4.9 second blank screen into an immediate response. Prompt length is the main lever on the processing that precedes the first token, so trimming instructions and unused context reduces that wait rather than merely masking it. The product owner's constraint on answer length rules out output-shortening approaches, leaving these two.

Distractor notes:
C: max_tokens is a ceiling, not a target, and raising it cannot make generation start sooner.
D: Batch is asynchronous and unsuitable for an interactive chat assistant, whatever it does for backend load.
E: Temperature affects sampling diversity and has no meaningful bearing on time to first token.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-latency

verdict.note: A tier downgrade must clear the pre-agreed 2-point bar on the same held-out set (CS-D2-01, the cheapest tier that clears the eval bar). A fair comparison also gives the smaller model a prompt tuned for it. To keep the result attributable (CS-D4-08), score the small model with the unchanged prompt and then with the re-tuned one; quarter-long production monitoring and an eval filtered to incumbent passes cannot answer the question.

stem:
A subscription business wants to move its churn-reason classifier from a frontier model to the fastest small model to cut cost by roughly 70%. The classifier feeds a retention campaign, and the analytics team says a 2-point drop in macro F1 would be tolerable but a 6-point drop would not.

Which TWO steps make this a responsible experiment? (Select TWO)

options.text: Score both models on the same held-out eval set and compare against the stated 2-point tolerance before switching.
Re-tune the prompt for the smaller model rather than reusing the frontier model's prompt unchanged.
Switch in production and monitor campaign conversion for a quarter to see whether it moves.
Assume the smaller model is equivalent because it shares the same tokenizer and API surface.
Reduce the eval set to the cases the frontier model already gets right, to isolate the regression.

explain:
A model swap is a change like any other and needs a measured comparison on the same eval set against a pre-agreed tolerance, which the analytics team has helpfully supplied. Re-tuning the prompt matters because prompts optimised for one model are not automatically optimal for another, and a fair comparison should give each model a reasonable prompt. Together these tell you whether the 70% saving actually costs 2 points or 6.

Distractor notes:
C: Learning from campaign conversion takes a quarter and confounds model quality with a dozen other campaign variables, so it cannot answer the question in time.
D: Shared API surface says nothing about task accuracy; capability differences between model tiers are exactly what is being traded away.
E: Filtering the eval to cases the incumbent already passes builds in a bias and hides regressions on the harder cases that matter most.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview

verdict.note: The identical 40k-token taxonomy is about 96% of input, so caching it is the dominant lever and does not affect quality (cache reads are billed at a fraction of base input). The job is non-interactive, so Batch's 50% discount stacks on top (CS-D4-13, PF-API-02/03). A model downgrade is the only quality-affecting lever, so it goes last behind an eval gate; summarising the taxonomy both risks labels and breaks the stable prefix.

stem:
A media company must cut inference spend by 60% on a document-tagging pipeline. Each request carries an identical 40,000 token taxonomy plus a 1,500 token document. The pipeline runs nightly with no interactive consumer, and quality is currently acceptable.

Which sequence of optimisations should be attempted first, in order of expected saving per unit of risk?

options.text: Cache the taxonomy prefix, then move the nightly run onto the batch API, then consider a smaller model only if the target is still unmet.
Switch to the smallest model first, then cache the taxonomy, then move to batch.
Move to batch first, then reduce the taxonomy by summarising it, then cache what remains.
Reduce document length by pre-summarising each document, then cache the taxonomy.

explain:
Caching a 40,000 token identical prefix is the largest saving available and carries essentially no quality risk, since the content sent to the model is unchanged. Batch adds a further discount and the workload is already asynchronous, so it costs nothing but a scheduling change, and the two discounts stack. A model downgrade is the only lever that can change output quality, so it belongs last and behind an eval gate.

Distractor notes:
B: Downgrading the model first puts the one quality-affecting change ahead of two free ones, so you may pay a quality cost you did not need.
C: Summarising the taxonomy changes the classification labels the model can see and is a real accuracy risk, and it also destroys the stable prefix that makes caching effective.
D: Pre-summarising documents discards the detail the tagger needs and addresses the smaller share of tokens; the taxonomy is over 90% of each request.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

verdict.note: Both keyed measures come from Anthropic's 'Reduce hallucinations' guide. Best-of-N consistency across runs detects ungrounded claims, and a pass that finds a supporting quote for each claim (retracting any claim without one) prevents unsupported claims reaching the analyst; the 3x cost headroom pays for both. Caching is a cost lever for a constraint that is not binding, and forcing a confident tone removes the uncertainty signal.

stem:
A ratings agency's research summariser must not assert facts absent from the source filings. Cost per document may rise by up to 3x, and outputs are reviewed by an analyst before publication. The team wants a detection mechanism as well as a prevention one.

Which TWO measures fit this brief? (Select TWO)

options.text: Run the same prompt several times and flag documents where the outputs disagree on material facts.
Add a verification pass in which the model must locate a supporting quote for each claim and retract any claim it cannot support.
Increase the summary length so more of the filing is represented in the output.
Instruct the model to write in a more confident tone so analysts can spot hedged claims.
Cache the filings so repeated requests are cheaper.

explain:
Best-of-N style repetition is a detection mechanism: inconsistency across runs on the same input is a strong signal that a claim is not grounded in the source. A verification pass that requires a supporting quote for each claim, with retraction when none exists, is the prevention mechanism, and the stated 3x cost headroom accommodates both. The analyst review then operates on outputs that are already filtered rather than raw.

Distractor notes:
C: Longer summaries increase the number of assertions and therefore the number of opportunities to be wrong.
D: Encouraging confident tone removes the hedging that currently signals uncertainty, making unsupported claims harder to spot rather than easier.
E: Caching reduces cost but has no bearing on factual grounding, and cost is explicitly not the binding constraint here.

Reference: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

verdict.note: A forced model migration is a measured change: score the new model on the existing suite, study the regressions, adapt the prompt, re-measure, then cut over well inside the deprecation window. Cutting over on the date relies on production detection, and the rollback target disappears at retirement. An exception is not a plan, and a from-scratch rewrite throws away encoded domain knowledge.

stem:
A payments company pins a specific model snapshot in production. Anthropic announces that the snapshot will be retired, and the team must move to a newer model within the deprecation window. The prompt has been tuned over 14 months.

What is the right migration approach?
