A longer TTL, a trimmed block or packaging as a Skill all leave the ordering broken.

stem:
An analytics team reuses one prompt about 8,000 times a day. It opens with the customer record being analysed, then a 6,000-token block of fixed methodology and output schema. Costs are triple the projection and caching appears to do nothing.

What is the fix?

options.text: Extend the cache TTL
Shorten the methodology block to cut input tokens
Reorder so the fixed methodology and schema come first, with the record after the breakpoint
Package the prompt as a versioned Skill

explain:
Static before dynamic. This is the single most testable caching fact in the module, and the scenario telegraphs it: a large fixed block sitting behind a small variable one. At 8,000 calls a day against a 6,000-token prefix the saving is the whole point. Note what the other options are: each is a real technique that is right in a different situation, which is how distractors are built in this domain.

Per-option notes:
A: A longer TTL cannot help a prefix that is different on every single call. There is nothing stable to keep alive.
B: Trimming the methodology block reduces tokens but leaves the cache broken. It treats the symptom and abandons the largest available saving.
C: Caching matches on a stable prefix. With the per-customer record first, the prefix differs every call and nothing is reusable. Methodology and schema first, record after the breakpoint.
D: Packaging as a Skill addresses governance and distribution. It does not change the token ordering that is breaking the cache.

verdict.note: The stem says the existing AWS BAA already covers Bedrock, which clears the HIPAA gate. Bedrock carries its own compliance and sits outside Anthropic's API HIPAA scope (PF-GOV-03). Residency is the wrong regime, a second BAA duplicates cover the network already has, and Claude.ai Enterprise is a chat surface that does not fit an assistant embedded in clinical systems.

stem:
A healthcare network wants a clinical documentation assistant that processes patient records. The network already holds a BAA with AWS and has confirmed Bedrock is covered under it. A competing proposal suggests the direct Anthropic API with a separately negotiated BAA.

Which option names both the right choice and the deciding tradeoff?

options.text: Bedrock, because the deciding tradeoff is regulatory residency: it pins data to a US region
Bedrock, because the deciding tradeoff is governance: the existing BAA covers this configuration and eliminates the compliance risk first
The direct API with a new BAA, because the deciding tradeoff is control over how PHI flows
Claude.ai Enterprise with a BAA, because the deciding tradeoff is governance: Enterprise adds HIPAA-ready configuration

explain:
Bedrock, on governance. These items pair a choice with a reason and score the pair, so a right route with the wrong reason is wrong. The tell is that the scenario states the BAA already covers Bedrock. That is a constraint that has already eliminated options, and it outranks every preference in the room.

Per-option notes:
A: Bedrock is right, but the reason is wrong. Regional pinning addresses residency. HIPAA coverage is about whether a BAA covers this configuration, which is a governance question.
B: The existing BAA already covers this configuration, which removes the compliance risk before cost, latency or ergonomics are discussed. Governance eliminates options first.
C: Negotiating a second BAA adds time and risk to reach a position the network already holds. More control over PHI flow is not the binding constraint here.
D: Claude.ai Enterprise offers a HIPAA-ready option, but this is a documentation assistant embedded in clinical systems, not a chat product. The entry point does not fit the work.

verdict.note: In the course brief (not reproduced in this item), the senior associate is the fixed final reviewer. Auto-approving any clause category removes a stated requirement rather than tuning a variable, and only the owner can change it (L8, T-OWNER). Sampling and a well-evaluated classifier are sound in other settings but cannot override a fixed gate, and cost does not change.

stem:
Same firm, same brief. A fifth proposal arrives: API behind the approved gateway, parallelised clause review, playbook retrieved per clause, Sonnet with progressive context, iManage for fetch. The only change is that low-risk clause categories are auto-approved without associate review, to hit the 60 percent time saving more comfortably.

What does that change cost, and is it acceptable?

options.text: Acceptable, because sampling low-stakes work is exactly what the module recommends
Unacceptable, because it raises cost per contract above the target
Acceptable, provided an eval set confirms the low-risk classifier is accurate
Unacceptable, because the brief fixed the human gate and accountability sits with the reviewer

explain:
The gate was a requirement, not a preference. The strongest habit for this domain is to separate what the brief fixed from what it left to you. Fixed here: privilege, the gateway, iManage, the final reviewer. Left to you: pattern, sub-pattern, tier, context strategy, and where retrieval fits. An option that optimises a fixed constraint is wrong however sensible it sounds in isolation.

Per-option notes:
A: Sampling is the right tool for low-stakes actions, and the module recommends it. But the brief did not offer this gate as a variable, so redesigning it is answering a question nobody asked.
B: Cost is not what changed. Removing a review gate does not alter tokens, tier or context strategy.
C: Classification accuracy is a real risk, but the deciding objection is not measurement. It is that the brief fixed this gate as a requirement.
D: The brief states the senior associate remains the final reviewer. That is a stated requirement, not a tradeoff on the table, and in a privileged setting the reviewer is also the accountability answer.

verdict.note: The prompt changed to handle a new input class, but the 400-document golden set had no example of it. The 99.6% pass therefore measured the old behaviour. Refresh the set whenever the prompt's target inputs change, and score the new layout as its own slice (CS-D4-06, L7).

stem:
A bank's onboarding team runs a document extraction system with a full eval suite: 400 labelled identity documents, code-based checks on every field, a calibrated judge on the free-text notes. They revise the extraction prompt to handle a new passport layout. The suite passes at 99.6 percent. Ten days after release, operations report that dates of birth on the new layout are being read as issue dates.

What is the diagnosis?

options.text: The judge was not calibrated on the new layout
Field extraction should have been graded by a judge rather than in code
The golden dataset was not updated with the new layout when the prompt changed
The pass threshold of 99.6 percent was set too low

explain:
The dataset went stale. The prompt changed to handle an input class the golden dataset did not contain, so the suite went on measuring the old behaviour and passed. This is the contract-review Watch Out in a different industry: an eval suite that is present and out of date is the highest-risk configuration, because it looks like evidence.

Per-option notes:
A: The judge grades free-text notes. Dates of birth are structured fields under code-based checks, and those checks passed. Calibration is not the failing component.
B: Moving field checks to a judge would make them slower and less reliable. The field check was fine; it was checking the wrong set of documents.
C: The 400 documents predate the new layout, so the suite contains no example of the behaviour that changed. It passes because it tests the old system. The golden dataset moves with the prompt, or the pass means nothing.
D: A threshold is not the issue: the suite reported 99.6 percent on documents that did not include the failing case. Tightening it would not add the missing inputs.

verdict.note: The complaints come from the slow tail, which a median hides by construction. p95 measured under production concurrency is the SLA figure that settles the dispute (CS-D4-02). A single-user demo number and a 30-day mean say nothing about the slow minority, and cost does not answer a latency question.

stem:
A retailer's returns assistant reads a customer's message and a photo, and drafts a returns decision for an agent to send. In the demo it answers in 1.1 seconds. The production target is 2 seconds. The team reports that the median in production is 1.4 seconds and calls the target met. The agents' team lead says customers are complaining about waits.

Which measurement settles who is right?

options.text: The demo's 1.1 seconds, measured again on the production model
p95 latency under production concurrency
Mean latency over the last thirty days
Cost per request against the ceiling

explain:
p95 under concurrent load. A median of 1.4 seconds is compatible with a large minority of customers waiting five. The complaints live in the tail, and the design target for a user-facing path is the 95th percentile, not the middle of the distribution.

Per-option notes:
A: The demo ran one request at a time. Its latency describes a single-user, clean-input world and predicts nothing about concurrent load.
B: The complaints come from the slow tail, which the median hides by construction. p95 is the value 95 percent of requests finish under, and it is the number an SLA is written against.
C: The mean is dragged around by outliers and still says nothing about how many customers waited too long. It is not the SLA figure either.
D: Cost per request is a real production number, but it does not answer a latency dispute.

verdict.note: Sizing clears easily: about 150k short emails a month on a small tier costs a few hundred pounds against a £1,000 ceiling and fits in 10 s. Throughput is not the binding constraint; the writes to the order system are. The verdict is feasible with constraints: code-based checks on the structured fields plus a gate before anything is written. 'Low-confidence' must mean system signals such as validation failures or a calibrated classifier, never the model rating itself (T-SELFCONF).

stem:
A freight forwarder wants an assistant that reads unstructured emails from hauliers, extracts the delay reason and the revised arrival time, and writes both into the order-management system. About 5,000 emails a day, a 10-second target, and a £1,000 monthly ceiling.

Which option names the verdict and the constraint that makes it defensible?

options.text: Feasible as scoped: a cached prefix on Haiku copes with 5,000 a day inside 10 seconds
Not feasible: the volume is too high for the ceiling
Feasible with constraints: a code-based eval on extraction accuracy, and a human gate on low-confidence extractions before anything is written
Feasible with constraints: emails must be chunked to fit the window

explain:
Feasible with constraints, and the constraint is the write. A wrong arrival time in the order-management system has real downstream consequences, so the verdict is governed by extraction accuracy, not throughput. The control is a code-based eval on the structured output plus a review gate on anything the extractor is unsure of.

Per-option notes:
A: At this volume Haiku plus a cached prefix would cope. But throughput is not what governs this verdict. The verdict is governed by what happens when an extraction is wrong and gets written to the system of record.
B: 5,000 a day inside 10 seconds is comfortably achievable. Volume is not the binding constraint.
C: The load-bearing constraint is extraction accuracy on a transactional write. Dates and reasons are structured and scoreable against the source email, so a code-based eval fits, and low-confidence extractions need a human gate before the write.
D: Haulier emails are short. Working memory is not the property under pressure here; next-token prediction on exact values is.

verdict.note: Current market conditions are live state outside the training data, and the proprietary risk model lives in the firm's systems, so both need tool calls. Whether those round trips plus generation fit in 2 s must be measured before any verdict (CS-D1-04). A human gate on every recommendation cannot fit a 2 s budget and does not close the data gap, and Opus closes no knowledge gap. A's wording ('not feasible' yet 'validate before a verdict') is awkward, but it is the only option that names the binding constraint.

stem:
A wealth manager asks for an assistant that gives clients a recommendation on a holding based on current market conditions and the firm's proprietary risk model, delivered inside 2 seconds.

What is the feasibility call, and why?

options.text: Not feasible as described: the live-state knowledge gap means a tool call to a market feed, and whether that fits in 2 seconds has to be validated before a verdict
Feasible as scoped: the model knows current market conditions
Feasible with constraints: add a human gate on every recommendation
Feasible as scoped: move to Opus to handle the complexity

explain:
Not feasible as described, until the round trip is measured. The knowledge property is the disqualifier: the data is live, so it comes from a tool, and the tool's latency has to fit inside the 2-second budget. Issuing a verdict before that is measured is the scoping call that skipped the constraints.

Per-option notes:
A: Current market data is outside the model's training and is live state, so it needs a tool call to a live feed. Whether that round trip, plus the model's response, fits in 2 seconds must be tested before any verdict is issued.
B: Training data has a cutoff. Current prices, positions and conditions are outside it, always.
C: A human gate mitigates the risk of autonomous recommendations. It does not answer whether live market data can be fetched inside the latency budget, which is the constraint that decides feasibility.
D: Opus may be slower, not faster, and tier does not close a knowledge gap. The missing piece is the live data, not model capability.

verdict.note: Putting compliance first is right, but the key's reason is outdated. Anthropic's Public Sector FAQ (support.claude.com/en/articles/13756069, updated 2026-03-25) says Claude Enterprise meets CUI requirements under a third-party NIST 800-171r3 attestation and is appropriate for most state and local uses. Only FedRAMP-required workloads are limited to C4G, Bedrock GovCloud or Vertex Assured Workloads, and the attestation covers Claude Enterprise, not the direct API that the stem runs together with it. The stem never says this state agency needs FedRAMP, so the real first move is to confirm which authorisation its CUI obligations require. B is still the least-wrong option, since redaction, a BAA and inference_geo all address the wrong regime.

stem:
A state agency wants a Claude-based assistant to help caseworkers summarise files that contain controlled unclassified information. The vendor proposes Claude Enterprise on the direct API, on the grounds that the agency already has an enterprise agreement and the team knows the product.

What is the architect's first move?

options.text: Accept the route and add server-side redaction of CUI before each call
Rule the route out: it is not FedRAMP authorised, and only Claude for Government, Bedrock GovCloud or Vertex Assured Workloads at the right impact level survive
Sign a BAA with Anthropic covering the configuration
Set inference_geo to "us" so the data stays in-country

explain:
Rule the route out first. Compliance is layer one and it eliminates. Claude Enterprise over the direct API does not stand in for a FedRAMP-authorised path, and no downstream control (redaction, a BAA, a region setting) changes that. Identity, data handling and logging are designed afterwards, on whichever authorised route the agency approves.

Per-option notes:
A: Redaction is a real control and it comes later. It does not change the fact that the proposed route lacks the authorisation this workload requires.
B: Compliance eliminates routes before any other layer. Claude Enterprise over the direct API has no FedRAMP authorisation; the eligible paths are Claude for Government, AWS Bedrock GovCloud and Google Vertex Assured Workloads, at the required impact level.
C: A BAA is the HIPAA instrument. It has nothing to do with FedRAMP authorisation for a government workload.
D: Pinning execution to a US region does not confer FedRAMP authorisation, and inference_geo only takes us and global anyway.

verdict.note: A stable prompt, index and claim mix together with a changed model version is the model-update signature, so the model layer is the right suspect (T-LAYER rightWhen). Confirm it by running the eval suite on the old and new versions, then pin a dated snapshot or roll back. The stem's 'three weeks after' timing is ambiguous, so the eval comparison, not the timing, proves the cause.

stem:
Three weeks after a model version update, the claims assistant's field-accuracy metric drops four points. Nothing in the prompt, the retrieval index or the claim mix has changed on the dashboards the team checks. The cost per claim is unchanged.

Which attribution does the evidence point to, and what is the fix?

options.text: Data drift: the claim mix shifted, so rebuild the golden dataset
A model update effect: the new version behaves differently on the same inputs, so run the eval gate and pin or roll back the version
A prompt failure: tighten the extraction instruction
Hallucination: add a retrieval step to ground the extraction

explain:
Model update, and the eval gate should have caught it. The three causes look identical on a dashboard and have different fixes. Stable inputs and a changed version point to the update; the mitigation is model selection through the eval suite, with the version pinned in configuration as section 3 said.

Per-option notes:
A: Data drift means the inputs changed. The claim mix is unchanged on the evidence given, so this is not the first hypothesis.
B: Same inputs, same prompt, a new model version and a moved metric: that is the model update signature. The fix is model selection gated by the eval suite, which should have run before the version changed.
C: A prompt failure shows up when the instruction changes or was ambiguous from the start. The prompt did not change, and the metric was stable on it for weeks.
D: Grounding fixes hallucination, and hallucination is a class of failure, not a cause of a step change that coincides with a version update.

verdict.note: The check has a known answer (does another claim's identifier appear here), so a deterministic code scan is the right instrument (CS-D4-04). High stakes justify a zero-tolerance threshold and alerting, not a pricier grader. An Opus judge is slower and less consistent, human review of every claim does not scale, and dropping the check trusts a design nobody has verified.

stem:
A colleague reviewing your framework argues that cross-claimant leakage is the most serious failure the system could have, so it deserves the most capable grader: an Opus judge with a detailed rubric, run on every claim.

What is the right response?

options.text: Agree. The highest-stakes check deserves the most capable grader
Escalate it further: human review on every claim, since a leak is unacceptable
Keep it in code: the identifiers are known, so the check is deterministic, and stakes set the threshold, not the grader
Drop the check: the architecture isolates claims, so leakage cannot happen

explain:
Code, with a strict threshold. The grading method follows the shape of the check, and this check has a known answer: does any other claim's identifier appear here. Seriousness is expressed in the pass threshold (zero), the alerting, and the review policy when it trips, not by climbing the ladder to a grader that is slower and less consistent.

Per-option notes:
A: A judge would be slower, dearer and less consistent than a scan for identifiers that are already known. Capability is not the axis that decides grading method.
B: Human review does not scale to every claim, and it is not needed: the check is deterministic. Reserve people for calibrating the judge and sampling novel behaviour.
C: The identifiers from every other claim in the batch are known, so a function can scan each summary for them. Stakes justify a strict threshold and an alert, not a change of instrument.
D: Removing the check because the design should prevent leaks is the eval-suite-that-measured-the-wrong-thing pattern: a behaviour you cannot test is a behaviour you cannot verify.

verdict.note: Training covers broad harm, not this hospital group's triage protocol, and a system prompt only steers. Nothing enforces the rule until the prompt is paired with a runtime output check outside the generating model, plus review where the stakes are high (L3, CS-D2-04). Anthropic's usage policy governs what operators may do, not individual responses.

stem:
A hospital group deploys a Claude assistant for ward staff. Its system prompt says, at length, that the assistant must never advise outside the group's approved triage protocol. In testing, Claude also declines every dangerous request the team tries. The security lead asks which layer enforces the protocol rule.

What is the accurate answer?

options.text: Trained behaviour, as the refusals in testing show
The system prompt, since the rule is written there in full
Nothing yet. The prompt steers; enforcement needs an output check paired with it
Anthropic's usage policy, which the hospital agreed to

explain:
The prompt steers; nothing enforces. Training covers broad harm, and the refusals in testing prove only that. The protocol is a domain rule the model never saw. It becomes enforced when the system-prompt instruction is paired with a runtime control, an output check against the protocol, with a review gate where a wrong answer is costly. Until then the rule lives in no layer that can stop a violation.

Per-option notes:
A: Training reduces broad harm classes. A triage protocol is a domain policy specific to this hospital group, and the model has never seen it.
B: A system prompt steers behaviour inside a request. An adversarial or merely unusual input can talk the model out of it, so instruction alone is not enforcement.
C: Deployment-specific policy is enforced when the instruction is paired with a runtime control: here an output check against the protocol, with review where the stakes demand it.
D: Anthropic's usage policies govern what operators may do with the platform. They do not enforce a hospital's triage protocol on individual responses.

verdict.note: The instruction arrived in retrieved content after the query screen had already passed, and a schema validator does not judge what a summary says, so neither existing control sees it. Retrieved passages and tool outputs need their own screen before they enter the context (PF-GOV-07, CS-D5-04). The structural fix to add: keep session tokens out of the model's context entirely, so there is nothing to exfiltrate (T-BOUNDARY).

stem:
A legal-research assistant retrieves passages from a firm's document store and summarises them. A document in the store has had a line inserted: an instruction to ignore the system prompt and append the reader's session token to every summary. The design has a model-based input screen on the user's query and a deterministic validator on the output schema.

Which control catches the inserted instruction?

options.text: The input screen, since it is model-based and reads for injection
The output validator, since the summary would break the schema
Neither. Retrieved content needs its own screen before it enters the context
Tool-call authorization, because exfiltrating a token is an action

explain:
Neither existing control sees it. The instruction rode in on retrieved content, which the module names as the dominant injection vector wherever retrieval or tools are used. Input screening had already passed the clean query; a schema validator has no opinion about what the summary says. The missing control is a screen on retrieved content and tool outputs before they enter the context, and it belongs in the risk assessment as a named gap until it is built.

Per-option notes:
A: The user's query was clean. The input screen passed it, and the instruction arrived later, inside the retrieved passage.
B: A schema validator confirms the output has the right shape. A summary with a token appended can still be a valid summary.
C: Retrieved content is the second injection vector. It enters after input screening has passed the request, so it needs its own screen, run before the passage is appended to the context, using the same classifier as the input.
D: Authorization gates actions with side effects. Appending text to a summary is content, not a tool call, so no authorization check is in the way.

verdict.note: The regulator asks about consistency across a quarter and wants one decision reconstructed. That needs a durable, queryable per-decision record of inputs, outputs and path, retained for the whole look-back period; 30-day logs and 7-day traces cannot answer it (CS-D5-11). Plain-language explanations serve the applicant, a runtime bias judge is prevention rather than evidence, and vendor evals do not cover the lender's own pipeline.

stem:
A regulator writes to a lender using a Claude-based decision-support system. The letter asks whether applicants with similar profiles received consistent recommendations over the past quarter, and asks for one named decision to be reconstructed. The lender has a health dashboard, a 30-day rolling application log with prompts and responses, and a per-request trace in the observability stack retained for seven days.

What is missing for this audience?

options.text: A plain-language explanation of each decision for the applicant
A lasting, queryable record of what went in, what came out and which path each case took, spanning the period asked about
A judge model scoring each recommendation for bias before it is returned
The model provider's published bias evaluations, attached to the reply

explain:
The regulator needs the durable, queryable record. Each audience asks a different question of the same log. The affected person needs inputs and a reason they can act on. The build team needs the full trace. The regulator needs evidence that comparable cases were treated consistently and that one decision can be rebuilt on demand, which means a record that is queryable per decision and retained for as long as the question can reach back. Seven days of traces and thirty days of prompts do not cover a quarter.

Per-option notes:
A: A plain-language explanation is what the affected applicant needs. The regulator is asking about consistency across cases and reconstruction on demand.
B: A regulator's question needs a durable, queryable record of inputs, outputs and the decision path, retained for the period the question spans. Thirty days of prompts and seven days of traces cannot answer a question about a quarter.
C: A model-based fairness judge on each output is a runtime control. It does not produce the record that lets comparable cases be compared afterwards.
D: The provider's evaluations cover the model stage. They say nothing about the lender's corpus, framing, examples or routing, and they do not reconstruct a specific decision.

verdict.note: Confidence says how likely an error is, not what it costs. An irreversible reroute with a six-figure downside goes to pre-action approval whatever the score (CS-D5-06, CS-D5-08). Calibration is a precondition for using a score at all, and after-the-fact sampling cannot guard a single irreversible action.

stem:
A logistics firm's dispatch agent proposes rerouting shipments. Its confidence score on a proposed reroute of a refrigerated pharmaceutical consignment is comfortably inside the firm's tolerance. The reroute cannot be undone once the truck leaves, and a spoiled consignment costs six figures. The team argues the case can skip review because the score is fine.

What decides whether this reroute goes to a person first?

options.text: The confidence score, which is within tolerance, so it goes through
Whether the confidence score has been calibrated
Reversibility and the cost of a wrong answer, which route it to pre-action approval
A sampled review policy, so some reroutes are checked afterwards

explain:
Cost and reversibility decide; confidence only sets the volume. The score being within tolerance is the distractor. It says how likely the output is to be wrong, not what a wrong output costs. A reroute that cannot be undone and costs six figures if wrong is high stakes on both counts, so it goes to pre-action approval with the inputs, the proposed route and the flag reason on the reviewer's screen.

Per-option notes:
A: Confidence filters the volume you route. It does not change what a wrong reroute costs or whether it can be undone.
B: Calibration matters, but it is a precondition for trusting the score at all. Even a perfectly calibrated score would not lower the stakes of this decision.
C: Reversibility and the cost of a wrong answer set the stakes. A confident decision still routes to a person when it is irreversible or costly enough, and this one is both.
D: Sampled review monitors the system over time. It does not guard an individual irreversible action, which is what this consignment needs.

verdict.note: HIPAA is an agreement-based obligation. The control is a HIPAA-ready plan or a HIPAA-enabled API organisation under a signed BAA. The evidence a reviewer can inspect is the signed BAA plus the enabled configuration and the eligible-feature list (PF-GOV-03, CS-D5-09). Prompt instructions are intent, not evidence, and a filter on health terms answers a different obligation.

stem:
The insurer's US health line will route claims containing protected health information through the same assistant. The register row says that HIPAA requires the protected health data to be processed under a formal agreement. Three proposals arrive for how to evidence it.

Which proposal would a security and legal reviewer accept, and for the right reason?

options.text: A HIPAA-ready plan, or the first-party API, covered by a signed BAA, with the signed agreement and the enabled setting as the evidence
The same HIPAA-ready plan and signed BAA, justified by the fact that the assistant's prompt tells it to handle health data carefully
A model-based filter that flags health terms in the text, on the grounds that it catches sensitive data as it flows

explain:
Control plus inspectable artifact. Two things have to land at once: the control must fit the obligation, and the reason must name what the reviewer can inspect. A HIPAA-ready plan or first-party API configuration under a signed Business Associate Agreement is the control; the signed BAA, the admin setting showing HIPAA compliance enabled and the eligible-feature list are the artifact. Instructions to the model are intent, not evidence, and a content filter answers a different obligation.

Per-option notes:
A: The control fits the obligation, and the reason names what the reviewer can inspect: the signed BAA together with the enabled configuration and the eligible-feature list.
B: Right control, weak rationale. What the model is instructed to do is not an artifact anyone can inspect. Name the signed BAA and the enabled setting, not the intent behind the control.
C: A runtime filter on health terms does not evidence an agreement-based obligation. It is the wrong control for this row, and a classifier's behaviour is not the kind of proof a reviewer accepts for it.

verdict.note: Items 1-3 each trace to something the operations lead said; item 2 turns 'drivers will not wait' into a p95 target that still needs confirming. Item 4 traces to nothing and quietly makes a privacy-sensitive retention decision, so it is the undocumented assumption: confirm it with an owner or record it as an assumption. The explanation's claim that item 2 is 'labelled as a target' is not in the stem, but D is still clearly the best answer.

stem:
A logistics company wants an assistant that helps dispatchers plan next-day loads. In the discovery call the operations lead said three things: dispatchers make the final call on anything hazardous, drivers will not wait on it, and it should pull the manifest itself rather than ask for it. The architect's requirements document lists: (1) hazardous loads route to a dispatcher for the decision; (2) p95 under 1.5 seconds on the driver-facing step; (3) the manifest is fetched from the transport system by tool call; (4) driver location history is retained for twelve months for route analytics.

Which item is an undocumented assumption?

options.text: Item 1, hazardous loads to a dispatcher
Item 2, the 1.5 second p95
Item 3, the manifest by tool call
Item 4, twelve months of location history

explain:
Item 4. Three items each trace to a sentence the stakeholder said. The fourth traces to nothing, and an assumption with no source is the dangerous kind, because nobody remembers deciding it. The move that catches it: ask the retention question in the must-prove bucket and record the answer, or write item 4 as an assumption with a named owner to confirm it.

Per-option notes:
A: Traces directly to the first statement. It is a must-not-do constraint, translated: the hazardous case routes to a human.
B: Traces to drivers will not wait on it. The number is the architect's translation of an experience word into a must-cost constraint, and it is labelled as a target that needs confirming.
C: Traces to pull the manifest itself. An integration requirement, bucket 1, with the owner of the manifest data outside the model.
D: No statement supports it. Nobody mentioned retention, and retention of location data is a must-prove constraint with privacy implications. It entered the document as a fact when it was the architect's assumption.

verdict.note: Only the goal and the volume are known. What the system must never do and what it must be able to prove are still open, and stakeholders rarely volunteer those answers. Hold the sketch and ask those questions first (CS-D6-01, T-SKIPDISC); model tier and a compliance referral come later.

stem:
Fifteen minutes into discovery with a credit union, you have heard the goal (members get faster answers on loan status) and the volume (about nine thousand queries a month). You can already see the shape: an augmented call over the loan system's API. The member-services director is warming up and asks what it would look like.

What do you do?

options.text: Sketch it. Showing progress builds trust and you can refine later
Say it is too early to draw, and ask what the system must never do and what it must be able to prove
Pause the call and refer the question to the credit union's compliance team
Ask which model tier they had in mind so you can size the design

explain:
Finish the buckets first. Two of four are open, and the two that are open are the ones stakeholders never volunteer. The sketch will be better for the wait, and the director's trust survives a fifteen-minute delay far better than a compliance surprise in week three.

Per-option notes:
A: A confident sketch this early is exactly the failure in the Watch Out. The director will take it as evidence that the questions have been answered, and the questions stop.
B: You have bucket 1 and part of bucket 3. You have not asked what it must never do, what evidence it must produce, or what a wrong answer to a member costs. Those questions come before any shape.
C: Compliance will need to confirm the proof obligations, but that is a later step. The call is where you find out which obligations exist to confirm.
D: Model tier is a Module 1 decision, gated by evals, and it depends on constraints you have not yet found.

verdict.note: The record-keeping duty is a regulatory gate. B drops the per-interaction record and C drops both the record and the quality gate, so both are out before latency or build cost gets weighed (L1). A is the portal's auditable-workflow pattern: code-defined steps, a validation gate and logged outputs.

stem:
A retail bank wants Claude to draft responses to written customer complaints. Conduct regulation applies, with a record-keeping duty. Volumes are large and predictable. The sponsor wants quality, and a record of every automated step that would stand up to a regulator. Three options are on the table. Option A: a workflow with per-interaction logging and a quality gate before anything is sent. Gains: full record, checked output. Gives up: a small latency cost from logging. Reversal: minor, logging can be tuned without a redesign. Option B: the same workflow, minus the logging step, to cut latency. Gains: quicker replies. Gives up: the per-interaction record. Option C: one augmented call with neither logging nor a human gate, picked because it is cheapest to build.

Which option do you recommend?

options.text: Option A, logging built in, quality gate before sending
Option B, faster by dropping the logging step
Option C, one call, no logging, no gate, cheapest to build

explain:
Option A. Start from the obligation: which option keeps a defensible record and which quietly drops it? A is the only one that fits the constraints as stated, and it is also the only presentation that names what a reversal would cost.

Per-option notes:
A: Fits every stated constraint: the record-keeping obligation, the quality demand, and the sponsor's need for a defensible record. Its presentation also carries all three elements.
B: Trades away the exact thing the obligation requires. Faster responses do not help a sponsor who cannot produce a record when the regulator asks.
C: Inappropriate for the constraints on two counts: no record and no gate in a regulated, high-volume workflow. Lowest build cost is the wrong criterion here.

verdict.note: Option A's write-up sets the pattern: gains, gives up, reversal. B states a gain (quicker replies) and a give-up (the record), but never says what it would cost to restore logging after the system has been tuned for speed. Compliance posture would be worth adding, but it is not one of the three required elements, and this item relies on the course's three-element frame.

stem:
Same bank, same three options. Option B is technically accurate and would run. Its presentation, as written above, has a hole in it.

Option B's presentation leaves out one element. Which?

options.text: What it gains
What it gives up
The reversal cost: the price of putting logging back once the design has been tuned for the latency it bought
The compliance posture this option creates

explain:
The reversal cost. Option B says what it gains and what it gives up, and stops. Restoring logging after the interaction layer has been built for speed is a redesign, and any gap period is an exposure that has to be disclosed and remediated. That is the sentence a stakeholder needs before their yes counts.

Per-option notes:
A: Faster responses is a clear statement of gain. It could be quantified, but the element is present.
B: Per-interaction record is named as the give-up. It could be spelled out more, but the element is there.
C: Nothing says what it costs to put logging back once the system has been tuned around the latency gain. In a record-keeping workflow that is the element a reviewer asks about first.
D: Compliance posture is the fourth question and worth adding, but the module's frame treats the three elements as mandatory and this presentation is missing one of the three.

verdict.note: The head of IT is asking why this design and not the other one, so answer with the trade-off. Retrieval gains simplicity and reuses the index. It gives up currency on coverage, which is live state from the system of record. Reversing a wrong coverage decision is costly. Citing an earlier verdict (D) decides for the stakeholder instead of framing the choice. Policy wording can still be retrieved while coverage status is fetched live (CS-D3-12).

stem:
In the insurer's technical review, the head of IT asks: why does the assistant call the policy system live for coverage instead of just searching a copy of the policy documents? Retrieval would be simpler and we already run a search index.

What kind of objection is this, and what does the answer need to contain?

options.text: Capability. Show that retrieval over policy documents works
Governance. Produce the control register entry for coverage lookups
Design choice. Give the gain, the give-up and the reversal cost of retrieval against live lookup
Design choice. Explain that Module 1 settled it: live state is a tool call

explain:
A design-choice objection, answered with the tradeoff. Retrieval gains a simpler build and a reused asset. It gives up currency: coverage changes and a snapshot cannot tell you when it went stale. Reversing it after a wrong coverage decision has reached a policyholder costs a redesign and an incident. Said that way, the head of IT is making a business choice, not losing an argument.

Per-option notes:
A: Nobody is asking whether Claude can do it. Both approaches work mechanically; the question is which one you chose.
B: There is a compliance angle to live coverage data, but the objection as asked is about a choice between two designs, not about whether the deployment can be evidenced.
C: It asks why this and not that. The answer is the tradeoff: retrieval gains simplicity and a reused index, gives up currency (coverage tables change and the index cannot know when), and reversing it after a wrong coverage decision in production costs a redesign plus an incident.
D: Deferring to Module 1's verdict is a justification, not a tradeoff. The head of IT needs the frame, not the citation.

verdict.note: Latency traces to the discovery requirement and quality traces to the eval acceptance gate, which is the portal's 'accuracy floor on an agreed eval set'. The 99.9% availability figure is borrowed from other vendors, not derived from what an outage costs the claims desk. A real SLA would also state p95 at peak with an error budget and a remedy, but no option raises that, so B is the only correct diagnosis.

stem:
The insurer's operations lead drafts three SLA lines for the claims assistant. Latency: p95 under two seconds, taken from the instant requirement adjusters gave in discovery. Availability: 99.9 percent, because that is what their other vendors quote. Quality: eval score at or above 0.85, the acceptance threshold the release was gated on.

Which line will not survive the first breach argument, and why?

options.text: Latency. Two seconds is too generous for something meant to feel instant
Availability. It is borrowed from other contracts, not derived from how critical the assistant is
Quality. An eval score is an internal metric and should not appear in an SLA
All three. SLA thresholds should come from the vendor's benchmarks

explain:
Availability. Latency traces to discovery and quality traces to the eval gate, so both are defensible. The 99.9 traces to what other vendors say, which is not a source. Ask what a morning without the assistant costs the desk, and derive the number from that.

Per-option notes:
A: It traces to the user-experience expectation from discovery, which is exactly the source the module names for latency.
B: It traces to nothing about this deployment. Availability should reflect how critical the assistant is to the claims desk; a number borrowed from other vendors is a target someone picked because it sounded reasonable.
C: It traces to the eval acceptance criteria, which is the source the module names for quality.
D: Two of the three lines trace cleanly. Only one lacks a source.

verdict.note: Production runs at about 23 times pilot volume, so set cost expectations before the first invoice. That means a forecast at production volume, the spend controls in place (caching, tier routing, budget alerts) and an explanation of how tiering changes unit cost. A pushes the conversation to after the invoice. B is a single number with nothing behind it. D is a detective signal that fires only after the money is spent.

stem:
The claims assistant's pilot ran at four hundred claims a week and cost the insurer a few hundred pounds a month in model usage. Production will run at roughly forty thousand claims a month. The CTO has asked for a launch readiness note.

What belongs in that note about cost?

options.text: A promise to review cost after the first month of production data
The pilot's monthly cost, scaled linearly to production volume
A consumption forecast at production volume, the spend controls in place, and the tiering story, before the first invoice
A budget alert set at the pilot cost times ten

explain:
Forecast, controls, narrative, in advance. Production traffic is one to two orders of magnitude above the pilot's, and a trivial pilot bill becomes a five-figure line. The stakeholder who has seen the forecast and knows what caching, tiering and budget alerts are doing reads the first invoice as expected. The one who has not writes the Section 3 note.

Per-option notes:
A: It defers the conversation to the invoice, which is when the module says the cost expectation breaks. The Section 3 CTO wrote their note after exactly this.
B: Scaling the pilot bill is a start, but a single number without the controls and the tiering story invites the same surprise when the number moves.
C: Forecast at production volume, the spend controls (caching, model tiering, budget alerts), and the tiering story, all delivered ahead of the first invoice. That is the module's pre-emption in full.
D: A budget alert is one of the controls, but an alert on its own is a signal without a decision. It tells you the line was crossed after the spend is committed.

verdict.note: An auditor needs evidence that the control is operating: a redaction log extract, the configuration or a sample query, and a note that it is current. Without that the row is only an assertion (CS-D5-11 pairs a control with an evidence record and an owner). An accountable team can own a control, and rejected alternatives belong in the decision log for successors, not the auditor.

stem:
The claims assistant's control register has a row for the insurer's data-handling obligation. It reads: Control: policyholder PII is redacted before any text enters the context window. Owner: platform team. The insurer's compliance reviewer reads the row and marks it as not audit-ready.

Why?

options.text: The owner should be a named individual, not a team
The control is described too briefly to be evaluated
There is no evidence artefact, so the row is an assertion the reviewer cannot accept
The rejected alternative redaction approaches are not listed

explain:
No evidence artefact. The reviewer does not accept that a control exists because a document says so. Attach the artefact (a redaction log extract, the configuration, a returned query) and mark the audit-ready status, and the row becomes proof rather than a claim.

Per-option notes:
A: The owner is named. A team is an acceptable owner if it is accountable; the row's problem is elsewhere.
B: The row does describe the control. Describing it is the assertion; the reviewer wants what comes after the assertion.
C: A control asserted in a document with no artefact is a claim. The reviewer needs the redaction log, the configuration, or a returned query showing redaction happening, and a note that the evidence is current.
D: Rejected alternatives serve the successor, not the auditor. The reviewer's question is whether the control is operating, not which other controls were considered.

verdict.note: Only a decision record can stop the successor, because it names the rejected alternative (retrieval over a nightly export) and the trade-off it settled (one network hop against current coverage data). It shows the hop is load-bearing. Diagrams, runbooks and test results record what the system does, not why the alternative was rejected (CS-D6-10 ADR).

stem:
Eight months after you leave the insurer, the claims assistant's new architect is chasing latency. They propose replacing the live coverage lookup against the policy system with retrieval over a nightly export of the policy tables. It would cut a network hop from every claim.

Which artefact, had it been written properly, stops them before the change ships?

options.text: The architecture diagram, kept current
The deployment runbook
The decision-log row with the rejected alternative and the tradeoff it resolved
The test-result summary from the release

explain:
The decision-log row. Module 1 rejected retrieval for coverage because it is live state. That reasoning is worth nothing to a successor unless it is written as a decision, a rejected alternative and the tradeoff between them. With the row, the new architect looks for latency somewhere else. Without it, the assistant starts quoting yesterday's coverage.

Per-option notes:
A: A current diagram shows the live lookup exists. It does not say why, and a successor chasing latency reads a hop they can remove.
B: The runbook says how to operate the lookup. It is evidence of what is done, not a statement of why the alternative was rejected.
C: The row would read: decision, coverage fetched live from the policy system; rejected alternative, retrieval over an export; tradeoff, a network hop against currency, because coverage tables change and an export cannot know when it went stale; a wrong coverage decision to a policyholder is the reversal cost. Reading that, the successor knows the hop is load-bearing.
D: Test results show the current design passed. They do not say what a different design would fail.

verdict.note: The deciding detail is the strict regulatory obligation. Under the portal's gate logic (L1), a board expanding a regulated deployment first needs an auditable control and a named owner of ongoing measurement, or any before/after figure is an unverified claim. Without the obligation, A would be the expansion case (as CS-D6-05 would lead with impact). Reuse potential is partner material, not board material.

stem:
The insurer's sponsor is preparing the claims assistant's outcome document for a board decision on rolling it out to two more business lines. The deployment carries a strict regulatory obligation. The sponsor has the use case written up and has time to fill two more fields properly before the meeting.

Which two fields do they fill?

options.text: Metric before and metric after
Control in place and measurement owner
Metric after and reuse potential
Scope boundary and reuse potential

explain:
Control and owner. The obligation level decides it. With no obligation, before and after tells the expansion story on its own. Under a strict obligation the comparison has to be auditable and someone has to own the measurement after the engagement, or the board is being asked to expand on an assertion.

Per-option notes:
A: Before and after is the expansion story for an unregulated deployment. Under a strict obligation the reviewer asks for the control and the owner first, and without them the after number is an assertion.
B: A strict-obligation deployment's outcome document is worth nothing to a reviewer without an auditable control and a named owner of ongoing measurement. These make the before-and-after defensible when it is added.
C: Reuse potential is partner-track material for transferring the pattern. It does not help a board deciding whether this deployment is worth expanding.
D: The scope boundary is already part of the use case field the sponsor has written. Reuse potential is the partner asset, not the board case.

verdict.note: Server-managed settings deliver settings JSON (permissions, hooks, env, a managed CLAUDE.md) at startup and on an hourly poll. No settings key carries SKILL.md content (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/server-managed-settings), so Skills need a Skills channel. Managed settings can register a marketplace and enable a plugin, but the stem rules plugins out. The course's 'four mechanisms' also leaves out Claude Code's managed skills directory, deployed by MDM.

stem:
The insurer's platform lead proposes a shortcut: push the triage team's Skills to every developer through server-managed Claude Code settings, since those arrive from Anthropic's servers on authentication and refresh hourly. No plugin, no upload, no repository.

What is wrong with the plan?

options.text: Nothing, except that hourly is too slow for a Skill fix
Managed settings deliver settings, not Skills. Distribution is one of the four mechanisms or it is not distribution
Managed settings cannot reach Claude Code installs
It works, as long as the spend caps are set first

explain:
Managed settings are a settings channel. They configure the tool for everyone who authenticates, on an hourly polling cycle. A Skill reaches a team by one of four routes: org-provisioned, plugin, project Skill, or API Skill. An exam item that offers managed settings as a fifth route is testing exactly this line.

Per-option notes:
A: Hourly refresh is fine for what managed settings actually carry. Speed is not the problem; the channel is.
B: Managed settings configure Claude Code. They are a settings mechanism, and the module is explicit that they are not one of the four Skills distribution paths.
C: Managed settings do reach Claude Code; that is their whole purpose. The objection is what they carry, not where they land.
D: Spend is a separate setup decision. It does not turn a settings channel into a Skills channel.

verdict.note: Giving access without enabling workflows stalls use at basic chat. The fix is to build tool use, repository-aware help and the packaged Skills into the editor, review and test loop, with a champion demonstrating them on real work. Logins and usage are input measures, not evidence of adoption (CS-D7-04), and a stronger tier does nothing for an enablement gap.

stem:
Six weeks after the champion rollout, the insurer's triage team mostly uses Claude Code as a place to ask questions about the codebase. Nobody runs the eval command through it, the policy-system MCP server is configured but rarely called, and the team's Skills for prompt-file conventions are installed and unused. Adoption numbers look fine.

What has gone wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: The model is too weak for the work; move the team to a higher tier
The team has stalled at basic chat. Enable tool use, repository-aware assistance and the packaged Skills inside the editor and test loop, and have the champion demonstrate them on real work
Set weekly usage targets so the higher-value features get exercised
Nothing; adoption numbers are fine, so the rollout worked

explain:
Stalled at basic chat. Every higher rung exists and none is being climbed, because giving access is not the same as enabling a workflow. The fix is integration: put tool use, repository awareness and the Skills into the editor, the review and the test loop, and let the champion show them working on a real change.

Per-option notes:
A: The tier is not the problem. A more capable model in a question box is still a question box.
B: This is the module's second failure mode. Access without enablement stops at the first rung; the fix is to configure and demonstrate the higher rungs inside the team's existing workflow.
C: Targets produce usage, not adoption. The module rejects mandated usage in the quiz for exactly this reason.
D: Adoption numbers were the misleading signal. Counting logins measures access, which the module says is not adoption.

verdict.note: Fixing the incident yourself is firefighting. Support is finished when the team can handle the next one alone: a runbook entry for intermittent tool failures (check auth, rate limits, error and retry paths) and a written escalation boundary (compare the CS-D6-11 handoff pack). Moving coverage into the prompt would pull live state out of the system of record.

stem:
You take the on-call engineer's message about the coverage lookup failing one call in twenty. In ten minutes you find it: the policy system's rate limit resets hourly and the assistant's retry logic hammers it just after the reset. You widen the backoff and the failures stop. The engineer thanks you.

By the module's standard, what is still missing?

options.text: Nothing. The fault is fixed and the team saw how
A runbook entry for intermittent tool failures pointing at auth, limits and error paths, plus a written note of when this class of issue leaves the team
A quarterly review of the dashboards so the pattern is caught next time
Moving the coverage decision into the prompt so the tool is called less often

explain:
The entry and the boundary. The fix was correct and the team watched, but watching is not a path they can walk. Write the runbook line for intermittent tool failures, name what the first line may change on its own and when the issue escalates, and the next rate-limit incident never reaches you.

Per-option notes:
A: The incident is resolved, but resolving it yourself is the module's definition of firefighting. The next occurrence will land on you again.
B: This is the second half of the support role. The runbook entry and the named escalation boundary are what make the next occurrence the team's to resolve, not yours.
C: A review cadence is what catches problems nobody connected to a cause. It is the failure mode of the Watch out, not the remedy.
D: Coverage lookup is live state owned by the policy system, as Module 1 decided. The rate limit is a tool problem, and moving the decision into a prompt would trade a fixable fault for an unfixable one.

verdict.note: Switching every department on at once produced lumpy adoption. The remedy is a champion in each department who proves one real workflow, ideally measured against a baseline (CS-D7-04), and then adoption seeded in batches. Usage targets count logins, not outcomes. Waiting makes the gap permanent, and the top tier fixes neither enablement nor spend.

stem:
The insurer switched Claude Code on for all four departments that touch the claims triage assistant at once: claims operations, underwriting, customer service and IT. Two months later, IT uses it constantly, claims operations barely opens it, and the other two are somewhere in between. Nobody in claims operations can name a workflow it has improved.

What is the best next move?

options.text: Set daily usage targets for every department
Enable a champion in each department, have them prove one real workflow, then seed adoption in batches
Wait until each department asks for help
Give every department the most capable model to encourage use

explain:
Champions, then batches. Uneven adoption after a simultaneous switch-on is the module's lumpy-adoption failure, and the remedy is the rollout pattern from section 2. The strongest-model option fails twice: it does not address adoption, and it ignores the spend posture team setup exists to bound.

Per-option notes:
A: Targets produce logins, not adoption. Usage under a mandate stalls at basic chat because nothing was enabled past it.
B: The champion-and-batch pattern: one person per department gets access first, proves a real workflow, then seeds adoption batch by batch. It turns access into adoption and gives each department a local expert.
C: Waiting is how lumpy adoption becomes permanent. The departments that would ask are the ones already using it.
D: Capability is not the constraint, and handing out the top tier also breaks the spend posture that setup should have bounded.

verdict.note: The Help Center says users can switch off an org-provisioned Skill individually and that group targeting means bundling it into a plugin. Plugins can be set to Required and updated through GitHub-synced version bumps (https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13837433-manage-plugins-for-your-organization). That is why only B guarantees one procedure that compliance controls centrally. Redaction must happen before data enters the prompt, so its deterministic part belongs in code (for example a plugin hook), not in Skill text alone.

stem:
Compliance signs off a procedure for redacting policyholder details before any claim excerpt enters a prompt. Every department must run it the same way, and compliance must be able to update it, or withdraw it, from one place if the regulator changes the rule.

How should it reach the insurer's teams?

options.text: Pasted into each team's shared chat as a standing prompt
Bundled into an organisation-managed plugin assigned to all departments, with org or group targeting, version-controlled updates and rollback
A Claude Code project Skill in the triage team's repository
An org-provisioned Skill uploaded under Organization settings > Skills

explain:
The plugin. Reach alone would allow the org-provisioned Skill; the second factor, central revocation and rollback, rules it out. The plugin is the only mechanism that carries group or org targeting and version-controlled updates with a way back, which is exactly what a regulator-driven procedure needs.

Per-option notes:
A: A pasted prompt has no version, no central owner and no way to withdraw it. Each team's copy drifts from the moment it is pasted.
B: Two factors govern: identical everywhere, and revocable and reversible from one place. Only the plugin offers org and group targeting together with version-controlled updates and rollback.
C: A project Skill is scoped to the repositories that carry it. The other departments never see it, and compliance cannot reach it centrally.
D: An org-provisioned Skill reaches everyone at once, which satisfies the first factor, but it has no version pinning and no native rollback. Withdrawing a bad update means a manual re-upload while the bad version is live.

verdict.note: Review and tests both existed, but nothing required anyone to verify security on generated code. A gate with a security dimension (inputs validated, no secrets, least privilege) on every generated change fixes the root cause. The key's explanation overstates B, though: SAST taint rules routinely flag path traversal (CWE-22), so a scanner is a strong complement, just not a replacement for the verification gate.

stem:
Since adopting AI-assisted coding, the insurer's triage team ships changes to the assistant twice as fast. Then a generated change to the claim-ingest path goes live: it trusts the filename on an uploaded attachment and writes it outside the intended folder. Review passed it. Tests passed it.

What was most likely missing?

options.text: A code-review SLA that exempted small generated changes from security review
A linter that flags known vulnerability patterns ahead of merge
A verification checklist, with a security dimension, that gates every generated change on its way to production
More frequent model updates so the model knows recent security patterns

explain:
The checklist, with its security dimension. Inputs validated, no secrets, least-privilege access: those are the security checks the module's model answer names, and a gate that omits them passes code a reviewer would have caught. The other three options fix scheduling, tooling or the model. None of them makes a person responsible for what shipped.

Per-option notes:
A: A review SLA is a scheduling policy. The gap here is not when review happens but what it is required to establish; the root cause is missing verification discipline.
B: A linter catches known patterns. It does not require anyone to understand or vouch for what shipped, and an unvalidated filename is a reasoning failure, not a pattern match.
C: Diligence turns trust-by-default into a repeatable gate. A checklist with a security dimension asks about validated inputs and least privilege on every change; this team had no such gate, so speed decided what counted as checked.
D: Model currency does not substitute for reviewer discipline. Nobody was required to understand and vouch for the generated code, and a newer model does not change that.

verdict.note: Green tests cover only the inputs someone thought of. If the author cannot explain why a range-written amount routes to the senior queue, the change is not verified, so hold it until they can (and add the range case to the tests). Rewriting it by hand or sending every merge to the architect puts the check in the wrong place; it belongs to the author and reviewer.

stem:
In review, a developer on the triage team is asked why their generated change routes a claim whose amount is written as a range, four to six thousand pounds, to the senior adjuster queue. They cannot say. The change passes every test, including the golden claim set.

What should happen?

options.text: Merge it. The eval score holds and the tests are green
Hold it until the author can account for the behaviour and say why it is right
Delete the tests and rewrite the change by hand
Escalate every merge on the assistant to the architect

explain:
Hold it. The human-understanding dimension is the one check no tool can run for you. A developer who cannot account for a routing decision on a range-written amount has not verified the change, whatever the test runner says. The merge nobody could explain in section 3 is what happens when this question is skipped.

Per-option notes:
A: Green tests are not understanding. The tests cover the inputs someone thought of; the range case was not one of them until the reviewer asked.
B: This is the human-understanding check: the author can explain what the code does and why, including for inputs it was not explicitly tested against. It is the gate that stops judgement erosion reaching production.
C: Throwing away the work is not the point. The checklist asks for understanding, not for hand-written code, and the tests are useful evidence either way.
D: Escalating every merge makes the architect the gate, which is the opposite of the self-sufficiency this module is building. The check belongs to the author and the reviewer.

verdict.note: Quality drifted with nothing deployed while underwriting was revising the retrieved corpus. Start from the layer that changed: check the model, the prompt and above all the corpus and its index, comparing failing and passing traces (CS-D4-09, CS-D4-14). A bigger tier, turning off caching (an exact-prefix cache cannot serve changed content anyway) and a rollback all act on parts that did not change.

stem:
The insurer's operations lead reports that adjuster emails from the assistant have got steadily less specific over the last two months. Dashboards have been green throughout. Nobody has deployed a code change in that time. Underwriting mentions in passing that it has been revising the policy-wording library.

Where does the architect look first?

options.text: Raise the model tier and let a stronger model cover the gap
Whether the model, the prompt or the retrieval corpus changed: connect the symptom to an architecture cause
Disable prompt caching so every call pulls fresh content
Revert the most recent deployment and run the integration suite again

explain:
Model, prompt or corpus, and here almost certainly the corpus. Underwriting has been rewriting the very documents the assistant retrieves clause wording from, and the index has not kept pace. The eval set shows the drift; the change history shows the cause. Tier, cache and rollback each act on a part of the system that did not change.

Per-option notes:
A: A more capable model does not repair a retrieval index that has fallen behind its corpus. The model is not the cause, so changing it treats the symptom and raises the bill.
B: Quality drifting with nothing deployed points at the model, the prompt, or a corpus that outgrew its index. Compare against the eval set, then find what changed. This is the symptom-to-cause reasoning the runbook should hold.
C: A cache hit needs identical prompt segments, so exact-match caching cannot serve changed content. Disabling it adds cost and latency and does nothing about a drifted index.
D: The scenario says there was no code change. A rollback has nothing to act on; the cause is outside the codebase.

verdict.note: The binding constraint is a fixed five-section output plus an auditable processing trail. That means the path is known in advance, so a code-defined workflow with logged per-section inputs and outputs is the right pattern. A single augmented call (C) comes second: it is simpler, but it leaves one opaque step with no per-section gate or trail. The agent (A) and multi-agent (D) options add autonomy that nothing in the stem varies enough to justify.

stem: A legal team needs contracts summarized into a fixed five-section brief, every time, with an auditable processing trail for compliance sign-off. Which pattern?

options.text: Agentic loop with document tools, for flexibility across contract types
A fixed workflow of model calls, one per section, with logged inputs and outputs
A single augmented call with the contract in context
Multi-agent decomposition with a contract-type router

explain: Fixed output structure plus auditability is the workflow tell. A and D add autonomy and complexity the requirement forbids rather than needs; C cannot produce the per-step trail compliance wants.

verdict.note: Evals show the failures sit in one measured hard slice (complex multi-policy questions) while the fast tier clears the bar on 85% of traffic. Routing that slice up a tier fixes quality where it fails without paying flagship prices on solved traffic. Few-shot examples (B) fix format, not reasoning depth. Fine-tuning (D) assumes labelled data and a fine-tuning route that the stem never gives.

stem: A support assistant answers 50,000 queries daily. Evals show the fast tier handles 85% of traffic at target accuracy but fails on complex multi-policy questions. The architect's move?

options.text: Upgrade all traffic to the top capability tier
Keep the fast tier and add more few-shot examples for the hard cases
Route: fast tier triages and handles routine traffic, escalating the hard slice to a capable tier
Fine-tune the fast tier on the failing queries

explain: Routing captures the cost of the easy 85% and the quality of the hard 15%. A pays flagship prices for solved traffic; B applies a prompting fix to a capability gap; D proposes heavier machinery where routing solves it directly.

verdict.note: A cache hit needs a byte-identical prefix, so a value that changes on every request near the top invalidates everything after it. The fix is to move the timestamp after the stable content (breakpoint). In the real API the prefix is always built as tools, then system, then messages, so tools placed first can still cache, but the large system and document block is lost, which is why savings are near zero. C is false (tool definitions are cacheable), and lengthening the TTL (D) pulls a lever that does not address the first changing byte.

stem: An agent's prompt begins with the current timestamp, then the system prompt, tool definitions, and reference documents. Prompt caching saves almost nothing. Why?

options.text: The reference documents exceed the cacheable length
The timestamp at the start changes every request, invalidating the cached prefix from position zero
Tool definitions cannot be cached
The cache TTL is shorter than the request interval

explain: A changing token early in the prefix breaks everything after it. The fix is stable-first, variable-last ordering. C is false, and A and D invent facts the scenario does not give.

verdict.note: Several client surfaces (Claude Code, a desktop assistant, a customer-facing agent) need the same live capability, which is the defining case for building one MCP server that every client reuses. Direct integrations (A) triple the build and maintenance. Agent-to-agent (C) is for independently reasoning systems, not a shared function. A prompt template (D) cannot fetch anything.

stem: Three product teams want the same internal knowledge-search capability from Claude Code, a desktop assistant, and a customer-facing agent. Integration mechanism?

options.text: Each team builds a direct API integration for full control
One MCP server exposing the search capability to all three surfaces
Agent-to-agent delegation to a search agent
A shared prompt template with the search logic described

explain: Build once, expose everywhere across multiple client surfaces is MCP's defining case. A triples maintenance, C adds autonomous-system machinery for a shared tool, D is a prompt where a protocol is required.

verdict.note: Traces show the top results are off-topic, which is a precision defect in retrieval. Quadrupling k pushes more noise, cost and latency into the window, so fix the retrieval layer instead: chunking, embeddings or query construction, plus a re-ranker over the candidates. Widening k is right only for a measured recall gap, and a bigger window (C) or a bigger model (D) blames layers that are not failing.

stem: A RAG system's answers are frequently wrong. Traces show the top retrieved chunks are usually off-topic. The team proposes raising retrieval from 5 chunks to 20. Assessment?

options.text: Correct: more chunks raise the odds the right one is included
Wrong: retrieval precision is the problem, so more chunks add more noise; fix chunking, embeddings, or query construction, and consider re-ranking
Correct, but only with a larger context window
Wrong: the model tier should be upgraded first

explain: Context-stuffing is the trap; when precision is low, volume amplifies noise and cost. D misdiagnoses (the failure table points at retrieval, since the wrong documents arrive).

verdict.note: A loan decision is regulated, high-impact and external, so the synchronous human gate belongs on the final decision before it reaches the customer (A). Fairness in that decision has to be shown by per-group outcome testing against agreed thresholds (C, CS-D5-12). A fairness instruction in the prompt (B) is not a control, the top tier (D) fixes no fairness defect, and reviewing every internal draft (E) spreads reviewer attention over low-risk steps and invites rubber-stamping.

stem: An underwriting assistant recommends loan approvals. Which two controls are required rather than optional?

options.text: Human review before any final approval decision reaches a customer
A system prompt instructing the model to be fair and unbiased
Per-slice evaluation of recommendation quality across demographic groups
The top capability tier for all underwriting traffic
Human review of every internal draft the model produces

explain: Irreversible, regulated, high-impact decisions demand HITL placement (A), and fairness in a regulated decision demands stratified evaluation (C). B is a prompt-guarantee, D is flagship-everywhere, E is all-or-nothing HITL applied to a low-risk internal step.

verdict.note: Judge scores rising while human complaints rise is the classic sign of a miscalibrated instrument. Recalibrate the LLM judge against fresh human labels and re-check agreement before trusting any trend. For an extraction system, the crisp fields should also be graded by code checks rather than the judge (CS-D4-04). A silent model upgrade, a small eval set or latency does not explain the divergence between judge and humans.

stem: Two months after launch, an extraction system's judge scores drift upward while customer complaints rise. What most likely broke?

options.text: The model was silently upgraded
The LLM judge's rubric no longer matches human quality standards; recalibrate the judge against sampled human review
The eval dataset is too small
Latency increased

explain: Diverging judge scores and human perception is the calibration failure mixed-methodology testing exists to catch: sample, compare, recalibrate. The others do not explain the divergence pattern.

verdict.note: Success criteria, a constraint inventory and a current-process baseline are all discovery outputs. A system that works but 'isn't what we needed' is what building before discovery finishes produces. Blaming design, monitoring or handoff attributes the failure to a downstream phase, and the stem gives no evidence for any of them.

stem: A pilot's stakeholders are unhappy: the system works but "isn't what we needed." A post-mortem finds no written success criteria, no constraint inventory, and no baseline of the process it replaced. Which phase failed?

options.text: Design, for choosing the wrong pattern
Monitoring, for missing quality regressions
Discovery, whose outputs (success criteria, constraints, baseline) were never produced
Handoff, for missing documentation

explain: All three missing artifacts are discovery outputs. The system "working" while missing the need is precisely what skipped discovery produces.

verdict.note: Preserving why a pattern was chosen over its alternatives is the job of a version-controlled ADR that records context, options, decision, consequences and why each alternative lost. Code comments hold the 'what', recordings are unsearchable fragments, and the system prompt encodes behaviour, not rationale.

stem: Compliance asks how the team will preserve the reasoning behind choosing a workflow pattern over an agentic one, so future maintainers understand the constraint. Answer?

options.text: A comment block in the orchestration code
An architecture decision record capturing context, options, decision, and consequences, version controlled with the project
A recorded meeting where the decision was discussed
The system prompt, which encodes the behavior

explain: This phrasing is the ADR question, nearly verbatim. Comments (A) capture what, rarely why-not-alternatives; C is unsearchable and unversioned; D encodes behavior rather than reasoning.

verdict.note: Team-wide conventions and shared MCP servers belong in committed project configuration: CLAUDE.md for the conventions and `.mcp.json` with `${VAR}` secrets for the servers, so every clone gets the same setup through review. The stem's word 'enforce' is loose, because CLAUDE.md guides rather than enforces. A non-overridable, all-repositories requirement would need managed settings, which are not offered here. User files (A) never propagate, a shared account (C) is the authorization anti-pattern, and a wiki (D) is invisible to the tool.

stem: A platform team wants every engineer's Claude Code to enforce the same review conventions and reach the same internal MCP servers. Where does the configuration live?

options.text: Each engineer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, distributed by onboarding doc
Version-controlled project-level configuration: committed CLAUDE.md and project-scoped MCP config with environment-variable secrets
A shared service account whose settings all engineers inherit
A wiki page documenting the conventions

explain: Team-wide behavior lives in committed project config. A depends on every individual complying forever, C is the shared-account authorization anti-pattern from Domain 3, and D is invisible to the tooling.

verdict.note: 'Every repository on every machine, never' calls for managed settings deny rules. The client enforces them above every lower scope, whatever the model decides. Org-wide coding standards are guidance, so they go in the managed CLAUDE.md. For a true network guarantee, also note that deny rules match tool calls rather than acting as an OS boundary, so pair them with managed sandbox network restrictions and managed MCP allow/deny lists (PF-CC-05, PF-CC-08). Committed project settings (D) reach only the repositories that adopt them.

stem: An enterprise must guarantee that no developer's Claude Code session can ever call external network tools, across every repository on every machine, and separately wants company coding standards applied everywhere. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Both in a managed CLAUDE.md deployed to all machines
Both in managed settings
The network-tool ban in managed settings (permission deny rules, which the client enforces), the coding standards in the managed CLAUDE.md (behavioral guidance)
The ban in each project's committed settings, the standards in each project's CLAUDE.md

explain: Enforcement and guidance live in different layers: settings are enforced by the client regardless of what the model decides, while CLAUDE.md shapes behavior. A puts a hard requirement in a soft layer, B puts prose standards in an enforcement mechanism that cannot express them, and D covers only repositories that adopt it, missing "every repository on every machine."

verdict.note: An eval set frozen at launch measures past traffic, so a steady 97% on it says nothing about the changed regional formats. Refresh the set from current production and score the new formats as their own slice with its own bar. Model drift (A) is not plausible against a pinned version, the judge (D) is not the component that decayed, and raising the target (C) tunes a number whose measurement is broken.

stem: Six months post-launch, the extraction system's weekly eval still scores 97%, but enterprise customers in one region report rising errors. Investigation shows the eval set was built from launch-week traffic and never refreshed, while regional document formats changed. What failed?

options.text: The model drifted and should be re-pinned
Eval dataset maintenance: the set no longer mirrors production distribution, so its score stopped measuring reality; refresh it and add the new formats as a scored slice
The accuracy target was set too low
The judge rubric needs recalibration

explain: An eval frozen at launch measures the past. The score stayed high because the test stayed easy, which is exactly why eval design requires refreshing as traffic drifts and scoring per slice. A invents model drift against a pinned version, C tunes a number the measurement no longer supports, and D points at the judge when the dataset is what decayed.
